title: Life under Lockdown
text:
Praise

“When the Covid-19 pandemic first hit, university students around the world were among those most immediately affected, their routines upended as schools and dorms shut down and classes moved online. In lieu of their regular assignments, economics professor Johan Fourie asked his students to maintain a lockdown journal chronicling their experience of daily life made newly strange. In the 335 entries he has selected here, the students grapple with the many ways Covid altered their lives, from the mundane to the existential, their voices combining to give the reader a perspective at once intimate and panoramic.”
Ruth Franklin, literary critic and author of Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life


“In one or two decades from now historians will be grateful to everyone who kept a personal diary under the pandemic. A relatively old-fashioned habit for a world moving at the speed of social media comes alive as part of a university course assignment. A great pedagogic experiment by Johan Fourie and Laura Richardson. If you think it might feel contrived, or that to read diary entries from the first lockdown might be boring and repetitive, think again. There is something deeply touching about these students’ reflections on the pandemic. From the very personal, such as the illness of a mother, to the very social, such as the realisation of the unfairness of privilege; from the celebration of the power of art to concerns about unemployment, these diary entries provide an interesting, readable and moving account of one set of experiences of the Covid-19 lockdown.”
Prof Lis Lange, Deputy Vice-Chancellor: Teaching and Learning, University of Cape Town


“This volume collates entries from an unusual diary task set for Stellenbosch University Economics 281 students during the initial month of South Africa’s (very) hard lockdown in 2020. With the sudden, unprecedented disruptions to lives and livelihoods caused by Covid-19, the journaling gave the students an opportunity to reflect, in the pandemic’s enforced pause, on the mundanities and mutations, on the privileges and precarities, of everyday life under the coronavirus. Rich in documenting the varied and changing thoughts, emotions, struggles and material situations of the young respondents’ daily lives during the first lockdown, the anonymised diary entries record valuable microhistories. They offer illuminating experiential insight into the bigger picture of facts and data-oriented coverage of these not yet post-coronial times.”
Prof Sally Ann Murray, Chair of English department, Stellenbosch University

title: Introduction
text:
Introduction
In addition to killing more than four million people globally in 2020, the Covid-19 pandemic shut down social and economic activity as governments across the world announced national lockdowns and travel bans. While mortality and morbidity statistics reflect the tragic death toll of the pandemic and the collapse of gross domestic products reveal its dire economic consequences, far less is known about what ordinary people thought, felt and experienced at the onset of this extraordinary period. This anthology is an attempt to (partially) fill that gap. As we explain below, we collected 335 diary entries of Economics 281 students at Stellenbosch University. These entries expose the fears, hopes and beliefs of young people living in South Africa during the first month of the national lockdown. The aim of this anthology is two-fold: to preserve and to reflect, both for those who experienced Covid-19 and for future generations.

title: Introduction
text:
Writing during the pandemic
On 12 March 2020, a day after the World Health Organisation (WHO) declared Covid-19 a pandemic, American literary critic and biographer, Ruth Franklin, published a tweet urging members of the public to keep a record of their experiences. “A suggestion for coping with Covid-19 anxiety: write down what’s happening. Whether you call it note-taking, keeping a journal, whatever – it’s calming and also serves as a useful record”, she wrote.3 A day later she reminded her followers to take some notes in another tweet: “Write down what’s happening, what you see around you, how you feel about it. Do it a few times a day, because by evening, what you were thinking in the morning may have been overtaken by new events. When this is over, we’ll want a record.”4 Again two days later: “Take a moment and make some notes about what’s happening. Call it your Coronavirus diary, your plague journal, whatever. It’s important. Later, you will want a record.”5
The idea to record people’s lived experiences during the Covid-19 pandemic would later be echoed by academics and journalists across the globe – so much so, in fact, that numerous writing guides and articles promising help to first time writers to “organize their thoughts during these difficult times” have now been published.6 The concept of a coronavirus diary has also prompted a range of fascinating new academic projects to emerge. Michael Ward’s CoronaDiaries project is a good example. The project aims to “record and archive the experiences of people living through the [coronavirus] crisis and after it by collecting written or visual documents, testimonies and accounts, similar to those collected before, during and after the Second World War in the Mass Observations Studies”.7
Historian Herbert Braun has launched a comparable, albeit slightly more targeted, project at the University of Virginia by inviting all of his current and former students to participate in a voluntary record-keeping exercise in which they write about their daily lives during this “unprecedented time”.8 University libraries all over the world are also in the process of collecting videos, personal diaries, artworks, photographs, newsletters, poetry and short reflections which explore the pandemic’s impact on different members of the university community. In recognition of the extraordinary period of history the Covid-19 pandemic represents, the University of Sydney Library is asking staff and students to share their experience of living through a pandemic. “We often miss what happens at ground level and don’t realise the importance of documenting the period we are living through which, with the emergence of social media, is more challenging than ever”, explains Catherine Storey, honorary archivist for the University’s School of Medicine and Royal North Shore Hospital.9
Despite small differences in format, the projects outlined above share similar motivations. Conscious that there is no shortage of factual information regarding the pandemic and its impact on a macro-level, these projects are generally not interested in simply detailing the measures being imposed (or advised) by governments and medical professionals. Rather, they seek to better understand how ordinary people are experiencing and coping with these measures, and how, to quote Michael Ward, “society is being made and remade” within the context of the pandemic.10 What kinds of strategies – both psychological and practical – are being adopted by individuals to manage this novel threat? How do these strategies differ between groups? What effect is social class, gender, ethnicity and sexuality having on people’s experiences of the pandemic? What kind of challenges are people facing both now and going forward? How are people thinking about the future? These are all crucial questions; questions which will influence how coming generations interpret the Covid-19 pandemic and its history.

title: Introduction
section: Lockdown and higher education in South Africa
text:
Lockdown and higher education in South Africa
South Africa reported its first coronavirus case on 5 March 2020, two months after the WHO announced that a novel coronavirus had been identified and was responsible for a cluster of pneumonia cases in Wuhan, China.11 The country had already faced dual HIV and tuberculosis (TB) epidemics, and with risk factors for infectious disease vulnerability, such as poverty and overcrowding, it could ill-afford an outbreak.12 Nonetheless, infection rates rose rapidly and within a matter of weeks the situation was judged serious enough to warrant extraordinary measures from government. First, a national ‘state of disaster’ was declared and then, on 23 March, in an attempt to control the number of infected persons and to allow time for additional medical facilities to come on-line, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a nationwide lockdown. The lockdown was set to last for 21 days, from 27 March to 16 April, but was later extended by a further two weeks.
During this period citizens were subject to a strict curfew and to shelter-in-place orders which prevented them from leaving their homes unless they were seeking emergency medical care, buying food, medicine and other necessities, or collecting social security cheques. Stringent public health measures were enforced, including a ban on tobacco and alcohol sales, prolonged closure of schools and public amenities, social distancing, as well as sanitation and mask wearing.13 Funerals were limited to a maximum of 50 people and all other social gatherings (e.g. weddings, birthday parties, conferences, etc.) were prohibited. Compliance, although difficult to guarantee, was affected through the use of fines and the deployment of police and military personnel, especially within the country’s poor and often densely populated informal settlements (known as townships). The police force also set up more than 190 roadblocks and 680 vehicle checkpoints across the country to monitor travel – a form of regulation which, despite its benign motivation, served as a painful reminder of the apartheid state’s restrictions on the free movement of black people.
The measures outlined did not halt coronavirus transmission; case numbers continued to rise throughout the lockdown period. This, though, was not the primary intention of the lockdown. Instead, the government spoke predominantly in terms of “flattening the curve” and, while not easy to test empirically, the measures adopted seemed to have slowed down the virus’s spread; preventing the country’s already strained healthcare system from being overwhelmed. Yet, the preservation of the country’s healthcare infrastructure notwithstanding, the government’s quarantine mandates precipitated much suffering amongst ordinary South Africans. Economic losses were substantial, food and income security were seriously compromised, and with informal settlements often lacking basic hygiene facilities such as running water and toilets, millions of under-resourced South African households found it almost impossible to heed the government’s Covid-19 regulations.
The lockdown also seriously affected access to basic and higher education. On 15 March 2020, the South African Minister of Higher Education, Blade Nzimande, announced that all universities and colleges would be forced to close from 18 March until 15 April as part of an ‘extended break’ necessitated by the lockdown.14 Basic infrastructure and maintenance activities, as well as on-site research could continue, but all in-person lectures, symposia and conferences had to be suspended; higher education institutions were advised to use the break to explore digital and online delivery methods which may have to be employed at a later stage.15 From 15 April onwards most of South Africa’s major public universities transitioned to online teaching and learning and continue to function in this way almost 18 months later.
Much has been written about this so-called ”online turn” and the impact that it is having on higher education in South Africa. Clearly, the Covid-19 pandemic has changed the face of university education in South Africa and the world, but what effects – both positive and negative – is this having on access to quality education and student and staff experiences within the sector? Educationalist and Senior Deputy Vice-Chancellor at the University of the Witwatersrand, Professor Ruksana Osman, contends that the pandemic “has provided the [South African] academy with a moment to pause, to reflect, and to propose new imaginaries, against a rapidly changing technological landscape”.16 For Osman, the pandemic, university closures and the shift to online learning, although extremely challenging for higher education institutions, have the potential to be facilitate new “knowledge architectures” which, coupled with strong, empathetic visionary leadership, could help to democratise and render academia more prosperous in the long run.17
This contention is supported by David Mhlanga and Tankiso Moloi’s research which suggests that, during lockdown, a variety of Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) tools were implemented in the tertiary education sector, providing this sector with much needed opportunities to assess the successes and failures of different technologies, to analyse the costs associated with them, and to look into scaling these technologies to improve educational access.18 Sfiso Mhlaba’s work, which emphasises the importance of self-directed learning and the role that it can play in advancing education in times of crisis, is also relevant here. Mhlaba’s main argument is that the pandemic has provided universities with a powerful incentive to prepare students to be self-directed in their learning, a skill which he contends would enhance student resilience in a rapidly changing world.
There are, however, serious obstacles to be overcome before these advantages can be properly realised. In South Africa, writes Saleem Badat, the Covid-19 pandemic has “laid bare and exacerbated inequalities” in all arenas of society, including the higher education sector.19 Badat argues that, in the post-1994 period, universities were given a mandate to promote transformation and social justice in and through higher education. Yet, higher education in South Africa still often functions as a “mechanism of unequal forms of social reproduction and exclusion of students from working class and rural impoverished backgrounds”, an uncomfortable reality which the pandemic and its attendant restrictions have served to highlight.20
Cramped and noisy learning environments, regular power outages, unstable data supply, and a shortage of digital resources (including laptops, tablets, etc.), now more than ever before, are likely to hinder the ability of less privileged students to engage with the available learning material, amplifying divisions already embedded in the education system. Limited access to physical facilities including student hostels, dining halls, sports equipment, counselling and healthcare centres, as well as libraries poses further problems, especially for poor students who rely on the support programmes, opportunities for personal development and the subsidisation of living costs which universities often provide. There is little question, for example, that university closures have led to a rise in student hunger with initiatives such as Stop Hunger Now at the University of Johannesburg normally providing up to 7 000 meals a week.21 It is vital that recognition of these inequaties “temper glib celebration of digital online learning”.22
It also needs to be acknowledged that while online learning can facilitate information acquisition and provide the basis for adequate credentialing, it cannot offer the sociability and in-person interaction between staff and peers which have traditionally been at the heart of the academic process; helping to foster the circulation of ideas and to enhance collaboration within and across fields. As Tawana Kupe, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Pretoria, explains: “Education is a social activity that connects people” and it is important that this aspect of learning process not be lost.23
Finally, there is the concern that reduced state funding post-Covid will increase the financial burden placed on South African universities, making it more difficult for them to hire and retain staff, fund research and to participate in activities designed to improve accessibility and contribute to community development.24 In these circumstances, institutional survival (through privatisation and increased fiscal conservativism) will likely be prioritised over more complex discussions regarding the purpose of universities and the part that they can play in transforming society at large.

title: Introduction
text:
The Anthology Project
Thus far, much of the research produced on the Covid-19 pandemic and its impact on South Africa has involved the collection of quantitative and survey data wherein the focus is on macro-trends and general responses to prescribed questions.25 This research initiative is different in that, like the projects described in earlier sections, it is being driven by a desire for unstructured qualitative data. Such information can provide a window into the lives of young people and their subjective experiences of the Covid-19 pandemic. Acquiring such information can however be difficult, particularly at short notice. A research project about the lived experiences of young South Africans would usually require months of preparation; time would have to be spent on funding applications, sample selection, data entry, curation and preservation and, importantly, on securing ethical clearance. Yet, because of the speed with which the virus spread, time was limited.
To capture and preserve the thoughts, feelings and experiences of South Africans during this first phase of the virus, a different approach was necessary. Johan Fourie, then Associate Professor in Economics at Stellenbosch University, was lecturing an Economics 281 elective course about global economic history to 84 second-year students. In mid-March, when it became evident that Covid-19 had spread globally, he requested that his students keep a diary. Instead of writing a short essay on one of the five prescribed topics, they would need to complete one diary entry daily for the duration of hard lockdown. As he explained in his initial email:
This book is a consequence of that project. Although the initial aim of the exercise was not to collate the diary entries into an anthology, when reading through what students had written, Fourie was struck by the insightful and often poignant nature of their comments and realised the value of such comments for future historians. Captured within them were the fears, hopes and beliefs of young people from across South Africa. Of course, the entries and the experiences which they convey are not representative of the experiences of the South African population at large, nor do they necessarily reflect those of the average South African university student, or even the average Stellenbosch University student.26 The following statistics confirm this observation: 51% of the students in the class were male; 70% were classified as white, 20% as black and 10% as coloured; 62% of the class spoke English at home, 26% spoke Afrikaans, 7% spoke one of South Africa’s other official languages – Xhosa, Southern Sotho, Tsonga or Tswana – and 5% spoke another African language – Shona or Swahili. Although most students were 19 years old in March 2020, the youngest individual was 18 and the oldest was 23.
We believe, nonetheless, that this collection of diary entries contributes to our understanding of the virus’s impact on the South African student community. As the entries demonstrate, even within this privileged group, there are diverse experiences of this unprecedented period of national lockdown. Just as we currently appreciate the records of Samuel Pepys,27 as well as the work of diarists relating to the 1918 influenza epidemic, the stories of these students may be of interest to a more general audience. We also hope that these entries will prove useful for future generations of historians and social science practitioners.
Although 84 students were enrolled in the course, only 76 submitted their diary entries as part of their Economics 281 assignment. The diaries were not graded; students were asked to write an additional ‘reflective piece’ that would be graded, but the diaries were a required component of the assignment. On 8 April, about three weeks after the project had commenced, the students were sent an email explaining the details of the ‘reflective piece’.28
While all students did give permission for reading and analysing their diaries at the point of submission, when requested to explicitly give us permission to publish their entries anonymously, only 59 responded. The second request was submitted in June after they had completed their assignments.29 As a consequence, the possibility of publication to a larger audience would not have influenced the way the students wrote.
We selected 335 entries from 59 of the 84 students.30 The original essays are safely preserved and secured in the Cloud.31 The selection process was an arduous undertaking. The entries were all moved from the original submission – some in Microsoft Word, some in Adobe PDF – to a CSV file. Author details were removed to make the entries anonymous. Personal particulars, like names of family and friends, were also removed. We chose not to remove place names as they provide useful context. Each of the entries were then printed to allow for easier sorting and comparison.
Ultimately, the 335 entries cover the period 21 March to 23 April. Eloquence and writing style did not form an important part of the selection criteria. We did alter the grammar at points to make the text more readable and logical, but were careful not to change the author’s meaning. We felt that some grammatical correction was necessary because otherwise readers might privilege the experiences of the eloquent and skip over the less fluent students whose writing was at times difficult to follow. Changes included splitting up long sentences, removing comma splices, capitalising when needed, and correcting typos and spelling mistakes.
We focused on gathering as broad a spectrum of thoughts, feelings and experiences as possible, whilst also deliberately including ideas and stories that touch on one of the following five themes:

mental health and coping mechanisms
student life (changes and similarities, future plans, etc.)
family or other important relationships/connections
inequality and privilege politics
local circumstances

These themes emerged as interesting during the initial reading process and then informed our decisions during the selection process. While we acknowledge that these themes reflect our subjective preferences to some extent, we have chosen to focus on them because we believe that the real value of the entries lies not in their regurgitation of global news, but rather in the fact that they shed light on Covid-19 in South Africa. They also bring to light the ways in which Covid-19 has impacted people’s private as opposed to public lives.

title: Introduction
text:
Text analysis
Upon submission, all students gave permission to use their entries for aggregate trend analysis. The plan was to use simple text analysis tools, like word clouds, to track themes as they emerged. One enterprising student, Steven Norman, created a dedicated website during the course of lockdown where students could enter their diaries (over and above the Word document they had to submit to us) and read the aggregated results of all the submitted entries. Although not all students submitted their entries online, it may still be interesting to look at patterns from a sample that is different from our eventual selection. On April 5, Norman sent Fourie a screenshot – Figure 1 – summarising the entries on the website. The most frequently used words were grouped into themes. ‘Community’ (with words like ‘home’, ‘friend’, ‘people’, ‘uni’ and ‘shop’) and ‘time’ (with words like ‘end’, ‘today’ and ‘now’) and virus statistics seemed to be the main themes.


Figure 1 Norman’s screenshot of topics

Ten word clouds were generated over the course of the project. Figure 2 is the final one. It is based on a frequency analysis of 27 000 words. The words ‘today’/‘day’, ‘home’, ‘virus’, and ‘time’ again feature prominently. Norman’s project ultimately faded as students lost interest.32


Figure 2 The word cloud on Steven Norman’s website

The 335 entries we analysed include more than 46 800 words. Similar to Norman, we began with a word cloud which reveals the most important words used by the students in their diary entries. The size of the word is correlated to how frequently it is used. Figure 3 presents the results. The most popular word across all entries is ‘lockdown’. This makes sense. The national lockdown was indeed the reason why students were at home and why they kept a diary. It is interesting, though, to note the other words that feature prominently. These include ‘time’, ‘people’, ‘day’, and ‘family’. Place, people and time.


Figure 3 A conventional word cloud of our full selection and one with sentiment analysis

We add sentiment analysis too, presented in the second plot of Figure 3. The sentiment of a word is scored with the bing sentiment lexicon, a general-purpose English sentiment lexicon that categorises words in a binary fashion, either positive or negative.33 The first finding is that ‘virus’ features most prominently in the entries that are classified. The word appears 152 times in the entries. A second finding is that students seem to use positive words – including the word ‘positive’ – frequently (if not more so than negative words). Common positive words include ‘support’, ‘privileged’, ‘healthy’, ‘productive’ and ‘excited’. It should be kept in mind that the context in which these words appear also matters. A student writing that he/she was ‘not productive today’ would, of course, use the word ‘productive’ in a negative context. The good news is that there are few examples of such negative use of the word ‘productive’ in the entries, which suggests that this is not a serious concern.34
Next we analyse the change in sentiment over the course of the first month. The method requires some explanation. The words used by the students are grouped by week and scored according to a sentiment lexicon. The score is then averaged across the week. The points in Figure 4 represent the average sentiment of the students’ diary entries in a particular week.


Figure 4 Change in sentiment and week-specific key themes

There are two important findings. First, sentiment is poor at the start, improves over the course of the month, and then collapses in the final week. Second, it is important to note that the average sentiment is negative for the entirety of the period. This seems somewhat in contrast to Figure 3, which shows a larger number of positive to negative words. This can be explained by the weighting of the words. The AFINN-111 dataset is a lexicon of English words rated for valence with an integer between minus five and plus five.35 The words were manually labeled by Finn Årup Nielsen in 2009-2011. An example of the scores assigned to words in the students’ diary entries is shown in Table 1.

While the word cloud exposes the key themes that students discussed in their diaries, we also want to know how these themes change across time. To do so, we use a tool that provides the weighted log odds ratio for each word across the six weeks of diary entries. This provides a quantification of how specific each word is to the week that it is used in.36 Figure 4 superimposes the week-specific words above the line graph that shows the evolution of student sentiment across the weeks.
At the outset there was anxiety about the lockdown, difficulties with internet access, traveling home and a worry about the rise in cases. On the first day of lockdown, one student wrote that “[t]here seems to be a dystopic fog or gloom that hangs all around”. This was followed by conspiracy theories and discussions of obligation and privilege. The collective mood improved towards Easter and was further buoyed by the announcement of a large stimulus package by the government. The focus also seemed to shift from the external environment to the internal. One student, for example, noted that “[e]ven though lockdown does have this over-arching gloom-and-doom feel, one of the things that I’ve really enjoyed about it is that I’ve really started to appreciate the smaller things again”.


Figure 5 Sentiment analysis and number of Covid-19 tests, cases and deaths

Finally, as case numbers continued to increase and a continuation of lockdown measures was announced, there was exasperation about the state of employment and livelihoods. As a way to demonstrate the relationship between the virus and sentiment, Figure 5 plots the number of Covid-19 tests, cases and deaths against the sentiment series.
It should be borne in mind that these diary entries were written during the first month of national lockdown, soon after the first case had been reported. Figure 6 plots the number of diary entries against Covid-19 case and death statistics from March 2020 to April 2021. This helps to contextualise the students’ thoughts, feelings and experiences: these entries are from a time before the virus’s health and economic impact would become evident.


Figure 6 Period of diary entries and Covid-19 case and death numbers from March 2020 to April 2021



Figure 7 Sentiment analysis, JSE All Share Index and rand/dollar exchange rate

We also want to compare the sentiment time series to other indicators of well-being. Because we do not have accurate daily observations of indicators like income or unemployment, we use two measures that should provide a rough approximation of investor sentiment, the Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index (JSE) and the South African rand/US dollar exchange rate, shown in Figure 7. The JSE, similar to many other stock exchanges globally, had collapsed during the first few weeks of March. It was, therefore, already on the road to recovery when Cyril Ramaphosa announced the national shutdown. The rand, however, continued to depreciate throughout the period, recovering somewhat after 6 April, but then returning to a high of R19 to the dollar by the end of April, the highest it had ever been. Although there are seemingly correlations between the three indicators, we are cautious to overinterpret these correlations. In general, the stock market improvement seems to correlate positively with the sentiment analysis, while the rand, surprisingly, seems to be negatively correlated; an increase in the sentiment is correlated to a depreciation of the currency. The safest interpretation would be that the levels – rather than the trends – indicate that the stock market, rand and students’ sentiment were at historic lows.
The approach above draws our attention to key themes in the diary entries. It exposes the generally negative feelings that the students experienced, but also important moments of temporal shift and the key topics which shaped this temporal shift. We believe these trends serve as useful context to guide close reading of the texts.

title: Introduction
text:
Microhistories
First developed by Italian historians in the 1970s, microhistory is a mode of historical enquiry that involves a reduction in scale – i.e. zooming in on an individual, a community or a unique event in order to illuminate what Edoardo Grendi famously called the “exceptional normal”.37 Following Grendi’s lead, we argue in this section that much of the value of the diary entries that follow lies in their interweaving of the exceptional (Covid-19 and the unique circumstances which it has generated) with the mundane (everyday social dynamics, habits and ideas). For many students the project represented a rare opportunity to write not about abstract academic ideas, but about the humdrum of everyday life; talking to friends, celebrating birthdays, shopping and cooking with family, exercising, studying etc. Read together, their descriptions provide much needed insight into the individual and collective coping mechanisms used to manage the threat of Covid-19.
Over the course of the last few months, researchers have emphasised that “[…] in addition to its staggering impact on physical well-being and mortality, Covid-19 is also taking an unprecedented toll on mental health”.38 This argument is borne out in our own research. For many students, lockdown was a time of struggle both practically and psychologically. It was extremely common for students to report feeling anxious, uncertain and overwhelmed – emotions which seem to have been heightened by exposure to the news media. Su, McDonnell and Wen et al. have suggested that “effective crisis communication” – that is, communication designed to provide accurate information, dispel fears and unify individuals in a collective fight against global political, health or economic crises – has not been forthcoming within context of the Covid-19 pandemic.39 Instead, global media outlets have presented audiences with a barrage of often sensationalist (read alarmist) news and statistics which tend to reinforce negative mental health outcomes. “Constantly being bombarded with the statistics and talk of economic collapse is mentally draining and not very useful when you are doing everything in your capacity to stay afloat”, explained one student. Later, a different student commented, “I’m going to try look for some interesting reads and download new books instead of anxiously checking the news every 5 seconds […] Twitter has been both a blessing and a curse in this time. It allows for quick transmission of news but on the other hand, because it is such a fast space, it generally makes me feel very anxious”.
Limiting their news intake was a strategy that worked well for some students. For others, though, the practical implications of the pandemic were too immediate to be ignored. Throughout the lockdown, students worried, for example, that a loss of family income or a lack of adequate technological resources would compromise their educational opportunities and possibly prevent them from finishing their degrees. The health of family and friends was also a constant concern. For one student, the health implications of the pandemic became extremely personal when the student’s mother was the first patient in South Africa to test negative after being admitted to ICU with what was thought to be Covid-19.
Most students found studying in isolation difficult, as well as disconcerting, even when they had access to adequate digital resources. As one student explained: “Its impressive to see how the lecturers have quickly adapted their teaching styles to suit the online platforms, but is also scary to see how all of this can be done from home and that we don’t actually need to be on campus to learn efficiently. What I did learn ( just from one day) is that I miss the social interactions I didn’t have today – they are definitely necessary for the ‘full university experience’”. Such comments lend credibility to Tawana Kupe’s argument that learning is a fundamentally social process.
In responding to the pandemic, though, students were able to draw on a range of alternative networks for support. Family ties, in particular, seem to have strengthened during lockdown, with one student going as far as to suggest that lockdown heralded a “restoration of the family unit”. Religious and faith-based communities also seem to have played an important role in helping students to manage their anxiety; students (and their families) often attended virtual services and sought comfort in communal prayer. In addition, a number of students spoke about how the virus had prompted new forms of sociality and solidarity to develop in the broader environments (both social and geographical) which they occupied. “In our community I have seen many organisations that have started doing grocery shopping on behalf of the elderly”, reflected one student, while another wrote proudly about how her stepfather swam several kilometres in order to raise funds for a local charity on Freedom Day. For some, Covid-19 even became an opportunity to rethink the future of community. Perhaps the pandemic could be used to fuel a new sense of global cohesion and interconnectedness? As one student commented, “[…] we are literally all in the same situation […] maybe this is all happening because a common threat would unite us globally. Could this be the antidote [to] racism, gender discrimination and xenophobia?”
Students grappled with the overall meaning of the pandemic in various ways. There were those who analysed the pandemic through a predominantly religious lens, sometimes using biblical metaphors to make sense of their situation. Others adopted an ecological viewpoint, wondering whether the pandemic wasn’t the earth’s response to the environmental damage wrought by human habitation. The past was also often used as a reference. One student drew inspiration from their own family history: “During the Spanish Flue of 1918 my great grandfather, his brothers and their father had the grim job of picking up the bodies of people who had died the previous night. Miraculously none of them caught the flu. My grandmother, when telling the story, always adds that she thinks they all survived unharmed because they were doing such a good thing.”
In a recent Op-Ed, psychologist Maggie Mulqueen argues that the Covid-19 pandemic has highlighted the tenuousness of human life, but that this shouldn’t necessarily be judged as a bad thing.40 Recognising our mortality, she suggests, can deepen our appreciation of the everyday and leave us with a sense of gratitude for the simplest of pleasures. The pandemic seems to have had this effect on many students. Drawing from Albert Camus’ La Peste, one student reflected on “the idea that we can, at any moment, be randomly exterminated”. He then wrote, “[…] [i]nstead of allowing this realisation to cause despair, however, it can lead to a renewed appreciation of our humanity”. Another student wrote: “[…] throughout this whole ordeal I’m becoming more and more grateful for things I never really took note of before.”
Especially for the more affluent students, lockdown also served as a reminder of their privileged position in South African society. “During uncontrollable times like these the rich will be ‘inconvenienced’, but still emerge relatively unscathed, while the poor are pushed further into a state of destitution”, one student said. Many others spoke about how lucky they felt to not have to worry about access to basic resources like food, shelter and safety: “I have a roof over my head, food guaranteed each day, two loving parents who do not abuse me (or any substances), two sisters to keep me company, the resources to keep up with academics and enough personal space. Many people are not so lucky.” There is, of course, a difference between the kind of awareness being expressed here and genuine structural change. The two are related though, and it is interesting that students used concepts related to privilege (e.g. the lottery of birth, the value of lived experience etc.) so fluently, perhaps suggesting the mainstreaming of a particular kind of privilege politics that was absent a decade ago.

title: Introduction
text:
Conclusion
This anthology suggests that the Covid-19 pandemic and the national lockdown to which it gave rise had a substantial effect on the everyday lives of university students in South Africa, many of whom suffered economic insecurity and acute psychological stress as they grappled with the personal and public consequences of the virus. Their experiences and the inequalities which they discuss are useful for assessing the impact that Covid-19 has had on higher education in country. Generally speaking, this anthology supports the view that, although the pandemic is capable of generating positive change within the sector, there is still much to be considered and accomplished before such change is likely to occur.
Ultimately, the purpose of this anthology is two-fold. First, to preserve. Covid-19 and the subsequent national lockdown(s) represent an unprecedented moment in South African history. The thoughts, feelings and experiences of young people should be of value to future historians. Second, to reflect. As we write this in July 2021, South Africa is experiencing a third wave. We have just come out of another level-4 lockdown and there are likely to be more waves of infection in future. These diary entries guide our own thoughts, feelings and experiences: how far have we come from that initial month of fear of anxiety, and how much are we still to endure?

title: 21 March 2020
text:
South Africa had 240 confirmed cases of Covid-19 – the second highest number of confirmed cases for an African country. The government began publishing the specific details of each case according to province. Gauteng province, for instance, had 16 cases, and one of the cases was “a 67-year-old male who had travelled to France and Ethiopia”. South African Airways announced that it would suspend all regional flights. In the United Kingdom (UK), Prime Minister Boris Johnson called for pubs, gyms, theatres, cinemas and restaurants to close immediately and indefinitely. The total coronavirus death toll for the UK increased by 53.

This term was clearly very stressful – the evidence is the spasm in my jaw from clenching my teeth. I went to the doctor to get anti-inflammatory medicine. However, these meds (sometimes) have severe cardiovascular side-effects and I started experiencing some of these symptoms including, wait for it, extreme difficulty to breathe. Needless to say, given that this is one of the symptoms for corona, I sort of freaked out because what if I contracted this virus [at] the airport and now placed my father at risk? Luckily, I figured out that it was the medicine and after a while it wore off. I’m usually a very calm-minded and rational person, but I have to admit, I did panic. The level of awareness that I am practicing at the moment is exhausting – not just regarding hygiene. I am checking my emails regularly for updates on SunLearn activities, academic deadlines, etc. I am also watching the news and cross-checking everything I hear to guard against fake news, which could be detrimental during this time. We hear so many statistics everyday that it’s hard to think in terms of actual people dying. I think there is a huge danger of people becoming desensitised to the effects of the virus.

* * *

Today has probably been the most challenging day yet. I feel like my mind hasn’t taken a break. There are just so many unknown factors right now and I don’t know how to fully prepare myself. I like to plan and to know how things are going to be. It is driving me crazy with everything being so fluid at the moment. I understand it must be difficult for the university to give us clear answers as to what is going to happen exactly in the coming weeks, but it is so difficult to know what head space to be in and how to prepare. […] I just feel like I need a break from it all to focus on other things and pretend that life is normal, even just for a minute.

* * *

I realised today that people only care about things that affect them directly. A family friend turned 50 today and I declined to go to the party, but my family still want to proceed with my grandmother’s 70th birthday party. This does not seem fair to me.[…] I’ve come to the conclusion that it is our civil duty to educate those around us on how we’re supposed to act and act in union with the rest of the world, even if said people are your own family.

* * *

Today I went hiking up Lion’s Head with two friends. Later, my family from Switzerland called me and informed me that their government implemented a state of emergency. From now on no stores will [be] open, apart from pharmacies and grocery stores. Hospital visits are only allowed for emergencies. Everyone is to stay at home and gatherings of more than 6 persons are forbidden. I suspect that South Africa will enforce similar arrangements if the situation gets worse. For now, I am glad that some gyms and stores haven’t closed yet. It still feels like a holiday at the moment.

* * *

There is so much going on around the world, as well as in my own life, that I don’t even know where to start, but I’ll begin with my arrival at home because that was quite a new experience. Normally, when I get home, I am greeted with leaps and licks from my little yorkshire terrier, and then three warm hugs from my brother, mother and father. This time the terrier was the only one who felt comfortable touching me – [this] human had just been through two airports. My family were happy to see me, but my mother gave me strict instructions to shower and change before we engaged in any physical contact (as is to be expected from a professional nurse turned nursing services area manager).

* * *

My mother is convinced that there will be a lockdown on Gauteng (despite the presidential spokesperson denying such plans) and is trying to force me to come home. Honestly, I think I’ll go crazy being with all my family everyday for the foreseeable future. If there is a lockdown in Gauteng specifically, I won’t be able to sell my clothes from home and madness will be inevitable. On the other hand, Stellenbosch has become a ghost town and I don’t know how much longer I’ll be okay here. Tomorrow, I’ll make a pros and cons list to decide. […] Everytime Stellenbosch gets quiet (supplementary [exams] time, etc.) people become unruly. Lately, my girlfriends and I are being harassed more than usual by random men.

* * *

This evening my sisters, my mom and I realised we haven’t watched our soapies in a while, so we binge watched Suidooster and basically spent the evening shouting at the TV screen, as most coloured families do. It felt good to just be home spending time with my family. I know that at some point during this pandemic these feelings are going to change, so I’m embracing them while they’re here. I don’t know how I’m going to survive being back home with both my parents and siblings at the same time. […] The number of confirmed Covid-19 cases in the country increased from 116 to 150 today. Apparently South Africa has the fastest growing rate of this virus compared to other countries. At this point it looks like we might have a complete lockdown.

* * *

I often go for coffee with my old high school English teacher when I am in Johannesburg and he suggested we continue our tradition despite the virus-related chaos that has gripped the city. I was reluctant at first as he is over 60 and is therefore classified as being part of the ‘high risk’ group, but he insisted. At the café the waiter offered us some hand sanitiser before taking our order. When I ordered a rock shandy, the waiter refused saying they are not allowed to serve alcoholic drinks anymore. I thought that was a bit funny – are they afraid of people becoming overly affectionate after having one too many? I know that I have not been taking the virus seriously enough up until now. From tomorrow onwards I will not be leaving my house unless it is absolutely necessary.

* * *

Today I had a really interesting conversation with my godfather, not only about Covid-19 and what’s to come for South Africa, but also about the state of South African universities – with special reference to NSFAS and its shortcomings.
On Covid-19
He believes as the virus becomes more widespread, it will shed light on government corruption and on persistent inequalities in the country. We laughed over a meme that’s been making the rounds that pokes fun at African leaders during this time. The meme said something along the lines of: “African leaders can no longer run away to rich countries to seek treatment if they are sick. Now we (as African citizens) are equal to them.” This made me pause and wonder, how are African leaders feeling right now? Does it make them feel better that the global North is in the same predicament as them, and that the situation there is far worse (for now)?
I thought, maybe for a lot of African governments and leaders, it must feel as though there’s an invisible countdown clock on their shoulder. They know what’s about to come, but to a large extent, they are unequipped to handle it. Not just because there is a lack of resources, but because within a lot of African governments there is a lack of competency. My dad said the Chinese are definitely being the ones to bring about a cure, I mentioned the possibility of Africans bringing a cure – I was met with silence and eye rolls …
On SA Universities and NSFAS
My godfather believes it is a failing system. I get him, I really do, but having friends who are recipients of NSFAS, I understand the necessity for a system like it. We spoke about how students exploit the system (by using funds for other ‘less academic’ activities), but we also spoke about possible alternatives to the system. Instead of paying students directly, why doesn’t it work in such a way that the Allan Gray Fellowship works (fees being paid directly to the varsity)? […] I had to note, though, that I speak from a privileged perspective. I am lucky enough to have received a fellowship that provides a lot of financial support. I often feel guilty when I take part in conversations like this. I think to myself: do I have the right to voice alternatives when I do not live that experience?

* * *

The news this week has been all about how people, from all walks of life, are reacting to the pandemic. In today’s edition of The Daily Maverick, there was criticism of those in high income positions who are either selfishly panic buying or not taking the pandemic seriously at all, instead continuing to socialise with their friends. A lot of recognition has gone out to the ‘helpers’ in this situation – doctors, nurses and the like. They are the superheroes in this story.

title: 22 March 2020
text:
The South African National Coronavirus Command Council met to discuss measures to address the coronavirus pandemic. In the Free State, authorities started tracing 480 worshippers from the Divine Restoration Ministry, which had five congregants test positive after a service. Italy recorded 800 new coronavirus-related deaths, with over 5 000 total deaths and more than 60 000 confirmed cases. The Italian government requested support from the United States (US) military stationed in the country in combating the virus. The Japanese Prime Minister, Shinzo Abe, spoke publicly for the first time of the possibility of postponing the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, and the Canadian Olympic Committee called for the Games to be postponed by a year.

I watched church online with my family this morning. After the service we had a family meeting to discuss the virus and what we as a family plan to do to stay safe and adhere to the government’s requests. We came up with various precautions in order to minimise risk of contracting the virus. We decided that if we needed to leave, we have to change clothes immediately when we get back home. We have a spare room near the front on the house so we will change there and leave those clothes there until they’ve been washed so that the germs don’t spread. We also won’t have unnecessary interactions with people outside of our household. There are hand sanitisers at the front door and in the kitchen and each family member also has their own sanitiser.
As we were speaking, I realised how many people don’t have the luxury of taking these precautions. Some households in South Africa consist of one room that is shared by nearly ten people. Throughout this whole ordeal, I’m becoming more and more grateful for things I never really took note of before.

* * *

Today I made the decision to accept our circumstances and accept fully our new reality without trying to question my actions the whole time. […] I also spent some time just mulling [over] how crazy it is that we can relate to people almost all over the world right now. We are literally all in the same situation. Maybe this is all happening because a common threat would unite us globally. Could this be the antidote [to] racism, gender discrimination and xenophobia? Could this make people across the world realise that things we have come to love and value are all so temporary and that relationships with others and how we treat and perceive others are so much more important? I’m so curious to see the world at the end of all this when we start to recover. I would like to think that there will be significant changes in what goes on around the world, for the better.

* * *

Speakeasy informed the public that there would be insane lunch specials coming up during the quarantine. My friend and I went to go check it out today. We asked them why they have these specials on and their response was that they need more business; they used to get double the number of customers before the outbreak. The waiter at Speakeasy told us that the tips she makes contribute to her rent. If she does not get enough tips, she will end up on the street. This is terrifying because it means that South Africa’s poverty could rapidly increase as the coronavirus infects more people.

* * *

I was extremely conflicted this morning. I received an invite to go to Jonkershoek nature reserve with a group of friends. Every day there is increased pressure on social media to self-isolate. There have been a lot of hateful comments directed at people who post things on social media of them doing things outside of their houses. This made me doubt whether I would be doing the right thing in going.
However, the government hasn’t restricted nature reserves or beaches yet. I also have the feeling that restrictions with regard to enjoying public areas are only going to intensify, so I figured that I might as well enjoy these things while I can. In a sense, we were isolated because our group wasn’t near any other people, and we had found a completely deserted and peaceful spot to spend the day. It was such a nice feeling to be in nature and it made me realise [that] we shouldn’t take it for granted.

* * *

So, it is Sunday today, I woke up around 7:00 am. I usually start preparing to go with the family to church in Bothasig, but no gatherings of more than 100 people are permitted. The church and the Bishop of Cape Town have used livestream technology to broadcast their masses, so I just attended an online mass. Pretty weird but cool to see the church adapt in difficult circumstances. […]
I have been hearing a lot of people say “this is the end of the world” or “it is a sign” etc. Uhm, I basically call bullshit and implore people to think rationally. During these times of distress and uncertainty, I think a lot of people [are] leaving themselves vulnerable to fake news, causing unnecessary panic and the spreading of further fake news.

* * *

Socially, having the virus or coming into contact with it almost seems shameful. I can compare it to the ancient responses towards those with leprosy. Organisations have been active in preventing the identities of those with the virus from being disclosed. There is a profound, negative stigma attached to having the virus.

* * *

My usual Sunday routine back in Stellenbosch includes going to church, but that’s not happening at the moment. Instead, church is brought to our homes. This is just one example of how organisations are using technology to their advantage and adapting during this time of crisis. My church is just one of many who are using online streaming to bring their sermons to the people. One should never disregard the effect of religion on the lives of people and the impact that believing in something bigger than yourself – a God in whom you can place your trust – has on your mental health. I see it with my friends and with my family – some are believers and others not. What strikes me is how frantic those are who place their faith in humanity because, let’s be honest, this is quite the battle we are facing and few people are able to see how we are going to get to the other side.

* * *

274 cases. Highly doubt this is accurate, apparently 75% of these declared cases have been privately tested, which means that the government has only tested and declared 70 people. This is ridiculous. Discussions abound on whether or not the disease has made its way to the townships, and what this will mean for the country. Many people in the townships have underlying health problems, are aged, or have weakened immune systems – the spread of the virus in these circumstances could be catastrophic and could result in many deaths.

* * *

It is Sunday now, and although everything is running normally, the rumours about lockdown [are] increasing. My family is practicing social distancing, and so we decided to not go to church. Many of our church members did not attend church due to the spread of the virus.
It was announced this afternoon that the president will be addressing the country this evening. Everyone is expecting a lockdown. The president has been meeting with all the other political leaders and business owners to make this decision.
It is a difficult decision as a lockdown involves the stop of most economic activities. Already the South African government is [in] a lot of debt and there are rumours about Moody’s deciding to downgrade South Africa to “junk” status. A lockdown will affect all businesses, their employees and families. There is much uncertainty about how and if salaries will be paid.

* * *

At first, I was surprised by how little my brother had to say about the Covid-19 pandemic. He was the first to alert me of its spread around the globe. However, once my father, who I have mentioned is quite involved in many decisions made by the government [in] preventing the spread of the virus, and my mother, who has always [been a] keen health enthusiast due to her profession as a nurse, started talking, I realised why my brother was exhausted by the topic. I haven’t been home for long so I don’t share his boredom and was eager to listen to my parent’s thoughts. My mother spoke of washing hands and using sanitiser constantly, always coughing in a tissue then discarding it, changing clothes after being in public and many other tedious but important precautions. My father did not hesitate to give me the scoop on what lay ahead for the nation. He knew that a nationwide lockdown was probably coming.

title: 23 March 2020
text:
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa announced that a national lockdown would be implemented to curb the spread of the coronavirus. It was explained that all South Africans would be required to stay home except for health workers, security services and those involved in the production, distribution and supply of food and other essential services. Individuals would only be allowed to leave their home to seek medical care, buy food or medicine and other essential supplies, or collect social grants. Amazon suspended more than 4 000 sellers because of coronavirus-related price gouging and false claims related to how products could benefit buyers regarding the virus. Cuban authorities announced that Cuban and foreign residents returning to the country would be required to undergo supervised quarantine for two weeks.

I woke up at 2:00 am. I was having corovirus related nightmares. […] I am starting to really think that this is God’s punishment to us. It would not be the first time. I have reached this conclusion because it is only humans that are getting it – then again, babies are not getting it. As ridiculous as it might sound, I have reasoned this to be because they are innocent. This is all in religious terms. There are probably scientific explanations for the virus. Why is this happening, though? Not how it is happening, but why; that is what I want to know, and I believe I can only find the answer religiously.

* * *

My domestic worker came in for the first time since Friday (she usually has the weekend off ). When she arrived, I feared that she may have picked up my flu as she could not stop coughing. I noticed that her cough, unlike my wet one, sounded rather dry – which is a symptom of Covid-19. After a bit of questioning, she explained that she also [had] uncontrolled and unnatural sweating since 21 March. I then said that, due to these strange times, she must not come to work, but will be on paid leave.
Like many South Africans, I have a close relationship with my domestic worker. She has looked after me since I was five and she is a part of my family. Because of this I, perhaps irrationally, decided to give her a lift back to her house, sharing the car with a possible corona victim. I did the best I could to prevent contracting the virus by wearing a face mask and washing myself thoroughly afterwards, yet this might not help. If I do contract the virus, it will be from this day.

* * *

A 21-day lockdown, effective from 26 March, has just been announced and I applaud it. From a political point of view, our president has shown immense leadership skills and has acted remarkably quickly and pro-actively – something which I honestly did not expect from South Africa. I think President Ramaphosa’s leadership has united the nation a little bit; people are feeling more certain now that we have a set plan of action and most of the people I know support the decision. From an economic point of view, I wonder whether stock prices won’t settle a little bit […]. Whilst I know that the economy will surely suffer under a three week closure, I think that consumers are a bit less apprehensive and uncertain about the short term future. However, I think this will still have immense adverse effects on our economy. Businesses are closing and a lot of citizens rely on their businesses or jobs being open to receive income – if businesses cannot pay their employees for these three weeks, living standards could decrease in the short term.

* * *

I’m sitting here trying to fight back the tears, while surrounded by a couple other extremely privileged white people who are going on about how horrible it is that there is to be a nationwide lockdown.
Never have I ever felt the guilt of my privilege like today. How can we complain about the situation that we are in? Do not get me wrong, I am not perfect, and I too have found myself being rather pessimistic at times about this situation, going on about how boring it will be etc. etc., but this has taken me right back to reality. A nationwide lockdown has been announced.
I am extremely lucky. I cannot stress this enough. I will never be able to understand why I was put where I am. I am in such a privileged position and I am aware of it, although it is easy to forget. I have always told myself that I want to use my position to do good, but in situation like this how can we? It seems our only option is to throw money at the problem which I do believe might be productive if given to the right people.
A nationwide lockdown. Who would ever have thought?
My mind cannot come to grips with what is going on: I cannot fathom how we can shut down a whole country that is so dependent on a day-to-day income. Yet I know it is the only thing we can do.
Children are being forced to stay at home with abusive parents, people living on the streets have nowhere to go, people cannot afford to buy food, and thus, if the virus doesn’t take them, starvation could …

* * *

Today the number of confirmed cases increased from 240 to 402 people. I was hanging up washing and I heard what sounded like guys playing rugby. So, I went to check outside and there were about 20 guys playing touch rugby in the park across the road from my house. I was so upset. I can’t believe that people are still not taking this virus seriously! I messaged one of my friends who was amongst the group. He seemed to think I was joking. I don’t understand why people can’t comprehend that it’s not just about themselves when their choices can put others at risk too.
This evening the president addressed the nation once again. It was decided that the country will enter a 21-day lockdown starting on Thursday 26 March at midnight. All citizens will be required to stay at home. Certain stores will still be open for households to get all their essentials in terms of food and medication. The president mentioned that social grants will be paid out earlier. I am worried for poorer households and what this lockdown means for them. After all, some people need their daily wage just to put food on the table.

* * *

I can definitely tell that life in quarantine is starting to affect everyone in my family. It’s just me, my mom and my dad at home, but the fact that they are not able to leave the house to go to work is making them feel restless and ineffective. I am, however, grateful that they are able to continue working from home. I hear so many stories of people sitting at home temporarily without a job or salary. Many companies are going bankrupt and having to lay off their workers. These are often people who cannot afford to be without a salary […]. This morning I went to buy groceries with my mom at the local supermarket and we bumped into a family acquaintance who spoke about how worried she was that the current situation might ruin a family trip to the United States in August. She mentioned all the money she might have wasted on Broadway tickets. What a luxury it must be to have that as one’s worry during a pandemic.

* * *

The day has arrived when our president has announced an official lockdown. I do not know whether to be thankful or disappointed. Reading the news out of China, where they have had their last infested person leave hospital, I am actually excited for South Africa to take responsibility for the virus and to implement this lockdown. The number of infected persons is rising at an exponential rate. My stepdad is a professor at Tygerberg hospital. He told me that they already have an entire hall of patients infected with Covid-19.

* * *

Cyril Ramaphosa addressed the nation a few hours ago, and amongst other things announced a national lockdown as of midnight on Thursday.
After beginning his speech by praising the nation for their combined efforts to curb the spread of the virus, as well as abiding by the recent regulations imposed by the government, Ramaphosa went on to emphasise the importance of the next few days. He also spoke about dangers the virus might pose to South Africa in particular.
South Africa has the largest HIV epidemic in the world (7.7 million people) and the world’s sixth largest tuberculosis [TB] epidemic, with this disease the leading cause of death in the country.
[…] I agree with the early implementation of a national lockdown, and I do believe the South African government has, as of this moment, handled the situation fairly well. I do fear though that those citizens below the poverty line may resort to desperate measures. I thus call upon the government, as well as other citizens, to assist those in need during this period. If we simply think of others and don’t put ourselves at the centre of the universe, we as a nation can very easily overcome this virus. My fear though is that humanity has become too self-gratified, and that Covid-19 will consequently take many more lives than necessary.
Prove me wrong Homo sapiens!

* * *

This just gets getting more and more surreal. Last week this time I honestly thought we would still possibly be going back to varsity soon after 30 March. Now that that has changed it makes me wonder what kind of space we will be in next week this time.

* * *

Today my father is travelling to Johannesburg for work. He opted to travel with a N99 mask and a pair of latex gloves in order to reduce his vulnerability to the virus. He reported to me that the airports, both OR Thambo and Cape Town International, remain fully functional and relatively busy. However, people are definitely making a conscious effort to reduce the spread of the virus by wearing masks and gloves. He also noted that the airports were being feverishly cleaned and that there was hand santiser everywhere. […] Also regarding Johannesburg, the SADF [South African Defence Force] were spotted in full effect at the Craighall barracks. This development comes after the army was mobilised just days ago.

title: 24 March 2020
text:
Most South African political parties welcomed President Ramaphosa’s announcement of a 21-day lockdown. Spain reported that it had over 4 000 infected health workers. The United Nations (UN) announced that it would create a fund to support the global response to the coronavirus. New Zealand commenced its own lockdown after experiencing a 30% increase in coronavirus cases. In the USA, the governor of Nevada, Steve Sisolak, prohibited gatherings of more than ten people in that state, and said that social distancing was the primary priority in defeating the virus. The UK entered its first lockdown.

Today I was kicked off the beach. The weather was beautiful and it was sweltering hot, so I thought it was a good idea to enjoy nature while it was still permitted. However, shortly after my arrival at the beach, I was approached by a member of the City of Cape Town law enforcement. He was incredibly polite and asked me to vacate the beach as all Cape Town beaches have been closed with immediate effect. Although the process was calm, it was startling to be removed from a public space whilst doing nothing wrong. I suppose this is the new reality.

* * *

Today, almost two years later, I finally got round to sorting out my matric books. It seems irrelevant to corona but it is actually not: one of our very close family friends is currently a matric student, who as a result of this lockdown, will not have class for at least a month (if all goes well). Needless to say, all of the matriculants are quite unnerved by the lockdown and their uncertain future. So, I decided to take my books and notes to her so that she has some sort of material to fall back on. While universities are already semi-online, no one knows how effectively the school system will be able to adapt to online learning. I also decided to take up an old money-making venture of mine again. The lockdown offers the perfect market to start selling school summaries as students will be desperate to get their hands on any helpful learning material. Apart from earning a little income on the side, I genuinely feel for these students. If learners from former model-C schools are under this much pressure, what about the schools without facilities to support online learning? What about the learners who depend on schools meal plans to be fed?

* * *

Not much to report today. Japan has finally agreed to postpone the Olympic Games. Rural dwellers are afraid that urban dwellers who want to return to rural areas before the lockdown commences will bring the virus with them. Limpopo will be doing screenings at toll gates to prevent the virus from going into the rural areas. The number of infected has now risen to 554 – the rapid increase in the number of infected persons is quite frightening. Hopefully, the lockdown measures work and will help flatten the curve. Consumers are still being urged not to panic buy. There are about 380 000 people infected globally.

* * *

My mother has been sick for a while now. This weekend our doctor came to our house because she was too weak to go to the doctor. He told us that she is feeling terrible because of her high blood sugar levels and gave her some medicine. We asked him if we should test her for the coronavirus. He said that it is not necessary because she does not have the right symptoms. She did not have fever, shortness of breath or a cough. My mother still demanded that she be tested and went with my father on Monday morning to have a test done. Yesterday morning I went to my mother’s room. She looked better and told me that she is feeling a bit better. While we were talking, the Department of Health called my mother to tell her that she tested positive for Covid-19. It was a big shock for us all because she had different symptoms. She had a painful headache, tiredness, vomiting and body pains. After we found out that she was positive we had to call everyone we were in contact with in this week because the chances are very high that our whole family might have the virus. Luckily, I only had to call two people. This virus just went from feeling like an apocalyptic movie to real life.

* * *

Today marks a very important day in my life: the day I received real independence. I finally got my driver’s license. Yes, it may be two years late, but nonetheless I still got it and I am delighted.
The day started off well. I remained calm and was very excited to finally get my license. An hour before I was scheduled to do my test, at 2:30 pm, there was a moment of panic at the traffic department, as one of the testing officers was informed that one of the people that she had tested earlier that morning may test positive for Covid-19 but is still waiting on their test results.
I panicked when I had heard this as I had come into contact with this testing officer earlier that morning and I started wondering if I had possibly touched any surfaces that she had also touched. I was also hoping that she wasn’t going to be my testing officer so that I didn’t have to be in a confined space with her in case she may have picked up the virus, because as we have learnt, the symptoms do not show instantly but rather after a couple of days.

* * *

I have realised that arts have such a soothing and wonderful role in this messed up world. What would we do without books, art, poetry and television in this lockdown? This is a good time to get to those things that we long promised ourselves that we would when we aren’t busy building our future. Quarantine is an opportunity to find ourselves again and to express the talents that we were blessed with but often cannot pursue in our rushed world.

* * *

It’s been a week since I started documenting my days in this diary, and so much has happened and changed during its course. My mother and I headed to the supermarket this morning, but much to my mother’s dismay, the place was packed with other mothers who had the exact same idea as her. I guess everyone wanted to prepare or the lockdown immediately so they could stay indoors for as long as possible, not needing another trip to the grocery shop for the whole three weeks by the look of it. People had trolleys full of the same thing and the store had signs indicating limits for certain products per customer. I found this amusing, because I suppose many took on the notion that “desperate times, calls for desperate measures”.

* * *

Today I woke at 11:00 am. I took a bath and had my breakfast of bread and butter. At 12:00 am, I went to campus to print some documents. Since the national lockdown has been implemented, I believe that I won’t have access to Wi-Fi and so I wanted to make sure that I printed enough hard copies to do my revision.

* * *

Panic shopping – something the president told us not to do, but which the majority of the nation did anyway. People are flocking to the malls. The traffic in Mosselbay was even worse than it is in December. Alcohol, flour, tinned foods and toilet paper were some of the first things to be sold out. The president could have said that shops selling necessities will also close and the outcome wouldn’t have been very different. […] Paranoia spreads even faster than corona, it seems.

* * *

There’s been a lot of talk of how, during social distancing, we should not mentally and emotionally isolate ourselves, and I have been wondering a lot about that. Even in my circumstances, not having had a phone, being away from res [student accommodation] and campus life, I already feel like a shadow of myself. I feel socially isolated from everyone. It’s a weird feeling. In feeling this way, I also feel guilty. I am part of the lucky few who even whilst in isolation have access to a lot of luxuries. There’s this weird balance I am trying to find whereby I do not invalidate my feelings of loneliness from my friends but also be aware of the fact that I am in a fortunate position.

title: 25 March 2020
text:
The South African government urged citizens not to panic buy as they rushed to shops to purchase goods amidst fears of possible food shortages. These calls went largely unheeded as South Africans queued outside grocery and liquor stores to stock up. Airlines around the world cut back on flights. Alaska Airlines, for example, reduced their flying schedule by 70%. The US Government called on retired medical military personnel to assist in responding to the medical crisis precipitated by the virus, while New York authorities set up temporary morgues in the city to prepare for coronavirus deaths.

My mind has shut itself off any good thoughts today. I wonder if coronavirus shall decrease the crime rate. Do gangs know about this virus? […] I have been awake since midnight, just staring at the roof and wondering.
I heard that Donald Trump has been giving hydroxychloroquine to the citizens of America. I know it is a cure, but it hits very strongly. My mother told me that they sold it in my country (DRC [Democratic Republic of the Congo]) and then they stopped because it was just too strong. One person apparently died from an overdose.
Unbelievable how someone can die and life still goes on. I heard someone playing music as they drove by … people are still visiting each other. I called my friend and for the first time I allowed myself to talk over the phone.
Even though this whole virus is making me afraid, it is also helping me understand where my interests lie and making me reconsider many things in life.

* * *

This morning my father came into my room. He asked me if I was showing any symptoms. I told him that I felt fine. He then explained that I should get dressed to greet my mother because he must take her to the hospital. He also explained that we will not be allowed to visit her until she has tested negative. I showered, got dressed and went to our kitchen. My brothers also stood there waiting. My father came to us and told us that we must decide for my mother, because she feels that she cannot decide on her own.
The two options were: go to the hospital and get physical support, but not any emotional support or be allowed to see us. The second option was to stay at home, still receive emotional support but without medical monitoring. I immediately told my family that we should not decide for ourselves but rather only take my mother into consideration, but we all knew that already. We called a hospital near us that is prepared for Covid-19 patients. They asked us the following questions: “What is her blood pressure? What is her blood sugar level? What is her blood oxygen level?” We answered all the questions. When they heard what her blood oxygen level was, they told us that she should immediately be hospitalised. Their next question was: “How fast can you get here?” It was decided.
The next moment my mom came out of her room. She was crying. She told us that she loved us. We tried not to cry and answered that we love her and that she would be okay. The worst part was that we could not even give her a hug goodbye. We were not allowed to touch her. After they left, we all just sat and cried – still not allowed to give each other hugs. After 50 minutes my father sent a picture with my mother smiling. He said that the hospital is going to take good care of her. He said that the nurses are friendly and will be able to give her emotional support as well.

* * *
