Today I woke up early because my friend and I planned to go get our hair cut in town. […] My barber owns the shop, so out of interest sake I asked him how this coronavirus pandemic would affect him. He told me that he won’t be able to generate income through the barbershop, but will still cut the people’s hair in his community. He also has a ‘side-hustle’ where he creates frames, furniture and other objects out of wood. He has a passion for this, so he won’t get bored. He also mentioned that being a small business owner, he rarely gets a holiday and so he will put this lockdown holiday to good use spending time with his family.

* * *

How many people are actually going to die from the virus? Is it really as bad as we think it is, or are people just overreacting?
I think this is so important to address, because the measures that are being taken are very extreme, and if things are not as bad as they seem to be, we might be putting our economy under a lot of strain for no real reason.
Do the benefits really outweigh the costs right now?
I think that many lives are going to be lost due to the lockdown. People will not be able to provide for their families if they are not working. Poverty is rife in South Africa and most people do not have a vast amount of savings to fall back on. This time is going to be hard for them, and there is a huge possibility that we could lose many people, economically active people, to things such as starvation and malnutrition.

* * *

The minister of health says we are allowed to go for walks but the minister of security is saying otherwise. Personally, I do not often go for walks, but lockdown is making me think that maybe that’s what I have been missing out on my entire life …
I am making a promise now that when the lockdown is lifted and we are free of Covid-19, I will take more walks.

* * *

Tomorrow the lockdown commences, and my family feels well prepared for it. My brother and I will be home and in isolation for the duration of lockdown. However, my parents are not so lucky. My father is obligated to work as his position in provincial government demands it. My mother is a health worker who has been tasked with the important duty of educating and coaching nursing services managers around the city in 60 clinics on the necessary procedures and measures that must be adhered to during the Covid-19 pandemic. Their jobs will keep them from home most days and put them at risk of coming into contact with the virus. They have bought masks and gloves to wear at all times while moving around. My mother should be provided with a mask at work, but masks are slowly dwindling as they have become very popular over the past few weeks. She has now decided to purchase her own reusable masks. My parents have assured us that they will be very careful.

* * *

Today I felt particularly anxious. Perhaps it is because the lockdown starts tomorrow night. […] I know that I have little to complain about: I am staying in a house with family that cares about me. Not all South Africans are this fortunate, especially not during times like these. I saw videos of the army roaming the streets of townships during the day and I could not help but think about similar photographs in 1985 after a state of emergency was announced in South Africa. Currently we are not yet in a state of emergency, only a state of disaster, but I can hardly see the difference.

* * *

Saw many old people out and about today. My one set of grandparents in Johannesburg don’t want to shop online. They are very set in their ways to do their shopping themselves, even though they are vulnerable. My other granny lives with us […] we are scared to infect her, so we have to speak to her and have tea through the security door.

* * *

Every Wednesday my boyfriend and I have date night, but this Wednesday we could not go out, so we decided to have our date night at home. We set a table with candles and my mom made us some spaghetti. My sister was our waiter and kept refilling our glasses. Later, we drove to McDonald’s to get our last McFlurry. It was so romantic; we didn’t even need a fancy restaurant.

* * *

Following the president’s address to the nation two nights ago, we received a communication that Stellenbosch University has had to extend the March recess by another two weeks. […] We are still unsure whether this means that we will resume contact teaching or if university will now operate online.
The thought of online classes is a bit daunting as nobody knows exactly what form they will take. This I suppose will also mean that students would have to work at their own pace and take their studies into their own hands. This could definitely be a struggle. There are usually a lot more distractions at home.

title: 26 March 2020
text:
In light of the impending national lockdown, President Ramaphosa called for a National Day of Prayer to be observed in the country. Further details regarding the lockdown also emerged, and these included the total ban of alcohol sales and the prohibition of exercise outside of homes. Thousands of South Africans attempted to leave cities in order to spend the lockdown with family and friends in rural areas. Once the lockdown commenced, public transport would be allowed to operate from 5:00 am to 9:00 am and from 4:00 pm to 8:00 am, and only to transport essential workers.

Today at midnight the lockdown starts in South Africa. My brother and I had to drive back to Cape Town to return our rental car. We didn’t realise that even the airport would close starting from 27 March. We arrived just in time before the rental car return closed and took an Uber back to our house in Cape Town. We have no groceries and no clean washing left […]. I start biting my nails when I’m nervous and today my teeth are sore from the biting. This whole situation has escalated very quickly.

* * *

The number of confirmed Covid-19 cases is increasing rapidly. I suspect that the virus is already in rural areas and informal settlements, but we just don’t have the infrastructure to test everyone. My friend and I called her mother in East London two days ago and she had no idea about the lockdown. When we got her up to speed, she denied the seriousness of the situation, saying that no soldier can stop her going about her daily life. This is the mindset of many people living in the townships: it’s a white person’s disease so it can’t be that serious for us. Also, what becomes of the people who don’t watch the news on TV and have no internet access? What becomes of the homeless?

* * *

I went to the shops today to buy some tea ( just tea, because I had run out). The shops were an absolute nightmare and it made me question whether the people of South Africa are really capable of complying with the rules of the lockdown. A lady in front of me bought 15 blocks of cheese, another quite literally ran past me, while yet another was stocking up on bread like there is no tomorrow … and all this when the president explicitly called on people to stop panic buy. A lot of people are trying to find loopholes to this lockdown. My thinking is that if people cannot work together for these three weeks, the lockdown will have to be extended.

* * *

A fellow work colleague (I am a part-time waiter at Eike Restaurant) is currently completing her Master’s degree in Neuroscience at Stellenbosch University. While she is loving the lockdown and the time she now has to spend with family, she is weary about the effect this situation will have on her career and that of many others. Her laboratory work for the past two months has had to be scrapped as a result of the lockdown, which means that as soon as the lockdown ends, she will need to work non-stop for the remainder of the year to complete her data work.

* * *

Today I woke up at 10:00 am. I received a bank notification to say that my R6 000 allowance had arrived in my bank account. I was pretty happy and had a little motivation within myself. I went to Spar to do grocery shopping but when I got to Spar, I did not find what I really wanted so I went to Checkers instead. I wanted to buy canned fish, canned beef, All Bran, corn, 6 x 2l milk cartons and 10kg of rice. I thought that maybe this food could last me through the 21 days of lockdown. It was worth R1 300 in the end.

* * *

This morning at 1:30 am I was still awake. My mother texted on our family group that they are moving her to ICU. I replied to her message to calm her down, but I knew that she would not be able to answer. After about half an hour I fell asleep. The next morning my father explained to me that they moved her so that they could check on her oxygen levels at all times. At 10:13 am my mother sent a voice note. In her voice you could hear all her fears. She urged us to clean the house and not to underestimate the virus. After that I sent a voice note to my mother praying for her and telling her not to be scared. At 2:00 pm my father and I decided to exercise. We had so much fun. I could feel the strain on my body because I have not exercised in a week. While my father and I were cooling down from our exercise my mother sent another voice note. She sounded happy, positive and ready to fight this battle. She said: “I hope you are all exercising because when I come out of here, I will come out running. I am ready to lead a healthy and fit life. There are so many adventures I still want to go on with you all.”

* * *

LOCKDOWN AS OF 00:00 am. The day that everyone has been preparing for has arrived. The panic buying is at an all-time high and what is rather humorous is seeing the long queues outside of liquor stores. Under the lockdown regulations, liquor stores will also be shut down and people seem to be very worried that they won’t have access to alcohol. I should admit that my boyfriend and I joined this trend and did our time standing in these queues. I heard the owner of the particular bottle store we were queuing at speaking to another customer. He said it was like double Christmas at the moment – which probably means he’ll be financially alright during the lockdown. […]
Our final ‘pre-lockdown’ plans are to get some KFC later this afternoon and to go for a coastal drive.

* * *

There seems to be a dystopic fog or gloom that hangs all around. The shops are already closed, there is no one frolicking in the bays, the roads are quiet, the land seems still.

* * *

It is the last day before lockdown starts. To obviously over exaggerate, I feel like an inmate just before death row. I know that the lockdown is not supposed to be that bad, but three weeks is a long time to stare at the same four faces every day. I checked in on all my friends and family to make sure everyone has a plan for lockdown and that no one will be left stranded at midnight. My cousin lives alone in Wellington, but luckily he could arrange with his firm to go home to Upington before lockdown starts. Everyone is doing his or her last bits of shopping. We refilled all our water bottles and made sure we have enough alcohol to last us for three weeks. We also stocked up on enough vitamins and immune boosters to last us the lockdown period. I went for a jog outside for what might be the last time in 21 days.

title: 27 March 2020
text:
On the first day of its lockdown, South Africa also recorded its first coronavirus death and its number of confirmed coronavirus cases surpassed 1 000. Meanwhile, in the US, coronavirus cases surpassed 100 000 and President Trump announced the country would acquire 100 000 ventilators in the next 100 days. UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson tested positive for the virus and began self-isolating at Downing Street. Cases continued to surge globally. More cities opened improvised morgues around the world. In Italy, a 102-year-old woman recovered from the coronavirus after spending 20 days in hospital.

We celebrated my gran’s 84th birthday today with cake and a little champagne. It felt a bit strange celebrating something on the first official day of the lockdown, but I believe that it made the day just a little more bearable.
I have quite a bad headache now and it is probably as a result of the sugar, but also because of all the anxiety that we are constantly exposed to at the moment. I cannot help but (irrationally!) think that I am ill as a result of the virus. Every little discomfort leads me to check the typical symptoms of Covid-19 sufferers.
Many people seemed to have ignored the lockdown and continued to go to shops (of course many people only received their payment today) – I wonder if it is going to continue like this if the army is going to be deployed to force people to cooperate. Ignoring the lockdown is seen as breaking the law and people can get arrested; I just cannot see what they will do with the people that have been arrested.
Earlier today it was also announced that the Prime Minister of the UK, Boris Johnson, as well as the UK health secretary, have tested positive for the virus. It is scary to think how many people they have been in contact with, all of whom are now possibly infected as well.

* * *

It is day one of lockdown and the streets are empty around my home. This made me proud as it means many have adhered to the warnings and decided to quarantine as instructed. I have received much conflicting or confusing information from the university during this period, but I believe that we will be having an extended holiday until online lessons commence on 20 of April. I’m thrilled! This gives me much time to mentally prepare myself for studying while at home. I have a feeling a lot is about to change for me. The country is changing, the world is changing, the economy is destined to change for the worse and my life is changing. I have decided that the best way forward is to ensure I keep myself informed on what is happening around the world and in my country.

* * *

I cannot take 20 more days of this. I need to get out for the sake of my own mental health, I feel trapped and caged. I do not know my own personality well but believe that I am generally a reserved person; my emotions tend to be masked around others. Only in brief moments of self-isolation do my emotions come to light and I address them. These moments of solitude provide me with personal insight and help me to de-stress and de-depress. I find I am the most revitalised after a long car ride to or from Stellenbosch. These car rides, or other moments alone, are when I can truly be vulnerable without having to put up a front or wear a mask. I find that now, even around my family, I still resort to the same defensive techniques. I fear that with this lockdown, I have no safe place to express my emotions.

* * *

In our house, today was all about Trump. My parents are quite tuned in to news about Trump and his shenanigans given that my sister studies in America. To quote The New Yorker, “The President‘s mendacious nightly press briefings on coronavirus will go down in history for their monumental flimflammery.”
Once again, I am reminded of the effect that sound leadership can have on a country during trying times: In contrast to President Ramaphosa, whose leadership and character are undeniable, the ‘Leader of the Free World’ makes spur-of-the-moment proclamations and creates doubt amongst his people.

* * *

Day one of lockdown. Our nation’s first confirmed Covid-19 death was recorded today. Rest in Peace.
Oddly enough, today just feels like a normal day at home. Perhaps it could be a particularly lazy Sunday or a public holiday. The streets are empty and the city is quiet, except for the police and army in and around the CBD [Cape Town Central Business District].
According to reports, in Langa and Nyanga, lockdown hasn’t been taken so seriously – videos have emerged of people loitering in the streets, attending social gatherings, going to the stores, and not really obeying the lockdown rules in any capacity. Also, in Yeoville, the police had to open fire on residents socialising and also questioned a News24 media agent.

* * *

Today is the first official day of lockdown and it feels like the beginning of a strange new era. Something that’s been bothering me is that the government has been granted access to data tracking in order to monitor the spread of the virus. This seems like a misuse of power and it also creates a very slippery slope. First of all, the data tracking could perhaps track one or two criminals, but what about the rest of the nation who are abiding by the lockdown? Furthermore, if government has been granted such broad power, these powers could easily be exploited and misused when the pandemic blows over. A lot of people have been arguing that there is often a trade-off between rights/privacy and protection, and while I do agree that it is true in some cases, the problem then becomes what if you lose both?

* * *

Today I genuinely had a great day. Who knew that there was so much to do in one’s own house?
I started the morning off with a lovely session of yoga with my mom. I personally have never been someone that is the biggest fan of yoga, but throughout this period of being trapped inside the space of four walls, I have really come to understand how some people can view yoga as an escape. It really allows you to open your mind and free your thoughts, while making you stronger and feel better.
My recent yoga has made me realise [that] I can be close minded about things and has taught me to open myself and try new things.
I read for a while, made myself a healthy breakfast and plucked up the courage to sit behind my desk and actually do some work. In a time like this where your days are empty and the clock seems to slow down, it is easy for me to get into my mind that there will always be time to do my work and catch up what I have missed. However, almost two weeks have gone by since university ended and I still haven’t managed to sit and work. So, I made today my day.
I learnt that being productive makes you feel better; efficiency is a good thing to practice.
After lunch it was time to set up my different stations, I gathered all the art supplies from around the house and all the gym equipment and accessories that I could find, and I put myself to work. I set up a station for my mom and I to do our art in the studio and organised a little home gym for the family.
And then I drew, and drew, and drew. And then suddenly it was dinner.
Art is my passion. If I had it my way I would be studying it, yet still before today, I could not remember the last time I had allowed myself to get lost in it to the point where I allow the hours to pass me by with little or no realisation. It was amazing, and I felt more like myself today.

* * *

I had a very different picture of how the next week or two was going to go and didn’t think a lockdown was on the cards. I do think that it is necessary and our country is taking the necessary precautions in the right time, it just feels so surreal though … like a dream, or more like a nightmare.

* * *

Today was the first official day of the lockdown in South Africa, and the measures taken have not exactly gone as planned. Many citizens carried on with their lives as if there was no order to stay home. Many people were arrested today in the Western Cape and Gauteng, including cyclists, runners, surfers and just normal pedestrians who were not out to buy food or medicine.
Alexandra seemed to be the biggest issue of the day; most people living in this informal settlement were found walking outside interacting with others like normal. In the news a resident was interviewed and said there was no point for them to isolate since they were already six to ten people living in a one-bedroom shack. The SADF were present and attempted to contain the situation but struggled as residents resisted which resulted in a few arrests by the military.

* * *

I don’t know how to describe today because it was kind of weird. The usual Friday energy that makes you excited that the weekend is here wasn’t there because I guess in a weird sort of way for the next few days every day is a weekend.
South Africa has had their first deaths as a result of Covid-19. My friend told me that she thinks the gravity of the virus will be felt in SA [South Africa] once there are deaths. Sad, but I understand what she means. For me, Covid-19 is a sort of mysterious virus. We know people are dying but they are also recovering. You can self-isolate it away, but it can also leave you in critical condition.
In related news, my mother thinks the shutdown is going to last until June … I really don’t want to think about that possibility.

title: 28 March 2020
text:
On the second day of lockdown, Gauteng was the province with the most active cases in South Africa. The UN secretary general called for a coordinated response to support developing countries in managing the virus and predicted that $3 trillion [USD] would be needed to provide that support. As countries around the world scrambled to put appropriate measures in place to curb the spread of the disease, fashion brands such as Burberry started producing masks instead of items of clothing. Meanwhile, those stuck at home started coming up with creative ways of keeping busy. One man in the UK ran 26.2 miles by doing over 1 000 laps in his small garden.

Unsurprisingly, day two of lockdown presented many of the same challenges as yesterday. […] Police were greatly outnumbered and were left looking foolish in their efforts to disperse crowds in populated townships. Informal workers do not have the luxury of staying at home and receiving paid leave; nor do they have the cash at hand or the space available to stockpile food. As a result, they have no option but to queue for hours to feed themselves and their family. Poverty fuels contagion. Contagion deepens impoverishment. However, the virus is not selective. When everyone is concerned with their own wellbeing, and risk and uncertainty is rife, the welfare of the vulnerable population is often neglected. We are only beginning to see the predicament facing developing countries. This is a somber thought considering that even the wealthiest countries have been unsuccessful in their efforts to restrain the virus. Death tolls are rising and the virus is yet to reach the poorest places on earth.

* * *

Today I really miss my friends in Cape Town. We have been speaking regularly, but it’s not the same as seeing each other every day and having a natural conversation in each other’s presence. Cellphone relationships versus in-person relationships are very different things, and I definitely prefer the latter. Desperate times call for desperate measures though, so this is how it will have to be until we see each other again.

* * *

My biological alarm clock has fully resorted to slob mode; mornings where I was conscious and concise at 5:00 am seem to be a distant memory. I only got out of my bed at around 10:00 am today, which is problematic given my recent tradition of having an hour nap in the afternoon.

* * *

Despite the fact that the country is in lockdown, I see people on the streets talking and listening to good music. They greet me as they pass, making me want to go out as well just to hear the music.
The university decided to extend the break to 20 April. I am a little displeased. I spend time reading ahead for all my courses but never quite grasping what I am reading. I shall find this time particularly hard for me. I am not a person who keeps contact with friends or individual[s] outside of my family, unless I want to find out something important. I fear that I am losing relationships that I have put a lot of effort into forming.
One thing I am starting to understand though, is myself. It is not nice when things that were distracting you from seeing what is problematic in your life suddenly stop. I do feel for those who have to return home to a father who beats them too often, or parents who are uncaring. This is sort of a time where people are forced to face the problems that they have been avoiding.

* * *

The class difference in South Africa has become very apparent over the last few days. While more affluent people could afford to buy groceries earlier this week, some South Africans living hand-to-mouth are still struggling to buy food and supplies. Across South Africa people are waiting in long queues, hoping to find what they need while endangering their health.
In other parts of Africa, military forces are using violence to enforce the lockdown. In Kenya, for example, military forces were recorded beating people with batons. In South Africa, rubber bullets were used to control a gathering crowd outside a supermarket in Johannesburg.
South Africa has recorded an overnight increase of 17 cases. Sadly, it was announced that 13 of the 1 187 infected persons are health workers.

* * *

As the sun rose early in Gauteng, I was still fast asleep. I have discovered a new tactic to get through this lockdown. I sleep until around 12:00 pm, wake up for breakfast, chill a bit, exercise a little bit and before you know it the day is almost done.
I spoke to my domestic worker who is staying with us during the lockdown. She sounded very stressed as she falls into the vulnerable category regarding Covid-19. After this chat, I began to understand just how privileged I am, especially during this time. I have food on my plate, fast working Wi-Fi and I live in a house where I have a lot of personal space.
For supper my mom made spaghetti and we prayed together that the nation and the world will get through this pandemic.

* * *

Today I do not feel better unfortunately. My body is sorer than it was yesterday and my fever is worse. My ears have also started to become painful at random times throughout the day. […] I am so scared that I maybe could have come into contact with the virus somewhere, maybe when I went shopping on Tuesday or even somewhere before that. If I did, my whole family is at risk of getting infected. With the numbers suggesting that older people and people with cardiovascular diseases are more at risk, I am really worried about my parents. But for now, nothing is certain so I’m trying not to dwell on the negative thoughts. If I feel worse in the next few days, I’ll contact a doctor; in the meantime, I’ll just rest and keep on drinking my immune boosters. And to be honest – aside from all the possible bad things that might come with having Covid-19 – I think it could be quite cool to say you had the virus that brought the whole world to a halt! Definitely a good conversation starter if you ask me.

* * *

My sister’s friend let us know that it doesn’t seem like there’s a lockdown happening in her area as the people are still walking around as if this virus does not exist. She lives in a rural area.

* * *

It still does not feel like we are under lockdown. It feels as if I have had a lazy long weekend. But the landscape around me is stark. I had slight cabin fever, so I went out for a drive, of course. I ran the risk of being pulled over by police, but I was willing to chance it. My drive took me all around the Atlantic seaboard of Cape Town. What stunned me the most was the number of homeless persons loitering in the street. Along a 5km strip, I counted roughly 200 displaced persons. This just goes to show how rampant general homelessness is in Cape Town. I feel very sorry for these people as they must already be very hungry as many of them rely on petty cash gained from begging. News outlets are claiming that the homeless should wait along the Sea Point promenade where they will be picked up by police and relocated.

* * *

Today is my stepsister’s birthday. Even though our parents aren’t married, we still tend to refer to each other as stepsiblings. She opened her presents and then we had a really nice breakfast to celebrate her birthday.
At the moment I am staying with my mom who lives on a golf course. The nice thing about this is that from 6:00 am to 6:00 pm we are allowed to walk around the estate. Who knows if this will last the full three weeks though?

* * *

This morning I slept in and only woke up at 10:00 am. At 11:00 am I used an app called Houseparty. My four best friends and I chatted on the app. We could all see each other and played games like trivia, heads up and 30 seconds on the app. For a moment it felt like they were here with me.

title: 29 March 2020
text:
In Mozambique, 60 people went missing after a deadly jihadist attack on the town of Palma. Amongst these were several South Africans, and rumours soon arose that the SADF would be deployed on a mission to rescue its citizens. Spain recorded 838 new coronavirus deaths while UK citizens were told to prepare for a ‘significant period’ of lockdown measures. The first major international research study into the treatment of Covid-19 was initiated by the World Health Organisation (WHO). The study, called Solidarity, began treating patients at the Oslo University Hospital in Norway and treatments to be tested included the malaria drug (hydroxychloroquine/plaquenil), the Ebola drug (remdesivir), as well as an HIV treatment (Iopinavir/ritonavir).

We’ve received emails from the university and from lecturers trying to gauge our situations in terms of internet access. It’s good to hear that the university is taking care to establish what our current circumstances are, but I am wondering what will be done to accommodate learners who genuinely don’t have any devices or internet connectivity – surely a computer plus internet access cannot be given to every student, and it would go against the guidelines of the lockdown to bring said students together where there aren’t the necessary internet facilities.

* * *

Coronavirus is causing a lot of death. I feel like it was a plan set forth by some evil people in the world who wanted to decrease the world population. My parents refuse to go to the shops. Not even for bread. They will only go when they feel it is really necessary. I am afraid that the toilet paper might run out.

* * *

Third day of lockdown. They haven’t released the number of new cases today. The government also only released 17 new cases yesterday, which is impossible. They say it is because of the delay in getting test results and analysing them and then releasing them to the public. I started the day off with live stream church. Think it is good families are praying to God together and seeking His word and advice during these tough times. I watched Netflix and played computer games most of the day. Time seems to go fast that way. I started a yoga challenge and practiced piano. Family did puzzles and boardgames together. I miss going out to restaurants and seeing friends on the weekends. The fridge is starting to look empty again and the snacks in the cupboard are depleting; almost time to go out to the shops for groceries again.

* * *

On this Sunday evening I am feeling a sense of deep gratitude for the privileged position which I occupy. I have a roof over my head, food guaranteed each day, two loving parents who do not abuse me (or any substances), two sisters to keep me company, the resources to keep up with academics and enough personal space. Many people are not so lucky and that thought truly saddens me.
The family unit, the basic building block for a functioning society and thus also the economy, is being restored in some sense, yes. But the broken homes, those affected by child abuse, social work cases and lawsuits aren’t being restored – and even though I know it would’ve been the case regardless of the virus, this just makes me extremely aware of how lucky I am, lucky to have this type of family and also lucky to know that all my family members are safe under one roof. Maybe the restoration of the family unit will bring about a realisation of what is actually important in life. This new found sense of compassion could replace the habit of exploitation we see every day in the business world. If not, humanity is more lost than I thought.

* * *

This Sunday we tried to keep the day as normal as possible. We obviously could not go anywhere, but we decided to have a good family lunch, discussing the effects the lockdown would have on small business owners and employees. We agreed that, with the first positive case in the township of Khayelitsha have been reported, stopping the virus could become more difficult. The township is densely populated with bad sanitation. It would, therefore, not be surprising if more people in townships test positive in the next few days. It is important for the government to take action.

* * *

Even though today is a Sunday, I feel extremely guilty. It has been a week and a half since coming home from university and it seems like I have not been able to do any work. Although I did try to go through a few chapters from some of my modules, I do not know if anything has really sunk in. Speaking to my friends, going through Twitter and other social media platforms this seems to be a common thread. Quarantine has ignited a productivity obsession and we all feel like we are failing miserably at it. From articles and posts that discuss how some of the greatest writers, artists and innovators created some of their best work while living in isolation, to us feeling like we have more time now than we have ever had and ever will have, people seem to be putting a lot of pressure on themselves to write that novel, learn that instrument or get ahead with work.

* * *

Today it dawned on me what a negative economic impact lockdown will have on South Africa. I saw a video of a convenience store being ransacked and I can’t help but think that this lockdown may be more harmful than helpful. As much as South Africans hate to admit it, we are still a third world country. Can we really sustain a period of no work, no economy at all for three weeks? I doubt we can without there being very serious consequences. My reservations may come from the fact that I am Zimbabwean and I know that circumstances can actually get worse even for those at the lower end of the poverty scale in this country. Perhaps, though, my thinking has also been influenced by my typically cynical (and probably right to be) economics lecturers who have taught me that even before this crisis, the projections for South Africa weren’t good. Either way, I think it is important, especially economically thinking, to be aware of the costs that may be incurred as a result of this lockdown.

* * *

Our church is now being held online. It felt weird, but this whole situation is weird. We all just sat in our lounge in front of the T.V. During the first half we were all still having our breakfast. Not good, I know, but yeah. We do feel more relaxed though because we can finally wake up a little bit later. It is a more relaxed life; we work around the house, and it feels like the earth is telling us to take a break. I think this is how people in the past used to live, without much competition.

* * *

The first case was reported in Khayelitsha today. When I imagine the effects of this virus on townships, for some reason the image I conjure up is that of a domino falling and then seeing the whole township fall down. CNN did a cover on townships in SA not adhering to lockdown rules, but the reporting seemed so one-sided. It didn’t delve deeper into why people weren’t isolating; just that they weren’t.
How can a family of six stay in a one-bedroom shack? This was the question posed by one of the residents in the report. The profile on the township just angered me. Not because they weren’t adhering to the rules but the fact that people couldn’t understand why they weren’t. When looking at lockdowns in townships, how can we get angry that people are not adhering to the rules? They live in confined spaces with limited resources. If I’m going through mental hoops every day in the space that I have, I can’t imagine being in their situation. […] To be angry, in a way, would not only be naive but ignorant of their circumstances over and above the commonality that we all share – the virus.

* * *

Today I woke up at 10:00 am. My brother and I walked to the nearest Woolworths. We only saw about ten people on the way there and maybe eight inside the store. It feels like one of those movies where a zombie apocalypse hits earth, and all the towns and cities are deserted. It’s actually a bit scary. I wouldn’t feel safe to walk to the store by myself.

title: 30 March 2020
text:
South Africa reported its second coronavirus death and recorded a total of 1 280 cases. To aid those collecting social grants, public transport times were extended for one week. In the US, President Donald Trump announced that stay-at-home guidelines would remain in place until the end of April, although initially it was hoped that the economy might be up and running again by mid-April. In Massachusetts, 11 veterans died in a care home for ex-soldiers. Five of them tested positive for coronavirus.

Tonight President Ramaphosa spoke on TV, and even though I only caught a little bit of his address, I liked what I heard. He thanked all the essential workers, called them our “unsung” heroes, and encouraged the nation to continue practicing social distancing. I think this speech boosted morale, and the fact that he took the time to give such an address even though it wasn’t critical, really shows character.
I said that I was going to start ‘working’ today, but we ended up having a Harry Potter movie-marathon instead. I constantly find myself judging my actions if they don’t really add value to my life in the form of academic knowledge (general knowledge, new literature, knowing more about world affairs), but I’ve made peace with the fact that I am okay to sometimes just watch movies the whole day.

* * *

Today it came to my attention that there are only 4 000 ventilators in the South African private health sector, and around half that number in the public sector. Multiple solutions are being investigated since ventilators are essential for treating critical patients and preventing the mortality rate from escalating. This is a huge concern for South Africa and all of its vulnerable people, the majority of whom will probably need critical attention.

* * *

Another day in lockdown: no excitement at all. All I’ve been doing is eat, sleep and being busy on the phone. I tried doing some schoolwork but I can’t concentrate, and I know I should be using this time to study and prepare, but it’s very hard to focus as I’m constantly worried. I’m worried about my bursary; I’m worried about my family back home. […] I must say this pandemic messed up my finances, I used to have a door-guard job at res and now because of this pandemic at my res there are no door-guards shifts anymore. So, because I don’t have a job, I have decided to go back to Forex. I have been busy with a demo account for a month now. Initially my plan was to trade with a real account from 1 April, but because of this pandemic, I’ve been advised to wait. However, over the coming days, I’ll see what’s happening on the market. I’ll do some technical analysis and check the news as well. I usually watch the news, but lately I feel like I’ll end up being depressed so I limit myself.

* * *

This morning I woke up and checked my phone. I had received some amazing news. My mom’s test results were back. She tested negative for the coronavirus. The doctors said that they are waiting for her lungs to recover and then she can come home. I am so thankful for every prayer our family has received. In this time so many people supported us. My mom is the first patient in South Africa who has been to the ICU for the coronavirus and has tested negative.

* * *

Today was not much different to the last three days, though somehow, I did manage to be quite productive. I must say, it is a very confusing time to be a student. We have already completed a large portion (though not the majority) of the semester, but I have personally only handed in one piece of written work so far. I am wondering if we will be tested on the topics we have already learned, or whether I should be trying to study or to learn ahead.
As I am writing this, I realise that must be how it is for everyone right now, […] interesting times to say the least. Another interesting thing to watch is how the world is trying to stay connected to each other during this time – though there is a kind of singularity about it. I am referring to the world of social media. I have been off social media for about three months now, but my friends are still on it, and I see them trying desperately to let the world know that they are still alive, or maybe to use a better word, relevant. What a time to be alive.

* * *

President Cyril Ramaphosa addressed the country tonight. He didn’t give much news, but I think the government is working hard to fight the situation. I hope the economy doesn’t suffer too much. The government might struggle to borrow more money to cover its expenditures, especially in difficult times like this. Apparently, there were two more deaths today in South Africa. People died while collecting their social grants. This is heart breaking, as the reason they got the virus is probably because of poverty and the myriad of problems that it creates. First case recorded in the township; this is surely bad news. I am finding it hard to keep faith.

* * *

This is so insane. I woke up this morning feeling basically completely better! I have all my energy back again and the fever and body aches are gone. I am quite relieved that it wasn’t something more serious.
I feel like today I have been in one of the best moods that I’ve been in for the past two weeks! I spent most of my day playing outside with our dogs and just enjoying being in the garden. I played tennis with my father and my brother which I really enjoyed – the exercise really helps to make me feel like I am doing something meaningful with my time!
My parents are both working from home, but even though we are all in the house the whole day every day, at least we can all get some time ‘apart’ from one another. Not that I don’t want to spend time with them or anything, but it can become too much for me sometimes.

* * *

I went for another drive today. I enjoy the headspace of being able to see some motion and a changing landscape. It feels quite historical as I drive around the deserted streets of the city. I noticed that there are still many refugees in St. George’s square, in the CBD [Cape Town]. I am wondering what will happen to them – they have no access to basic resources and the streets are incredibly unfit for habitation. Furthermore, there are still a large number of homeless persons walking around – I’m not sure that the SAPS has been very effective in relocating them to central locations. […]
Ramaphosa addressed the nation again this evening. He said: “Using mobile technology, an extensive tracing system will be rapidly deployed to trace those who have been in contact with confirmed coronavirus cases and to monitor the geographical location of new cases in real time.” This may sound like a very positive thing, but to me it’s terrifying! I have an aversion to being tracked and using such systems seems very similar to George Orwell’s 1984. It also begs the question: if they have the technology readily available, surely they’re already doing it? I am sure it will help with curbing the spread of the virus, but I do not believe it is strictly ethical.

* * *

I woke up to my laptop pinging with my calendar notification: “END OF RECESS, TERM 2 STARTS TODAY”, and I found myself just staring at the notification for a while. I wrote that notification into my calendar in January. My routine has changed so much and so quickly. I accomplished the first academic goal of lockdown: finishing one of my English seminar novels. It took me an obscenely long amount of time to read the book. But nonetheless, I have achieved my goal. I’ve always thought myself to be quite a goal-oriented person, but during this time I am finding it hard to set goals for myself. It has been suggested to me by multiple people that one way to stay sane during quarantine is to set clear goals for yourself … but how do you set goals when time seems so indefinite?

* * *

The purpose of today’s diary entry is to share my opinions on the implementation of the police and armed forces to curb the virus. I feel that police searching vehicles and people on the road is important because we have to ensure people are not unnecessarily outside. A video on social media is circulating where people in the area of Delft (Cape Town) were dispersed by the police by using water cannon[s]. Even though it was a large crowd, people argue it was not necessary. Many other stories have surfaced saying that the police force has been too aggressive. To see the other side, there have been areas in South Africa where people have been roaming the streets with no reason and refusing to listen to the police. In my opinion, we do not want a situation where the people and the police are divided as it will result in panic, violence and most likely more positive coronavirus cases.

title: 31 March 2020
text:
The South African Government announced that it would launch a mass testing initiative, which would include health workers going door to door in some communities to monitor the prevalence of Covid-19. Opposition parties called for the army to act within the law at all times amidst reports of brutality and the use of excessive violence from members of the SANDF. Hand washing and sanitisers became the focus of attention in the fight against the virus as various organisations, health workers and famous people produced videos on how to wash hands properly. A chemical firm in the UK built a hand sanitiser production plant in ten days which had the capacity to produce up to one million pocket-sized bottles a month.

Today started extraordinarily. I woke up with my family at 6:00 am to exercise. For the first time in our family’s history we exercised together! I was helping my dad with certain exercise and my sister was helping my mom. We then all went to go enjoy breakfast together and I started with a diet (the banting diet). After breakfast we all went our separate ways. I logged onto my PlayStation account and played online games with my friends. They all feel just as trapped as I do within the confines [of their] respective homes.

* * *

Lockdown continues. I have resumed my university studies. I went through some of my summaries and continued to add to them. I really want to be dedicated to studies as I think the country needs hard workers to get it out of the mess it is in and I want to be a part of that […] but it can feel sort of pointless to work during this time as there is no certainty or finality regarding when this whole situation will be over. I think everyone is going to come out chubby and hairy after this ordeal.

* * *

As I mentioned yesterday, this whole lockdown is getting more and more depressing with each day that passes. I miss my friends and the student life we had in Stellenbosch. Being locked inside doesn’t feel natural and I am very bored. My siblings are getting more annoying now that we see each other every single day and can’t get away from the house for some privacy. Additionally, I feel very tired the whole time. I sleep more than I normally do, but somehow, I don’t feel fit during the day to do much. I take every chance I get to help with chores or cooking. The more things I can do the less bored I am and the quicker the day passes. It’s sad to think in this way. Counting days until everything goes back to normal. Now I regret missing out on plans I cancelled before the lockdown, and I appreciate the times we were able to go outside and see our friends and attend lectures.

* * *

Today I committed two criminal offences – I went for a swim and I walked my dog. Saying that feels incredibly weird because these are two very ordinary activities! I recognise that it was not the best idea, but I have become incredibly restless and I am craving interactions with nature. I find myself staring with binoculars, looking at Table Mountain, Lion’s Head, and Signal Hill. Usually, I swim at the beach (on average) three or four times a week. When I’m at home, it’s closer to five or six times. Not being able to get out into the ocean is really impacting my psyche, as pathetic as that sounds. In the grander scheme, this is a really nice problem to have; I am incredibly privileged that I am not worrying about food, water or safety.

* * *

I felt extremely unmotivated and a bit lacklustre yesterday. I managed to go for a run every day (fortunately we have a treadmill in our house), which I am very grateful for. Not getting enough exercise and not being able to move around really does contribute to feelings of frustration and hopelessness – I can hardly imagine what someone sitting in alone in a small apartment must feel like during times like these.

* * *

I began my day by waking up to the gentle sounds of rain. The rain brings a sense of calmness; it feels as if it is washing away the stress and anxiety I have felt for the past few days. Today I started working out trying to keep my view and mind from clouding. The mood in the house seems to have calmed down a bit. I made some breakfast for my family today, started to catch up on a bit of work and worked on one of my assignments. […] All in all, it was a productive day.

* * *

One of the positive things that has come out of this lockdown for me is the fact that I have more time to strengthen my relationship with God and spend more time with Him. I’ve really enjoyed being able to extend my quiet time. I think that’s also kept me really calm throughout the whole situation. I’m not saying the virus isn’t a scary thing, of course it is. It’s completely unfamiliar and we’ve never dealt with something like this before, but I have faith in God, and I think that has just given me a lot of peace during this time.

* * *

Today I woke up at around 7:00 am and ate a breakfast of All Bran. I then had to go to campus with my iPad for internet access since the internet coverage in my apartment block is not good. I went and stood outside the mathematical sciences building where there is good Wi-Fi and downloaded the work I needed to. I then went to Pick n Pay to buy some fried chicken. […] In the evening I watched some of the history documentaries that I had downloaded earlier.

* * *

Today I spoke to one of my closest friends via Facetime. She is one of my biggest inspirations – one of those people who have an endless capacity to give. She inspires me and challenges me intellectually. We love thinking together and sharing interesting thoughts, and today’s conversation was no different. The ultimate conclusion to our discussion can be summarised as follows: development is caused by the imminence of problems that arise around us and the eagerness to solve them.
Most people deal with the problems directly facing them at a given point in time. Fewer people identify potential problems and put plans in place to conquer them in the future – these are our innovators. It is our belief that, in order to slow down the speed at which our problems come crashing down on our world, and in order to minimise the effect of these boulders, we need to inspire more innovators!
It all starts with education. Education should not be reflected by how many degrees the average person in a country has. Rather it should be seen as how many people can read in order to gain knowledge, create ideas, develop existing ideas into even better ones and how many people can translate these ideas into actions. I believe that this concept is more relevant than ever before where we all are now sitting in our own corners of the world topping over life and how to make it better.

title: 1 April 2020
text:
Taxi associations in South Africa threatened a nationwide strike in response to the lockdown restrictions that only allowed taxis to operate at 50% capacity. Gauteng still had the most active coronavirus cases. The Western Cape had the second most active cases. The investment ratings agency, Moody’s, downgraded a number of state-owned enterprises to sub-investment grade. Countries around the world planned attempts to repatriate their citizens. The Zaandam cruise ship sailing towards the Florida coast had 83 passengers and 136 crew on board exhibiting flu-like symptoms. The ship also reported that eight passengers had tested positive for the coronavirus and four passengers had died, although the causes of their deaths were not known.

I’ve missed the last few days of reflections on account of my mental health … being home for extended periods of time presents some challenges, like not having any time or space to myself. This experience has revealed to me that I’m not very adaptable, and in times of stress, I shut down. The lockdown has been difficult for me (and many people across the globe, I imagine) in that sense.
I’ve had to start taking my antidepressants again. We can’t pacify ourselves with alcohol, tobacco, drugs, food and whatever else in the same way we did before the lockdown.

* * *

Even though I had nothing to do over the past few days, I have been very lazy! I find that hilarious and disturbing at the same time. On one hand, having nothing to do makes you anxious and keen to get going, on the other it encourages lethargy. The days are starting to merge into one. […] My regard for time has gone out the window.

* * *

There are 16 days left until the ‘end of lockdown’, but from the knowledge I have gathered from news, statistics and my parents, I really don’t see that happening. The economy is struggling, businesses are losing money by the minute and profits are dwindling, unless you count supermarkets and essential service providers. Even pastors are struggling and have had to shift their thinking. Most churches require people to congregate regularly, but that has become impossible. Today I spoke to a friend of mine whose parents are both pastors. Covid-19 has forced them to close their church. This means they cannot preach to their church members in the traditional way. Instead, they have had to go online. This has proven difficult because people are so used to interacting and praising in person. Attendance at online services has been less than they hoped, and their salaries have dropped drastically.

* * *

Today I experienced, more consciously than ever before, just how dependent the world is on the internet. The absence thereof is truly an impediment on our ability to execute our daily tasks. This is because our Wi-Fi is not working. We can’t seem to fix it, and due to lockdown regulations, cannot even get a technician in to fix the problem. The only temporary solution we have is for all five of us to share my personal Wi-Fi modem that I got when Inetkey at Stellenbosch University was still a very expensive item on a student budget.

* * *

I found today to be a rather mentally challenging day. Up until now, I have been very good at remaining positive and optimistic about the future and dealing with lockdown, but today that energy wasn’t there. I really felt claustrophobic and overwhelmed when I came to the disappointing realisation that we have only been in lockdown for six days. I miss my friends more than ever. I miss my boyfriend. I miss my family. I miss the beach and the outdoors. I miss going for an innocent jog around my neighborhood. Yes, I am staying in contact with these people in my life through face time, phone calls and messaging, but it’s just not the same. I am craving human interaction.

* * *

Yesterday I was watching the CNN News Channel around noon. They were just beginning to cover a story (in America, of course) about a single mother of six children who had previously won her battle against breast cancer. Her children became worried after their mother began showing severe symptoms related to the virus. They rushed her to hospital. Two weeks later she passed away as a result of Covid-19. The children’s father had passed away in 2011.
Due to the strict regulations imposed to control the spread of the virus, the family had to say their final goodbyes via walkie talkie, whilst looking at their mother from behind a glass screen.
Although not quite the same, my family too has felt first hand the effect of such regulations. Five weeks ago, my mother underwent a hysterectomy, and after many complications, it was discovered she had arrhythmia (an irregular heartbeat). Yesterday we took her to the hospital to have a cardiac ablation procedure. Due to fears of the spread of the virus, not one of my family members was allowed to accompany my mother into the hospital or to see her before, during and even after the surgery. This was very scary.

* * *

Wednesday – otherwise known as Hump Day, since it’s the middle or peak day of the week – called for a lazy day, so my sister and I slept till noon and didn’t do much else with the day. Spending time with the family and appreciating each other has become something of the norm and I’m quite enjoying it. This much time without any new stories is prompting my parents to tell old stories from when they were our age – some are very relatable, and others are just plain interesting.

* * *

I didn’t really think about what is happening in the world today. It almost feels as if I have lost contact with the outside world, and I am living in my own world. The isolation has become my reality […] so much changed in a week.

* * *

There are few things as satisfying as when your cash flow statement balances … at least when you are in lockdown and have to walk into the same rooms and see the same people every day. This morning I started my Financial Management project that I have been putting off for longer than I would like to admit. The feeling of having accomplished something – even if it is just having finished half of a section of a three-section project – is a feeling I welcome. There is one feeling that I hate more than anything and that is the feeling of aimlessness. Unfortunately, the past few weeks have been filled with feelings of aimlessness and to accomplish something small like balancing a cash flow statement or getting up and doing a small at home workout really helps me to get through the day.
I have been ploughing through books, and this afternoon, I’m going to try look for some interesting reads and download new books instead of anxiously checking the news every five seconds. Twitter has been both a blessing and a curse in this time. It allows for quick transmission of news which helps when I would like updates on the latest news that other online platforms have not yet published, but on the other hand, because it is such a ‘fast’ space, it generally makes me feel very anxious, so I have been trying to limit my time scrolling through my Twitter feed.
One thing I am grateful for is that I am not currently in America. This is always my sentiment but at the moment, with Donald Trump in charge of managing the Covid-19 outbreak, I feel gratitude particularly strongly. In a matter of a few days, they have managed to top the list of international Covid-19 infections which I find a little worrying.

* * *

It’s April fool’s day today. I’m hoping that tonight the government will make an announcement saying that the whole virus pandemic was just one big April fool’s joke, but maybe that is a bit of stretch. Currently the number of infected nationwide stands at 1 353, and the number seems to be gradually increasing. Today is the sixth day of lockdown, there have been a few people who have tried to ignore the lockdown rules, but the police force and army seem to be enforcing the law. There have been some instances where the police and army have been seen abusing their power; this could lead to a huge unrest among the people if the situation is not dealt with as quickly as possible.

title: 2 April 2020
text:
After initially increasing the capacity of taxis to 100%, the Minister of Transport, Fikile Mbalula, decreased the allowance to 70% of capacity. While South Africa experienced a slowdown in infections, with only 27 new cases on this day, globally, coronavirus cases neared the one million mark. France, Italy, Spain and the US were the first four countries to report over 4 000 coronavirus deaths. In the UK, 10 000 coronavirus tests were being conducted a day, but Health Secretary, Matt Hancock, announced that this would be expanded to 100 000 tests a day. This announcement came as health officials in the country expressed frustration at a lack of progress in increasing the number of coronavirus tests.

Today was a day of resting – resting my mind, my body and shutting down my natural instinct to keep busy. I truly believe that once in a while, in order to regain strength and to boost future productivity, we need to rest. This concept can be expanded to the whole economy. This lockdown and the shutdown of the economy can be seen as a resting period in which we can choose to repurpose ourselves, regain strength and regroup in order to put back the broken pieces of our world in a more effective way than before.
That being said, there are people who are not experiencing rest or time to regroup. Our medical professionals were called to the frontlines in this war against the coronavirus and for them, this is no time of rest. It is thus our job to pick up the pieces of our economy while they make life and death decisions and put themselves at risk to save the people of their country. And this is not only the case in far off in Italy anymore. According to recent accounts from South African doctors (and medical interns), this fight has come home. Our people are also starting to die.

* * *

“Everyone has it inside themselves this plague, because no one in the world, no one, can ever be immune.” – Albert Camus, La Peste.
About a week before classes were suspended, my French class was assigned Albert Camus’s The Plague. I thought it fitting, but at the time would never have been able to imagine how eerily similar our situation would be to that described in the novel. The story opens with a description of an ordinary world with its inhabitants leading busy, distracted lives. Then out of nowhere rats start dying in their masses and soon afterwards, the inhabitants themselves become infected with a virus. Camus wanted to highlight our fraught mortality – the idea that we can, at any moment, be randomly exterminated.
Instead of allowing this realisation to cause despair, however, it can lead to a renewed appreciation of our humanity. Instead of being absorbed in our day-to-day activities, this pandemic has brought everything to a standstill, forcing us to take a step back and re-evaluate what we want to prioritise (family, our physical and mental health, hobbies that add meaning to our lives etc.). A ‘plague’ is not something backward that belongs to history; we as a modern, technologically advanced society are equally susceptible to its devastating consequences. If there is any philosophical meaning we can draw from these events, it must be this: there is no escaping our frailty.

* * *

Lockdown day seven. The amount of infected [persons] globally continues to rise on a daily basis. In my opinion, though, the coronavirus pandemic is not as big as the world is making it seem. Looking at the number of deaths worldwide and the number of infected persons, the percentages are actually relatively small. Personally, I think that the only reason people are fearful is due to the fact that the virus spreads unbelievable quickly and endangers those with weak immune systems. In situations in which people feel that their lives are threatened or in danger, they will also try to protect themselves and all the values we were taught – such as respect, kindness, help those who are suffering, etc. – are going out the door.

* * *

One week down, two to go. I can’t decide whether time has gone fast or slow. The days feel extremely long, but then when I sit back and realise it’s already been a week, then it feels like time is passing by quickly. I don’t want to sound negative or that I’m wishing time away, but I do want these next two weeks to be over as soon as possible. I really do miss my pre-lockdown life and routine. I know that I will most likely never have this much time for myself again, and I should utilise it to my best advantage, but I really can’t wait for things to be ‘back to normal’. I put that in inverted commas because I don’t think life will ever be as normal as it was when we come out of this. This pandemic has certainly changed our way of life and also will impact our lifestyles in the future.

* * *

I have been noticing that as the days go on, I am waking up later and later. I hit a new record today and woke up at 12:00 pm. Pre-Covid-19 this would have really worried me, but at this point all I can say is: it is what it is.
I ended the day with a much-needed phone call with a friend where of course the main topic of discussion was the pandemic. As she is from UCT [the University of Cape Town], we compared notes on how our different universities are dealing with the crisis. She said that from now on, for the foreseeable future assignments would be graded PASS/FAIL, not specific marks. So far, Stellenbosch hasn’t said anything similar, but things could change at any moment.
We also spoke about what the pandemic meant for our futures. She seemed quite optimistic, but I (having fallen into another YouTube rabbit hole earlier that day) was not so optimistic. We will be entering the working force next and having to deal with the repercussions of this pandemic. Suddenly my future didn’t seem so exciting and filled with possibility – just incredibly scary. So as not to end the conversation on a sombre note, we promised ourselves that once this pandemic was over, we were going to take hold of every opportunity that presents itself. I will go to the next wine tasting!

* * *

With each passing day, my enthusiasm weakens as I come to write. I have started to resent my previous days’ work as I all too easily come off as a pretentious pseudo-intellectual.
Though sitting on my growing resentment, I managed to get a bit of work done; my statistics project is looking promising.
I also managed to stumble upon Gil Scott-Heron’s Comment #1, which may in fact be the highlight of my day. Though I understand Gil Scott-Heron wrote this poem in a different time for different people, it gave me much to think about as I listened to it on repeat. Sadly, these journal entries are not meant for poem reviews, so I will slickly and quickly try to mention one line that hit close to home. Gil Scott-Heron instructed a “pale face” SDS [member of the group Students For A Democratic Society] student to find his own revolution, as the students fight in the revolution cannot be compared to Gil Scott-Heron’s struggle. Gil Scott-Heron aims to acquire the basic luxuries that the students most likely already possess.
It made me question what real struggles I have really faced growing up as a middle-class straight white guy in South Africa. I latch on to other people’s revolutions because of the luxury of not needing to fight in any of my own. No struggle. My only fight is my own psychological one.

* * *

I was looking at good stock picks on the JSE [Johannesburg Stock Exchange] today. Every disaster can be an opportunity and I intend to make full use of this opportunity. I’ve been looking at buying Woolworths for a while now. They have a new CEO, and although their financials are in a dire condition, at the current discount they’re trading at, I believe the buy is worth it. I don’t think they’ll collapse or liquidate themselves. Another good buy could be the banks. On top of the stock market crashing, they’ve taken a beating from the downgrade recently. Capitec looks like the most attractive option. I don’t think I’m going to buy just yet, though, I think worse is still to come, and I plan to time this perfectly.

* * *

Today marks the [end of the] first week of lockdown. In light of this, we did a family fast. We had a good praise and worship session before we broke our fast. Straight after that I had a Bible study video call with two of my friends. It was so good to see them and just be able to speak about our experience with this lockdown from a Godly perspective.

* * *

I am starting to find a good rhythm during lockdown. I think my balance between work and play is solid. I had an educational conversation with a friend regarding the coronavirus. We discussed whether the government has an accurate way of measuring the effectiveness of the lockdown. One obvious answer is by tracking the number of new cases per day in South Africa. […] My biggest concern is that the government will only focus on the number of people who are infected and not [those] affected by the virus. Small businesses will crumble and people living day-to-day will need to take drastic measures in order to survive. Although the spread of the virus needs to be contained, it is important to realise that not everyone can survive more than three weeks without a salary.

* * *

I was watching a programme on a news channel today. They were discussing conspiracy theories regarding the coronavirus. All these theories relate to China creating and/or spreading this virus. It will be interesting to see what happens once all of this is over. My mum is very vocal with how she feels; she thinks that all the countries should ban or boycott any trade with China because she is convinced that China did this purposely for economic power. I do not know what to think.

title: 3 April 2020
text:
On day eight of lockdown, the South African government announced the relaxation of some measures. These included the reopening of spaza shops (and other informal food traders) and allowing the relatives of deceased persons to travel interprovincially. The BBC lauded South Africa for its swift and efficient response to the virus, but also questioned some of its methods, saying “South Africa seems to have acted faster, more efficiently, and more ruthlessly than many other countries around the world”. The US had the highest number of infections in the world, but Italy had the globe’s highest death toll. In China, restrictions tightened amidst fears of a second wave of infections.

There have been some days where I have deemed it appropriate to say nothing much really happened. But today, when I say nothing happened, I mean absolutely zero happened. This lockdown period has really shown me what it means to have nothing to do. […] I have tried to be ‘productive’ and learn about music theory, study a bit of philosophy etc., but I find it difficult to find inspiration in anything when I am consistently looking at the same walls, eating the same food and seeing the same two friends (the fact that I am lucky to have friends to see is even more disturbing).
I am second guessing my decision to stay in Stellenbosch and in South Africa in general. I am Zimbabwean, and although I know that at home I would already have been butting heads with my parents, life might be a tad more interesting at least.
It may seem that I am writing with an undertone of sadness, but that isn’t what I feel at all. The word should be indifference. I am simply indifferent about everything right now. This must be what happens when you don’t have any choices in life. Not sad, angry, frustrated or happy, just indifferent. It is a very weird sensation to notice.

* * *

Today seemed to fly by. I attempted to clean my room but didn’t get very far, but I guess it is better than nothing. I also spent some time doing some academic work and planned a new project for myself. I feel like I’m slowly starting to get used to this and everyday seems a bit more normal than the last. I feel like I have completely distanced myself from what is going on right now. I am living in my little bubble and don’t hate it. Sometimes I watch the news, but I find being unaware of the stats and what is happening is better for my mental wellbeing than being completely consumed by the news, which is how it was for a while.

* * *

I’ve noticed that more and more people in our neighbourhood are starting to come out of their houses, not in a way that is breaking the law, but rather by utilising their gardens and driveways more. We live in a crescent, and because of this it feels a lot more interactive. Everyone can see what is happening on the opposite side of the crescent. I like this because it reminds me that people do still exist. It is very nice to hear kids playing and laughing. I enjoy silence but can only handle it for so long. This time must be so tough for people living alone.

* * *

Cabin fever is a real thing. Lockdown is starting to get to me psychologically and emotional. Being so far from my friends and having to adjust to home life again is taking its toll, but at the end of the day I do realise that lockdown is necessary and only for my benefit.

* * *

We are living through an incredibly difficult time. Our lives have been placed on hold and we have no idea what the future will look like.
Even with no guarantee of the future, I am still grateful for our president, Cyril Ramaphosa. Unlike many presidents across the world (e.g. Donald Trump), our president has come forth as a formidable leader, exhibiting the characteristics of compassion and composure. He has been efficiently imposing restrictions that are aimed at ensuring the safety of all South Africans.

* * *

I am starting to suffer from cabin fever. I decided to take my chances and to walk 10km along the [Cape] Peninsula. It was an incredibly good idea because it was an amazing release and it put me in better headspace to be active and specially to see the sea. Despite many police vehicles patrolling, not a single one stopped me or even looked twice – a few even waved hello to me! This makes me question how seriously the authorities are taking the lockdown in certain areas and how flexible the rules actually are…
Previously, I voiced my concerns over the safety of refugees living in St. George’s Square in Cape Town. They have since been evicted from the Methodist Church they were staying in, and they travelled by bus to Belville. Here, marquees have been set up for them to live in and be provided with basic resources and amenities. The action was taken on the basis of health and safety concerns.
The government confirmed again that you may not buy cigarettes. They did say it’s just “for now” though. The number of cases in SA has now broken the 1 500 mark and the number deaths have jumped to seven. However, experts (both local and international) are praising South Africa for its swift and extreme approach, keeping the number of deaths and the rate of infection low.

* * *

For the first time since its inception, I participated today in clapping and whistling for those going out to work. I had initially decided not to do so as I didn’t want to mindlessly follow a herd mentality, but today I whistled as hard as I could at 8:00 am. If felt therapeutic.
I wonder if the apocalypse were to begin tomorrow, and the lockdown were therefore to go on indefinitely, would these cheers become the new form of church? Or take over another form of social integration? It produces a simple pleasure knowing that you are not alone; there are other families too outside the four wooden fences encompassing your home.
I think I have mentioned it a few times before in this diary, but I am really missing the outside world. My house has never felt so much like a claustrophobic environment. I miss the feeling of getting lost in places and finding new spaces. I think most of all I miss unfamiliar faces.

* * *

My friends and I discussed the Covid-19 virus over the phone. There were many ideas floating around about how the lockdown will affect the economy and if it will completely stop the spread of the virus. Current times are very uncertain, and it is very difficult to predict what next week will look like, much less next month. I strongly believe that the lockdown is a necessary measure in slowing the spread of the virus and helping the long run economy. I also believe that an extension of the lockdown will slowly begin to destroy the economy. Yes, we must stop the spread of the virus because, if half of South Africa get infected, our economy will collapse. A strong counter argument is that, if we extend the lockdown too long, then the majority of local businesses will go bankrupt. The government needs to analyse these arguments and decide on a middle ground. The economy will collapse if either of the extremes are adopted. The government is faced with a difficult decision. Do they risk the health of the nation by lifting the lockdown restrictions? Alternatively, do they risk the future of every non-essential business in the country?

* * *

The health minister has made plans to make 60 mobile testing units available across South Africa in order to help ramp up daily testing. Without efficient testing the government will never grasp the full image of the virus and will struggle to implement effective strategies to help combat its spread. The number of cases continues to rise. The deputy minister of health also mentioned that the government is struggling to get access to the necessary medical supplies needed for the health workers on the frontline. […] 17 people have been arrested in Johannesburg for not complying with the lockdown regulations.

* * *

Today I woke up at 7:00 am. I had laundry to wash and a room to clean. I began my day by making a hot lemon solution and after that I did my laundry for two hours. I prepared myself a breakfast of jungle oats and fresh milk, and then started making my meal for the day. I was planning to prepare rice, beetroot, chakalaka and beef stew. I started with the rice and then went to Checkers to buy canned chakalaka. When I got home, I changed my mind and made fried fish instead of making stew to save time. I prepared the hake and when I was done, I invited my friend […] for lunch. He brought some Fanta Orange to drink with the meal.

title: 4 April 2020
text:
The rand weakened after Fitch Ratings agency downgraded South Africa’s credit rating. According to Fitch, one reason for their decision was the lack of a clear path to stabilise government debt. The funeral of renowned South African author and sangoma, Credo Mutwa, was held on this day after his death on 25 March 2020. In the US, shortages of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) meant that medical staff had to look for different ways to protect themselves. Rain ponchos and garbage bags were suggested as replacement surgical gowns.

It has been raining in Johannesburg for nearly four days straight, which means that sitting outside is now also not really a possibility. According to the weather report, however, the rain should clear up by the end of the day and the sun should be out for the coming week. I can feel the weather getting colder, which means that winter is around the corner. I am actually grateful to be home during this time because I find it quite difficult to cope with bad weather when I am staying in my residence room. On the other hand, the new season is not good news for the spreading of the virus. Apparently, it spreads most easily in colder temperatures. Of course, South Africa is now only starting to feel the effects (according to the statistics the numbers are still quite low, but the authorities are only managing to test 5 000 people per day).
