I went grocery shopping today and of course the streets were deserted, apart from the occasional car on its way to buy ‘essential goods’.
How goods are classified as essential or not baffles me. No alcohol is allowed to be sold. Cigarettes are also not allowed to be sold, but surely the lung damage cigarettes cause cannot be reversed in 21 days. I do not really see the logic in it. Also, would a prohibition on cigarettes not just lead to a spike in black market dealing, especially in informal settlements? I suppose we will only be able to tell after all this is over.

* * *

This morning when I was doing my chores, I casually looked up and out through a window facing the street. I saw one of my neighbours outside on their front lawn. It was a really weird moment because it seemed somewhat unreal to be seeing another person in the flesh.
Today my dad decided to bake coconut bread. It was quite weird. He’s never really been one for baking, but he loves cooking. I guess everyone’s trying out things they wouldn’t usually do, however big or small those things might be.
This evening, my parents decided to bring out the tennis table. This table tennis board had been sitting in the garage probably since we’d moved into this house, which was 2015. So, this was a momentous occasion. Evidently, they were trying to find new things to do.
I’ve also noticed how the initial conflict between my family, which was the result by being confined to the same space for a prolonged period, has decreased. We’ve learned how to live with and around each other during this period by giving each other the space that we all need.

* * *

I have not mentioned this before, but my aunt is a nurse. Fortunately, she is a paediatric nurse; there have been no reported cases at her place of work. My heart still aches for her though. She comes home every morning complaining about the ill-treatment nurses are getting. She says that hospitals are refusing to spend money on protective equipment. They were instructed to use only one mask per week.

* * *

Today my thoughts were filled with the uncertainty of what next year brings for me, provided I graduate this year (which I am on track to do but the lockdown may have an effect on). […] I know that this is something that will have a huge impact on my life, so it is only natural to be lost thinking about it for hours at a time, especially when there isn’t much else to do. I did realise that a lot of the ideas I had for my life, starting next year, were contingent on the world that existed before this global lockdown. And it dawned on me that the world probably will be completely different after this. After all, this is the first time in over 50 years that something has really shut down the whole world, and certainly the first time in my lifetime. I am still excited to get out into the real world, similar to the feeling I had after high school, but at the same time the world could be different in so many ways that any ideas I have now might turn out to be obsolete. […] My mind is all over the place.

* * *

One of the unintended, but surely expected, consequences of the national lockdown is a surge in reports of gender-based violence [GBV]. With no chance of escaping one’s abuser, South Africa is one of the most dangerous places for a woman to be right now. Victims have fewer opportunities to seek help and less support is available to them. This trend is not unique to South Africa but can also be seen in other countries that have initiated lockdowns. China saw the incidence of GBV (and other domestic conflicts) fuel divorce rates after the quarantine period. Couples may be stressing about job security, financial health, teaching their children and chores to name a few things. It must be true that distance makes the heart grow fonder, and I wonder if South Africa will see the same effect on marriages.

* * *

Another cold, wet day … I found myself incredibly sad today. […] I don’t know how to describe it, but it just wasn’t a good day. Then top it all off, my mom said her “insider sources” have confirmed that it is definite that the lockdown will be extended. I was too annoyed to ask for more information.
I’m trying to break up the monotony of my days but it’s kind of hard. I didn’t think I would say it so soon, but I really do miss Stellies [Stellenbosch]. I miss seeing lots of people (even if I don’t know who they are). I miss complaining about res food and vowing not to eat another res meal ever again. I miss going to polo practise and fighting about who should have scored a goal in a game. I always thought myself an introvert, but this lockdown is really showing me otherwise.

* * *

Today I woke up at 8:00 am determined to study, but how can I study without proper internet connection. My main problem is that, to access SunLearn, I will need a proper internet connection, but right now I don’t even have a phone. I think I will need to talk to [friend] later about buying a phone, but what if the market for phones is closed in the current situation? […]
A friend told me about someone selling an iPhone 6 for R2 000. I had to take the offer. Now I have a phone to call my relatives.

* * *

The arts are grossly undervalued for the impact they can have, not only on the mental state of people, but as a medium of expression, protest and inspiration. Many entrepreneurial pursuits are either birthed from or inspired by art, and thus one can argue that art is a necessary driving force of the economy.
Being a creative myself, I became acutely aware of how people gravitate towards the arts during difficult times. I am part of various creative communities who have all initiated different projects during this nationwide lockdown to ensure the continuance of the arts and also to ignite or rekindle an appreciation for such things.

* * *

The Western Cape government plans on moving thousands of people out of informal settlements in [an] attempt to de-densify areas. However, many residents are refusing to leave and opposing the plans for logistical, social, financial and emotional reasons. I don’t think that the government’s plan is viable. There are still many homeless people on the street that the police were supposed to relocate. I also believe that help should start at the bottom levels and work upwards, and that initial promises should be delivered on. Thus, protecting the homeless population should be a priority, and the previous statements need to be supported through action.

* * *

Today, on the ninth day of lockdown, I have decided to limit the amount of time I spend reading Covid-19 news. Since I have been home, I have developed the habit of spending hours reading the news and watching related videos. Staying up to date is very nice, but this is obviously fuel for anxiety.
Speaking of news, today I read an article based on a speech by Akinwumi Adesina. Africa’s public debt is estimated to increase above $2 trillion [USD] as a result of the virus. […] Seeing how developing countries are struggling to keep afloat during this time is shedding light on the vastly different lives that people live. On Twitter, I see many American celebrities saying that we are all in the same boat when we are clearly not. The virus might not specifically affect those of a certain race or class, but in fighting the virus we are not on an equal playing field; money and power helps.

title: 5 April 2020
text:
Gauteng province still had the highest number of cases in South Africa. UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson was admitted to hospital for Covid-19. Kobe Bryant, the basketball player who died in a helicopter crash in January of 2020, was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame. While Melania Trump was tweeting about the value of wearing masks to combat the spread of the coronavirus, President Donald Trump stated that he would only wear one if he ‘thought it was important’. Italy recorded its lowest Covid-19 death rate in two weeks.

The weather has been really gloomy today which has made me feel quite demotivated. I feel like I am in a constant battle between wanting to be aware and up to date with what is going on, but at the same time wanting to completely distance myself from it all and to retreat into my own little world where I can forget what is actually happening. It feels lonely removing oneself from reality, but being part of it is kind of scary.

* * *

As a student, a big part of my life is socialising. While I am smart and capable of excelling at university, for me it is more important to make human connections. You cannot go through life alone, regardless of the amount of knowledge that you have.
As it is quite likely that lockdown is not only going to last for these three weeks, I’ve realised a big chunk of my university period is going to be scrapped. This leaves me thinking about all the people I am not going to meet and all the opportunities that I will miss.
And I am not the only one. The whole country is in the same boat as me. The opportunity cost of lockdown is immeasurable. I am still sitting here wondering if this is the right choice in the long run.
It definitely makes sense currently. A lockdown is needed to flatten the curve and to get protective equipment into place so that our healthcare workers are. However, once we have managed to achieve this, I think it would be wise to start opening the economy.

* * *

We happened to be sitting around our outdoor table, basking up the sunlight, while a chicken-potjie was brewing over the fire. My younger cousins and brothers were swimming and bouncing about on the trampoline. Us adults were having a fully-fledged (and highly competitive) game of 30 seconds. Not quite the scene one would expect during a global pandemic.

* * *

I saw a Zapiro comic today commenting on the fact that, since the lockdown, the South African police have killed eight more people than the actual virus itself (N.W.A. music intensifies). I found it weird that this shocked me. Maybe I have been turning a blind eye to the news, but I should not be so naïve to assume that crime stops because society does. I also read a tweet predicting that Home Affairs is going to be drowning in paperwork when this lockdown is done because of an exponential rise in the divorce rate as a result of people having been quarantined with their partner.
On more personal news, I learnt Morse Code today. It was simpler than I expected. […] Hoorah for me, if I am ever captured by ISIS, I can blink something in the propaganda videos they produce.

* * *

Day ten of the national lockdown. Today I woke up and felt differently to how I have felt on the other days. I felt discouraged and without hope. I examined the statistics online and saw no hope for the next few months. I do not know how the world will recover from this … people are dying all over the world; the economy is in shambles; my father’s pension that he has worked so hard for over the years has decreased by 30%. […] At dinner I could see the pain in his eyes, but he was keeping it together to look strong in front of his family. Today has been an eye opener for me and, emotionally, the worst day of the lockdown.

* * *

I celebrated my birthday today. I am twenty … twenty! It is at least good to know that I shall not be dying soon. I don’t feel death creeping up on me yet, and I have not been out of the house. I have not chatted to anyone on social media. It feels sort of good to not feel pressured to please people.

* * *

Today has been the first sunny day in quite some time and I am so grateful for it. Every day seems to melt into the next, making it increasingly challenging to distinguish them. The South African statistics seem to be staying the same and I think that is more worrying than seeing large numbers. At least then we would have been closer to knowing the truth. I also think that the peace and quiet we see around us (in my neighbourhood) is deceptive and a far cry from the actual current situation in the country. Over the news there have been some reports of violent encounters between the police and the public, but no major cases have come to the forefront yet.

* * *

At the end of February, my boyfriend’s parents went on a work-related trip to Italy, Spain and Germany. They arrived in Europe without any problems but left ridden with disease. After returning to South Africa, they immediately went into self-isolation. Tests revealed them both to be positive for Covid-19. […] Luckily both are still feeling well and showing barely any symptoms, but they admitted to having sleepless nights worrying that things might change for the worse. […] Realising that I know two vulnerable people infected with the virus has changed my perspective.

* * *

I haven’t written for a few days, but there has been absolutely nothing to report. I’m starting to really miss varsity life. I miss physically walking from one class to another, I miss grabbing coffee with my friends, I miss being surrounded by people, I miss the walk to campus and the mountains around me. I’ve read a lot of posts lately that basically says if you’re privileged, you don’t get to be sad about this. You don’t get to miss your normal, privileged life when there are people currently locked in their houses with abusers or with ten other people living right next to them. At the risk of sounding extremely selfish – I disagree. This pandemic has changed every single person’s life, and whether we are locked down in luxury or in less-than that, every person deserves some time to be sad, to miss their old life. However, I do think that with this privilege comes an obligation to not rub your privilege in others’ faces; an obligation to be humble about what you have and an obligation to be sensitive to the situations of others.

* * *

A distant family member of mine has tested positive for Covid-19. I haven’t had any contact with her or anyone that has visited her. She is in hospital now, although we do not know for sure what condition she is in. This news has made me realise that anyone can be affected by this virus. I knew it was spreading in South Africa, but it didn’t feel real until today. We often take our own health for granted.

title: 6 April 2020
text:
50 people were arrested for attending a wedding at Nseleni near Richard’s Bay; those arrested included the bridal couple, the pastor and some of the guests. Boris Johnson was moved into intensive care as his symptoms worsened. To curb the spread of the virus, Chile announced that from 8 April 2020, it would be mandatory to use face masks when travelling on public and private transportation in the country. In the US, the State of California suspended all evictions and set a $0 bail for minor misdemeanours.

Today was the beginning of a local sanitising drive in Stellenbosch. Stellenbosch’s Municipality Water Services began disinfecting hotspot public places in an effort to combat the spread of Covid-19. The Kayamandi and Bergzicht taxi ranks were washed and scrubbed with sanitising solution. There were many teams of people all dressed in protective suits and accompanied by a water truck filled with the sanitising solution. The areas that were disinfected also included Plein Street, Andringa and Merriman Street where I live.

* * *

A very blue Monday this morning. Lockdown is starting to affect my whole family and there is an underlying tension amongst us. I am worried about my family’s future. My father is a lawyer, and his firm will suffer big financial losses if the lockdown is extended. Many countries overseas have extended their lockdowns, and this is a very real possibility for South Africa. I am also stressed about our academic year. I seriously cannot extend my studies by another year.

* * *

Had another chance to leave the house today for [the] purpose of dropping essential food items at my Ouma (grandmother). On the drive, I noticed that the grass on the sidewalks had become overgrown. The roads were petrifyingly quite; it felt more like driving through the outskirts of Winterton, a farming town, than through Meadows, a Pietermaritzburg residential area.
On passing another car I received a friendly greeting, followed by a look which seemed to say good luck. On the way back I stopped to fill up the car with diesel. A petrol clerk with his mask on greeted me in a friendly manner. My overall analysis of the trip outside is that the place looks deserted, yet people are careful and in a weird sense caring and friendly.

* * *

When I woke up this morning the latest stats were: 1 655 confirmed cases and a total of 11 deaths. It is very difficult to see how well South Africa is doing with regard to flattening the curve. We are definitely in a better position than many other counties (e.g. the US, where the daily death toll is at a global high), but people say it is just a matter of time before the tsunami hits us. I’ve read articles saying that our curve hasn’t even begun and that we have no idea what we are in for yet. Very scary and pessimistic things to think about, but what if these predictions are right? What if a 21-day lockdown isn’t enough and that if it is only after the lockdown, as we continue with our lives, that the real catastrophe happens?

* * *

We rarely get the chance to listen to Queen Elizabeth address the UK, and indirectly the world. Last night, exactly this happened. In her address the Queen thanked health workers on the front lines and urged citizens to remain at home. […] If the weight of the situation was not felt before, it certainly is now.
Meanwhile, across the pond, America is having its worst week thus far. The death toll continues to rise and some states like Louisiana are running out of ventilators. President Trump keeps changing his story. After boasting about re-opening after Easter, he has now backtracked, acknowledging the threat that the virus poses.

* * *

There are ten days left until the nationwide lockdown will be lifted. I am not too sure how to feel about it. Will the coronavirus be contained by then? How will we know who has it and who does not? There are people walking around that have the virus but are showing no symptoms? How do we avoid mass transmissions?
The police and army have been deployed to patrol the streets and ensure that the restrictions are being respected, but they have been performing their duties in a rather thuggish and disrespectful manner. Shooting, beating and humiliating civilians who are not heeding the president’s calls.
[…] We are currently experiencing the calm before a devastating storm. There is a need for quick but efficient decision-making that will ensure that we are not left worse off once the storm hits. We need to prepare for the battle that lies ahead.

* * *

For me, the biggest frustration is the absolute uncertainty that we are constantly living with. I hate uncertainty and I think others do as well. That is why we make to-do lists, create a productive ‘self-isolation study/work routine’ and do at home workouts day in and day out (or at least try, and then beat ourselves up when we cannot stick to it). At the risk of sounding very existential, I believe that this pandemic is making us come face to face with the idea that not everything can be planned, has meaning or is particularly significant. I wish I could end off on a positive note or try to see a deeper meaning to the crisis that our society is currently facing, but I seem to be unable to do so now. I am feeling a bit hopeless and frustrated and stuck, unsure of where we are headed and when this will all come to an end.

* * *

Today we’re getting into coronavirus conspiracy theories. I used to be a fan of watching all genres of conspiracy theories at ungodly hours until I was swallowed by the flat-earthers and developed an intense paranoia. Dark days indeed, but [I] digress.
These are just a few theories making the rounds: China developed the virus to eliminate unproductive (elderly and overweight) members of Chinese society; the US developed the virus as a biological warfare agent to be used against China; coronavirus is spread through 5G frequencies (an actual lol [laugh out loud]); and the emergence of Covid-19 was predicted by author Dean Koontz in a novel published in 1981. That last one is quite tempting to believe.
Conspiracy theories can be fun until they’re used to support racist ideologies and policies (US, I’m looking at you). I would have imagined it to be common sense for political leaders not to perpetuate harmful, unsubstantiated claims like some of those I’ve mentioned, but China and the US have shown me to be wrong. What would the result have been if these countries stopped trying to discredit each other and joined forces against a common enemy instead?

* * *

Many high-earning stakeholders around the world are slashing their salaries in order to help pay staff their more humble allowances. This has been seen in football clubs – with players foregoing large portions of their salaries – and other institutions. Today, Woolworths announced that senior executives would be taking 30% pay cuts in order to help those “who find themselves in extreme hardship as a result of the current crisis”. Mr Price also stated that “annual salary increases for head office associates have been delayed until further notice” and that its “executive management and board of directors have committed to a cut in salaries and fees”. These are highly appreciated sacrifices, but they raise greater economic questions.
How and why have we created a system wherein fractional pay cuts for the elite are able to fund a majority of bottom-earners?
South Africa has some of the most disproportionately spread levels of income distribution in the world. […] Will the global pandemic exacerbate inequality in the country, or could it end up operating as an economic leveller?

* * *

Today I woke up at 7:00 am. I washed my face and brushed my teeth. Then I called my friends so that we could go to campus and fetch the food parcels that we had heard about. When we got to campus, I met one of my oldest friends. He was giving out the food parcels. The parcels consisted of oats, soup and a packet of noodles.

title: 7 April 2020
text:
The UK government reported that Boris Johnson was in a stable condition. Switzerland experienced a rise in cases, making it one of the countries in Europe with the highest incidences of coronavirus per capita. The US reported a total of more than 10 000 coronavirus deaths. Almost half of these were in New York, where funeral homes were overwhelmed because of the increase in demand for funeral facilities. China, by contrast, reported no new deaths from the coronavirus for the first time since January. In New Zealand, the health minister was demoted after breaking lockdown rules by driving his family to the beach.

Lockdown has proved irrefutably that modern living is too privileged and without struggle. I wondered at first if this was a generational thing (i.e. that our generation has gone soft), but then changed my mind as it seems to be result of exogenous factors.
My point being: I, along with many of my friends have found lockdown to be a terrible bore. A waste of time. A lesser punishment of sorts.
I am only a few weeks into lockdown, yet I seem to complain as if my father was Josef Fritzl himself.
I would hate to be insensitive by comparing my mild inconvenience to the situation of Anne Frank but shall for the sake of argument [do so]; Anne lived in an attic for two years, without luxuries such as Netflix or YouTube. Modern middle-class living, though, has evolved to include constant entertainment.
I guess what I am trying to say is the consumer standards have resonance beyond simply making us sufficient in our own homes. I feel like the government has put me in time out.

* * *

Today is my grandmother’s 77th birthday. She lives in Durban, and we would have gone down to see her for this weekend (and for Easter). She is incredibly upset that we can’t be with her, and I think it’s a perfectly valid feeling to have on one’s birthday. I would be upset too. I’m just glad that her and my grandfather (who will be 84 in June) are actually taking this virus seriously and not leaving their home unless it’s for essential business (which, today, warranted buying a cake).

* * *

Today was such a good day. I finally learnt to bake something. I made Hertzoggies [a South African desert], some with jam and some with caramel. They turned out pretty well, but I had no idea baking something from scratch could take so long. I now understand why my mother doesn’t bake as much anymore. I took me nearly the entire day to make 54 Hertzoggies. In a family of five that means around ten each. […] I put each person’s share in their own container. I’m not sure about other households, or whether this has anything to do with us being coloured, but whenever anyone makes anything, there’s always one person who doesn’t get enough. So, in our household we divide everything equally so no one can complain, and when your share is finished, it’s finished. My mom also made soup and bread, which is my absolute favourite in this rainy weather.

* * *

I cannot believe it has been 22 days of not seeing the outside world! I don’t know; it feels like it has been forever already, but on the other hand it also doesn’t feel like almost a month has already gone by. Today is also my 20th birthday – I have no doubt that this will be an unforgettable birthday, even if it’s not necessarily the most exciting. […] My mother made me spaghetti bolognaise (which is one of my favourite dishes) and my sister baked me a cake. They didn’t have any gifts for me because they didn’t expect me to still be here on my birthday and they couldn’t go to the shops after finding out, which is totally fine – I really had an amazing day and everyone made me feel special which was more than enough for me!

* * *

I happened to watch a report by a journalist on Sky News today that pertained to South Africa. Cape Town gangs have called a temporary truce and are spending their time taking meals to households that need them the most. Many of these poverty-stricken families are unable to obtain food items because of the nationwide lockdown. These neighbourhoods are regarded as some of the most dangerous in the world due to the constant gang-related violence. Both civilians and gang members are killed during gunfights daily. Despite their good deeds, there is no justification for portraying such gangsters in a positive light, no matter the circumstances. They may have stopped shooting at each other, but just this morning there was an attempted hit on prominent Cape Town lawyer, William Booth.
Around 240 fewer murders than is usual have occurred in South Africa during this two-week period. The lockdown is certainly saving lives, but maybe not in the way it was intended to.

* * *

I did not manage to get any work done today and I felt very demotivated. […] The only confirmation that we have received from the university is that online classes will start from 20 April. We do not know when or in what form our first assessments will take place. All this uncertainty is driving me crazy.
Next year’s plans also feel very up in the air. The current third year BCom (International Business) students will not be going on their exchange semesters this year, which means that they will have to go during the second semester next year (when we are supposed to go). I wonder if this will influence our options (only a certain number of students per university are allowed). I am also very worried about how the semester will be funded – financially my family is not functioning optimally, and I do not know if a year will be enough time to turn that around.

* * *

I expected myself to feel greater fear of missing out on ‘life’ during lockdown. However, I almost feel peaceful knowing that the rest of the world and the country are in the same situation as me. Nothing much is happening within these four walls, but beyond these gates, there is a subdued but bubbling world.
I have taken to driving as a means of respite. Lone, windy afternoon drives around the Cape Peninsula. During my meander through Hout Bay, I noticed that the inhabitants of Imizamo Yethu informal settlement are not adhering very strictly to the lockdown regulations (although, who am I to judge as I drive past?). It was interesting, nonetheless, to see children going about their normal lives – many were skateboarding in the streets and a large group had occupied themselves with a game of pavement football.

* * *

We are heading towards the end of the nationwide lockdown. The number of coronavirus deaths has increased to 13 nationally. The number of confirmed cases in the country has reached 1 749.
The talk of the town at the moment is the Minister of Communications, Stella Ndabeni-Abrahams. She is said to be in trouble for breaching the lockdown regulations. A picture of her and the Higher Education Deputy Minister, Mduduzi Manana, and his family, was taken and posted on social media during lockdown.
It makes it extra difficult to enforce the regulations and encourage South Africans to respect them when an elected minister fails to do so [themself ].

* * *

Today was a day filled with work as we decided to buy large beef rumps and to cut up pieces for biltong to snack on for the rest of lockdown. I think this is an essential on most South Africans’ shopping lists. At the start of this lockdown, I really thought food might be scarcer due to panic buying and a possible lack of supply from very badly affected areas and countries, but it seems most food items are still found quite easily as farms and other businesses in the food sector have been allowed to carry on meeting demand. Finding medicines and immune boosters is still difficult though, as many people are hoarding these products.

* * *

When I woke up there was no electricity. My phone and laptop were dead and it [was] pouring rain outside, so I really had to think hard to come up with alternative activities. I decided to make pancakes on our gas stove for breakfast. Not only were they delicious but making them was also so much fun. I then went down to the stream to do some morning yoga. Once I was all stretched out from the yoga, I decided to start a puzzle. This puzzle was 1 500 pieces and had been in our house for about ten years. However, it has never been finished. I decided this was a prime time to change that. Having no electricity and nowhere to go really encouraged me to get up and do something productive and this made me realise how distracted we usually get by social media.

title: 8 April 2020
text:
President Cyril Ramaphosa, on a visit to the Rand Water Office, said that the pandemic provided an opportunity for the country to speed up service delivery. A team of 15 Chinese medical officials arrived in Nigeria to deliver $1.5 million [USD] worth of medical equipment to the country. At this stage, cases in Europe were doubling every three to four days. A panel of prestigious scientists told the White House that warmer weather would not make the coronavirus go away. Singapore banned all social gatherings, while in Wuhan, China, a lockdown of two months was lifted, and people were allowed to travel out of the city. Travel authorities expected 55 000 people to leave the city by train in a single day.

Another day spent with my family, us all on our individual zoom meetings. I had a res mentor meeting today where we discussed how we will be carrying on with our mentor sessions (with first years) during the lockdown via social media platforms and face time, zoom, etc.
Prior to the meeting, I found myself really excited to see all my fellow mentors. They form a big part of the ‘family’ I’ve made for myself at university and being apart from all of 23 of them has been strange. I went from seeing them every day, to not at all.
But seeing them via zoom, whilst extremely heart-warming, was also quite sad. It reaffirmed how much I miss them and the crazy chaotic energy that ensues whenever we are all together. The meeting confirmed, for me, that even though technology is amazing, it does have its limitations.
The organic nature of face-to-face communication is lost, and in some ways the conversation is stilted. I found myself grinning profusely whenever someone would speak about what they had been up to (which for most of us is not that much) and just wishing I could give everyone a hug.

* * *

I read this brilliant article from the New York Times today about what impacts the coronavirus could have on the world economy. A few things stood out, but the most interesting point was about the future of working from home and how it’ll affect women. Due to the large amount of people now beginning to adapt and working from home, it’s assumed that working from home will be easier and more socially acceptable in the future. Who will this help most? Women, especially those with small children. Hopefully Covid-19 can have at least one silver lining by enabling women to earn greater equality in the workplace.

* * *

‘Klein Saterdag’ [Friday] has lost all meaning during lockdown. I do not think I have ever gone this long without seeing my friends. […] The future of every student is uncertain at the moment, and we are all waiting for the next state of the nation address.

* * *

The number of positive Covid-19 cases in the Western Cape is now sitting at 510. Since the authorities rolled out the community screening in areas such as Paarl, Blackheath, Khayelitsha and Bo-Kaap, more than 3 930 people have already been screened in the province. It is good to see the government working swiftly to combat the virus and to detect its early spread within more vulnerable communities. South Africa is still struggling to source PPE from suppliers, [with] there being an overwhelming demand for such equipment worldwide.

* * *

I received an update today from the university telling us that we will be finishing the rest of the semester online, and that we will only have a two week break in July. This is something that will have a huge effect on me for obvious and not so obvious reasons. Obviously, learning and assessments will be completely different and will no doubt influence my ability to pass and graduate in one way or another. Not so obviously, though, this probably means that universities know something that we do not about the future of the country. They are projecting [that] we will need to do tests online well into July, despite the fact that this lockdown is meant to finish in the next week or two?
In other words, the lockdown will probably be extended. […] Something I can’t stop thinking is the possibility that because I am graduating in the very year that this is happening, my degree may end up being less credible than that of previous or future years. Online assessments are not the same as invigilated assessments.

* * *

Bheki Cele discussed the ban on alcohol and cigarettes yesterday. He noted that, since banning the sale of alcohol, there had been a major drop in crime, and that Groote Schuur hospital has experienced far fewer trauma cases. However, as I previously theorised, the ban is costing the government millions each day; without the sin tax revenue that alcohol and booze bring in, the government is losing just shy of R150 million per day.
I think this situation presents a catch 22 for policymakers, not just now, but also for the long term. It is clear that removing booze from the social equation is a positive thing (it makes for less crime and fewer trauma incidents), but it costs the government vital revenue. We find ourselves at the crossroads between ethics and economy … Can we even afford to choose at this point.
[…] I received an official communication from Stellenbosch University. Our testing and teaching policy has changed, with all classes and assessments moving online as of 20 April. I worry for those students that are in compromised environments or situations. The university has come up with a device loaning policy to help mitigate some issues, but I see a few logistical issues arising, especially surrounding network strength and access. Furthermore, the environment for some students may not be conducive to studying effectively.

* * *

I woke up this morning eager to have a productive day. I showered and went to go sit behind my laptop. I started with my Financial Management project and really got work done. After I finished with my work, I went downstairs for brunch. Afterwards my dad asked me to mow the lawn. For me, this was a first because my family has always been privileged enough to employ a gardener. I went to fetch the lawnmower from our storage facility and spent about 15 minutes with my dad trying to figure out how to turn the lawnmower on. After we finally got it working, I used my knowledge from movies to mow the lawn. It took me 45 minutes to cut the grass in the back garden and 30 minutes in the front garden. I could tell how impressed and happy my parents were that I was doing some work around the house. I finished just before sunset and went straight to supper.

* * *

Yesterday’s weather persisted. This morning was overcast, and the high today is 15 degrees [celsius]. The bad weather brought with it the bad news of a potential lockdown extension. Medical experts have commented on the likelihood of an extension, noting that South Africa is about to go into the winter flu season. This is likely to bring about some confusion as Covid-19 symptoms are similar to normal flu like symptoms, adding extra strain to the country’s healthcare system.

* * *

Despite claims that the ban on alcohol is reducing crime rates, many liquor stores in the Western Cape have been looted. Such actions undermine government’s efforts to curb the spread of the virus.

* * *

Last night after a very productive schoolwork day, I was thinking about trying out a four-day week to see if I would actually be more productive than working a five-day week. My only decision was whether I would be taking Wednesday or Friday off. That decision was made for me by my dad when I was woken up to help out in the garden since our garden servicers aren’t operational during the lockdown. I learnt how to mow the lawn (which requires a lot more strength that you would imagine, especially since we live on a hill), and how to use a weed whacker, among helping with other things. I must say it was quite therapeutic for the mind to be outside and actually moving around, instead of cooped up inside studying, reading or watching T.V.
After that morning of hard work, and also deciding today would be my day off from studying, I was in the mood to use the oven, and so my mom suggested I bake bread. Keeping in mind that I have minimal culinary skills, the end result was quite impressive, and the loaf didn’t last a full 24 hours before being finished by the family.

title: 9 April 2020
text:
On day 14 of lockdown in South Africa, President Cyril Ramaphosa once again addressed the nation and announced a two-week extension to the initial lockdown of three weeks. With 440 infections, the city of Johannesburg continued to be the epicentre of the coronavirus pandemic in Gauteng. In Cape Town, criminal lawyer William Booth survived what appeared to be an assassination attempt on his life. The first of thousands of British tourists stuck in South Africa began their journey home. In an attempt to stop the virus from spreading, Cuba suspended all forms of public transport, including taxis and buses. The city of Honolulu in Hawaii introduced a curfew just before the Easter weekend. The curfew prohibited most people from driving ‘anything with a wheel’ between 23:00 pm and 5:00 am each day.

Today, as we ended the second week of lockdown, our family fasted again. During our time fasting we prayed for the country, our leaders and all those that are still working to accommodate and protect us. We also had a little family meeting. My parents have been doing Bible study together and discussing the different roles in a family, and they wanted me and my sister to give our input. It was actually the first time I got to speak openly and honestly about my thoughts on how they have parented us. I think this lockdown has really created more time for us to have these conversations. We’ve also been spending a lot more time together.
President Ramaphosa addressed the nation at 8:00 pm. He announced that the lockdown will be extended by an additional two weeks. I am not surprised, as the number of Covid-19 cases has continued to increase despite the lockdown. The growth rate has slowed substantially though, from 42% in March to 4% currently. As much as I’m disappointed about not being able to see friends and family, I’d much rather see them in healthy condition after all this is done.

* * *

I woke up extra happy and excited this morning. There would have been exactly seven days left of lockdown and I had so much planned for when things got back to normal.
The first thing I wanted to do was return to Stellenbosch, because although I have been enjoying spending time with my family, I could really do with some quiet and fewer domestic interferences once online learning starts.
Deep down, though, I knew none of the things I wanted to do was going to be possible. In his national address this evening, the president announced a two-week extension of the nationwide lockdown. I assumed that there would be an extension, but I must admit that I was disappointed that my assumption had become a reality.
Although we are all disappointed, I believe it was a smart decision made by our government. At the end of the day, we all know that the government is fulfilling their duty to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all South Africans.

* * *

I took a walk to the shops today (about 1km from the house). If I’d known it would be that easy to move around with no questions asked, I’d have started grocery shopping every day for one item at a time weeks ago! I was nervous that I’d be stopped by police or the neighbourhood security, but they didn’t give me a second glance. The atmosphere at the shopping centre was something out of a Stephen King novel, but it was the most eventful experience I’ve had in weeks. I was disappointed, however, to find the Beacon chocolate-covered marshmallow eggs SOLD OUT the day before Easter. Under normal circumstances, those things last until June!
A student reached out to the leaders of the Stellenbosch University [SU] Anti Gender-Based Violence movement seeking refuge from domestic abuse. We sought help from university structures and tried to direct her to different institutions and shelters, but we weren’t very helpful.
The extension of the lockdown was certainly expected, although nothing short of disappointing. It dawned on me that, eager to get back to my life, I’ve been naively optimistic about the situation.

* * *

My question today is: is the coronavirus a biblical plague that will be the end of civilisation? The virus has now infected over 1.6 million people worldwide and killed over 95 000. Every time I check the new statistics, I am astonished. China was brought to its knees back in January when the pandemic hit the city of Wuhan and it has since then managed to expand to all four corners of the globe. This rapid spread, and the fact that there is no cure being discovered, has led me to wonder if it has a supernatural origin.
A verse from the book of Chronicles [in the Bible] reads: “[W]henever I hold back the rain or send locusts to eat up the crops or send an epidemic on my people, if they pray to me and repent and turn away from the evil they have been doing, then I will hear them in heaven, forgive their sins, and make their land prosperous again.”
I am a Roman Catholic Christian, and I was raised in church, so this definitely attracted my attention. I went online and saw many people were saying that God has held back rain in Australia, Africa is being swarmed with locusts and that the coronavirus is an epidemic. Many are saying that, according to the Bible, this signals the end.

* * *

Lo and behold – we learned tonight that isolation is being extended by another two weeks. I have mixed feelings about this. I was right about the extension and so I am kind of proud of my foresight. I also know that this is going to be dreadfully boring, economically draining and all the rest. However, I now have more time to learn things about myself that perhaps I did not know, which adds an element of excitement, if you want to call it that and be ironic.
Part of me is also starting to think that I should have gone home, back to Zim [Zimbabwe] for this lockdown. My parents are struggling to send me money for food and electricity because of their inability to trade Forex at the moment.
With this global lockdown, there must be many people stuck in foreign countries. I am one, though it is not affecting me too much as I have faith in my parents’ ability to get me money one way or another. But, I heard a story today about a South African family that was on holiday in Morocco and ended up not being able to leave, and are now homeless as they have run out of money.

* * *

My family and I had a celebratory dinner tonight to celebrate us surviving two week of lockdown. The theme was ‘Proudly South African’, and we all had to come dressed in our national colours. The evening was very festive until it was announced that lockdown will be extended. We were all disappointed, although we understand that it is necessary.

* * *

This morning, my mom woke me up and said that she was making a brunch for the family, and we all had to be done at 11:00 am. This was a nice surprise (also, a once-a-year type of surprise). We had banana-based flapjacks, hot-cross buns and scrambled egg. After this, I quickly did my chores, and then ended up playing table tennis for about two hours.
The main event of the day was watching the president’s speech. When Ramaphosa announced that he and his cabinet will be taking a pay cut and donating a third of their salaries for the next three months to the Solidarity Fund, I was very impressed. I believe that this was a perfect example of servant leadership. I also loved how he extended the challenge to other large company executives and public office bearers. […] Honestly, I can’t imagine what it must be like to be president during this period.

* * *

Tonight, President Ramaphosa announced that the lockdown will be extended by two weeks, making the lockdown period a total of five weeks (for now). Just before he made this announcement, I spoke to one of my personal mentors – she is doing her Master’s in Chemistry at the University of Pretoria. Her opinion is [that] lockdown has to be extended, since we haven’t even reached the peak of the virus in South Africa yet. But many others, especially those more focusing on the economic effects, would disagree.
In reality though, we cannot argue with the president’s decision. The counterfactual would be much worse, in terms of loss of human life, system overload and infrastructural pressure, to name just a few things off the top of my head.

* * *

In today’s entry, I want to address some of the main concerns regarding the implementation and subsequent extension of the nationwide lockdown. Many industry experts have expressed their disfavour towards the approach adopted by the South African government. While on the surface, the practice of basing one’s strategy on results obtained by other countries sounds reasonable, it fails to address the fact that the African continent faces a unique set of challenges. More studies are suggesting that by applying a “cookie-cutter” approach, countries – particularly poorer ones with vastly different demographics to those found in the western world – run the risk of an outcome even more detrimental than anything the virus is likely to conjure up. Africa has extremely high levels of poverty, which greatly reduces the effectiveness of a lockdown. These same experts argue that the economic fallout due to a lockdown will result in many deaths due to starvation and malnutrition, the victims of which are likely to be children (the same cannot be said of the coronavirus).

* * *

It was my cousin’s 21st birthday today. Like most people he had no choice but to stay at home and spend his birthday like a normal day. I know it’s not the biggest problem right now, but it is something which he had really been looking forward to.

title: 10 April 2020
text:
In South Africa, the mayor of Nkandla and other Kwa-Zulu Natal councillors were arrested for gathering in public. UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson was moved out of intensive care, though he remained in the hospital for the treatment of his coronavirus symptoms. By this time, the UK had over 65 000 coronavirus cases and over 8 000 deaths recorded. Singapore’s minister of education announced that Zoom would no longer be used for home-based learning because of the serious security breaches being experienced. According to scientists at Johns Hopkins University, New York state had more coronavirus cases than any country in the world, with 161 807 cases. After the US, Spain was the country with the second highest number of cases, with 157 022. Italy was third, reporting 143 626 cases.

Today is Good Friday; it is a very significant day in the Christian calendar. I really tried to put the thought of lockdown out of my brain, and to just absorb the beautiful day. It was a bit overwhelming considering that I had to deal with so many emotions. The lockdown puts a big strain on one’s emotional health. You stop feeling certain emotions and then all of a sudden you feel all of the bottled-up emotions welling up at once. You also do not have a clear concept of time because it is difficult to establish a routine. I knew from the start of the day that I was not going to do any work. I basically just ‘floated’ around the house all day. I tried to order all my thoughts and to gain some clarity. I learned that it is necessary to write down your thoughts, goals, plans and ideas. […] As soon as you write a problem down, you see it for what it is: ink on a piece of paper.

* * *

Today I discovered a hidden talent.
This morning my stepdad was mentioning how badly he wanted to go and have his haircut, but of course all the barbers are closed due to Covid-19. He asked me if I could give him a haircut instead. At first, I was extremely hesitant. I didn’t want to completely mess up his hair.
About an hour after he asked me, I decided I would give it a try. I certainly learnt a lot about how to cut men’s hair, using the different numbers on the shaving device. I was very impressed with myself in the end. My stepdad agreed that I had done a great job.

* * *

This morning I woke up quite late because my brothers and I played Monopoly late into the night last night. Earlier yesterday we had searched in all our drawers to find our old board games. During this lockdown, our family has grown close again. My brothers and I feel like children again: playing games, irritating each other, running around, playing with our dogs, fighting over who should do the chores, and even colouring again. I am trying to enjoy this time with them, for I know that it will pass just as quickly as my childhood.

* * *

The start of Easter! I grew up in a very religious household, so Easter is a very important part of our year. We woke up and immediately went to our TV room to watch our pastor from our church give his annual Good Friday service. The service revolved around the basics of Christ’s resurrection, but also included how a Christian can look at the coronavirus and try to find peace with it. After the service, my family had communion with other families in our cell group through a zoom call.
We then enjoyed a large Easter Good Friday family lunch, which consisted of braai vleis (which I braaied), salad, garlic bread and some beer to wash it down. It was a really great and spiritual day for our family.
Finally, I went upstairs and topped a great day off playing some Call of Duty with my friends.

* * *

Days feel like they are melting together, and I am starting to find it difficult to distinguish between them. This sense of purposelessness is difficult to come to terms with. I must admit that the last few days since Ramaphosa announced the extension of the nationwide lockdown have been very challenging, since it feels like this state is never going to end. I do think that South Africa has reacted in an appropriate manner (given the specific challenges we face), and Ramaphosa has emerged as a great leader that takes action when it is necessary to do so.
I have been trying to limit my news intake to once a day in order to stay informed about what is happening around the world, but also to make sure that I am not unnecessarily overwhelmed. Constantly being bombarded with the statistics and talk of economic collapse is mentally draining and not very useful when you are doing everything in your capacity to stay afloat. What else can we do but to stay put and wait until this virus blows over? The economic implications of it all is already being felt, but all we can do is carry on working and hoping that better days will come.

* * *

Today is the halfway mark: 21-odd days of a combination of social distancing and two weeks of lockdown, and 21 days left of lockdown … It feels as though this is never going to end.

* * *

Happy Easter weekend! My family is not Christian, in fact we are Gujarati, and I was raised (not very strictly) within that religion. However, we love celebrating certain holidays, such as Easter and Christmas, and appreciating family time. I guess it feels more like a South African tradition to us. I would have flown down to Durban this morning, had the circumstances been different, but instead, my mom is trying to keep our spirits high by baking hot cross buns. All the talk in the house today has been about how much travel has been affected – no one is flying or driving down to the coast this weekend from Joburg as they usually would. The ripple effect is incredibly large; the flight industry, the hotel industry, restaurants and all kinds of vendors would have pocketed months’ worth of income from this weekend.

* * *

Today is Good Friday. I woke up early to watch a church service online, but then went back to bed. After waking up from my nap I realised my aunts were here. They came to drop pickled fish; apparently they can no longer handle the lockdown. […] I’ve realised that my mom and her sisters are really people’s people. They grew up in an area where your neighbours were like family and everyone visited everyone’s homes. I think that’s why they are struggling with this lockdown. My aunts still live with my granddad in the house they grew up in. They are always visiting the aunty across the road and chatting to the people that pass by … it’s their daily life.
My aunt says that, in their area, people are still walking up and down the streets because apparently the police told them they need only be in their homes before 8:00 pm. I definitely think the rules of this lockdown need to be enforced more strictly in rural areas. I don’t think those people realise how important it is to minimise social contact.

* * *

Today, [the] minister of education addressed the nation. Possible (not definite) strategies to combat the effects of Covid-19 on the 2020 school year include: 1. The removal of June and September breaks: 2. Revision of curriculum outcomes. 3. Combining the 2020 and 2021 school years. 4. In the case of continued lockdown, screening/testing grade 12 and 7 learners, and phasing it down to grades 8 and R. 5. State-sponsored online education on television and radio programmes.
The last mentioned option is not ideal because there is a reason for classes and personal interaction. Some students cannot learn on their own and it is no indication of their intelligence but rather a reflection of the effect of a stimulating learning environment. Not all matriculants will make it through this year – the stress that comes with the uncertainty, the difficulty of studying on their own and the limited access to resources will definitely lead to a much smaller group of matriculants with university exemption. This might, however, not be as dire as it seems. Maybe this could be the perfect opportunity for a much-needed shift in the labour market? We need practical labourers, technicians, healthcare workers and artists. And who knows, with the consumer shifts taking place, new jobs will be created – some which don’t even exist yet …

* * *

The Bible warns of war and plague when the world is coming to an end, but experts have said that this pandemic does not actually fit the description spelled out in the Bible. What a relief. Now I can focus more on the economy and less on whether or not the world is ending.

title: 11 April 2020
text:
Gauteng still had the most coronavirus cases in the country with 801 persons infected, while the Western Cape had 541 persons infected, and KwaZulu Natal had 412 persons infected. The so-called wage-subsidy scheme was also applied retroactively to include days worked since 15 March 2020. Violent crime rates were reported to be falling globally. In South Africa, homicide rates fell from 326 to 94 in the first week of lockdown compared to the same time last year. Canadian lawmakers passed legislation to subsidise up to 75% of salaries in an attempt to discourage mass layoffs as a result of the Covid-19 pandemic.

I watched the Korean movie Parasite for the second time tonight. I saw it in the cinema a few weeks ago, but its message felt slightly different this time around. Posing as unrelated servants, a poor family con their way into the home of an upper-class family. As one unexpected, gruesome event unfolds after the other, the film begs the question: who should really be considered the ‘parasite’ in this situation? The film also discusses the idea of being trapped, both physically (characters unable to leave a space for years) and metaphorically (the idea that upward mobility is a farce and that having hope can lead to dire consequences). There is a scene in which a great storm causes the poor family’s basement home to become flooded and most of their possessions to be destroyed. This is juxtaposed against a scene in which also as a result of a storm the rich family end up feeling mildly irritated when they are unable to go on a camping trip. During uncontrollable times like these, the rich will be ‘inconvenienced’, but still emerge relatively unscathed, while the poor are pushed further into a state of destitution.

* * *

My day was dominated by my time in the kitchen. I had taken it upon myself to make authentic New York pizzas from scratch. This included crafting homemade dough and kneading it for nearly 90 minutes. The pizzas were a success and my family really enjoyed the experience. Despite the dreariness of lockdown, it is lovely to have such special and intimate moments with those around me. My love for cooking has also grown during this time.

* * *

Private banks across South Africa have begun to offer payment holidays, relief programmes, and various other initiatives in an attempt to minimise economic hardships felt by their clients.
While this may appear great on paper, I thought I’d dive a bit deeper into their reasoning behind these decisions. Firstly, this is a marketing scheme. Banks like FNB and ABSA are using this to not only appeal to their current clients, but to attract new clients as well. It’s safe to say that this lockdown has had a negative economic impact on almost every citizen in South Africa, and the idea of payment holidays or saving schemes is very appealing to many.
Secondly, how much do these private banks actually care about their client’s situations in these dire times? Unfortunately, from what I have uncovered, I believe the answer is very little. 32 years ago, my father, who was then 17, walked into United Bank (now ABSA) to open his first personal bank account. To this very day my father has remained loyal to this bank. Every payment, every credit card, every loan and everything financial he has ever had to deal with, he did in conjunction with this bank.
Following the announcement of these various payment relief programmes, my father approached his bank to apply for a payment holiday on his bond. Despite never missing or even being late on a payment, ABSA refused his application.

* * *

Everyone, with the exception of a few extremists (in my opinion the only thing extreme is their lack of common sense), seems to be on the same page that social distancing is the best way to counter the effects of the novel coronavirus. […] How to counter the effects of economies around the globe shutting down due to social distancing is another question. Various economic recovery strategies are being put in place for the post-Covid-19 period, and to my surprise, many of them include ecological focus points. I think people are finally starting to realise that we have angered the earth.

* * *

We had a party last night so we got up quite late this morning. We probably partied until 4:00 am. When I got up I had my daily cup of coffee and sat in front of the TV for a bit. We then had some brunch (eating the leftovers from last night’s braai). The rest of the day we just lay in bed and watched movies. Later, I cut up all the ingredients to make burgers because we had a build-a-burger night. We then climbed back into bed because it had started raining hard. I am not sure how long the rain lasted, but it was so soothing.

* * *

2 028 cases. 25 deaths. 75 053 tests conducted. The number of tests conducted is increasing, which is great and the government is even conducting more tests daily than private facilities which shows their seriousness. I think that this is very important as it will help assess the situation better to make more informed decisions. […]
I am beginning to believe that South Africa’s situation might not be that bad, as we have relatively few cases compared to other countries. It is encouraging to hear that Cyril called the nation to pray (he prays before he addresses us), and also that he was part of a church service on Good Friday. I think that he is impressing the country. I hope once this is over he can use this newly gained trust and his improved reputation to truly change and improve the country in all of its spheres.

* * *

Today I read an article released by the UN projecting that the number of deaths due to starvation in 2020 had risen by 130 million, largely as a result of the effects of economic lockdown in poor countries. I am now firmly convinced that the lockdown is the worst policy to have been implemented in these circumstances. […] I believe that many more lives would have been saved if this virus was treated in a similar way to previous outbreaks and not as some floating death serum.

* * *

Today my sister and I visited the shops for the third time since the beginning of lockdown. Just for the sake of a ‘change in scenery’, we decided to go to a shopping centre that was located slightly further away from our house rather than to the usual, closer shopping centre. If I’m being honest, this shopping trip was more a treat than a necessity. We got a few nice things for our Easter lunch tomorrow. We also felt a craving for sushi, which we were pleasantly surprised to find. The one thing that I did notice that was different to our usual Checkers was that, here, they had put up massive plastic screens between the tellers and customers. This is a hygiene measure I haven’t seen before and I think it is so clever. The employees don’t have to wear uncomfortable face masks and these screens create a proper barrier between them and customers. One of the perks of going to this shop was that it is on top of the hill, so when we were driving home, we got to see the ocean for the first time since lockdown started. Yes it was very distant, but it was a beautiful view and really reminded me of how lucky we are to live so close to the sea.

* * *

Today is Holy Saturday. We as a family thought back to when all the disciples were sitting around thinking that their saviour, mentor and friend was gone forever. We acknowledged their fear during this time and their faith. Just as we are uncertain about our future, all the disciples were living in fear and uncertainty. This, again, gave me a better perspective about the bigger picture. Although the coronavirus is a pandemic, it seems small compared to what the disciples faced. We need to keep faith and find peace in the fact that our God is bigger than the virus.

* * *

I guess that being productive today helped me feel a little better about things. This weekend I am really not going to look at the news, and rather just focus on trying to calm my thoughts, which are usually all over the place, but are even more so now. It’s Easter Sunday tomorrow, and I think it’s probably the first time I haven’t spent the day with my extended family. As the whole family won’t be coming, and we won’t have to be preparing food for the masses, I decided we might as well make Easter a little different. Slaving in the kitchen for hours when there is only me, my mom and my two sisters two feed, is nonesensical. I figured, instead, I would make nachos and we can spend the day in our lazy clothes, eating deliciously lazy food.

title: 12 April 2020
text:
Easter Sunday celebrations took on unusual forms across the globe due to lockdown restrictions. In the Eastern Cape, 23 inmates and three staff tested positive for Covid-19 at a prison. 18% of the New York Police Department were sick. Walt Disney World announced that it needed to furlough about 43 000 cast members and other employees because of the pandemic. In Ecuador, the president and cabinet took a salary cut of 50% due to budget constraints caused by the coronavirus. In the middle of a row with the US over the origins of the coronavirus, China imposed restriction on the publication of academic research into the beginnings of the novel virus. All papers on Covid-19 were required to have extra vetting before being submitted for publication.

I can officially say that I have experienced a ‘quarantine birthday.’ Even though the day wasn’t drastically different from the past few days in terms of what I did, I really enjoyed the day. I was really reflective today, thinking about my life and the times we are living in. It got me thinking of something my mom once said, “happiness is a choice”. I always disagreed with this sentiment. If your circumstances were bleak and opportunities were few, wouldn’t it be insensitive to say that happiness is a choice. As I went through the day, though, I began to realise that I was deciding to be happy despite what was going on around me. When I realised this, it really was a light bulb moment. As simple as my revelation was, I don’t think I’m going to experience it every day. I know as the quarantine furthers, I am going to experience a range of emotions. These past 28 days are an example of that. But it really was a good feeling today to have. Just to be happy for the sake of being happy.

* * *

I read that the cocoa industry has been suffering due to lowered demands for luxury goods, such as chocolate. This must be a massive blow to chocolate corporations as this is their peak season. Luckily, I’ve put it upon myself to help save these struggling corporations this Easter by ingesting obscene amounts of chocolate.

* * *

I am afraid that my corona diary is becoming awfully repetitive. Monumental events always seem much more interesting in hindsight, but for those living through them, they can feel almost anti-climactic (unless of course you are directly affected by the crisis).

* * *

2 173 cases. 80 085 tests conducted. No new deaths. […] Today was Easter. My family spent the day in [the] kitchen. We made a lamb shoulder and malva pudding with roast potatoes and vegetables, and even dove into the top shelves of the wine rack. It was lovely to spend the time together as a family. In the evening we watched [an] Andrea Bocelli concert that was live streamed on YouTube from Milan. […] My cello teacher who had tested positive is now fully recovered. My parents are hoping their businesses will open soon and that their cash flow can resume.

* * *

According to a report I read on News24 today, due to the two-week lockdown extension, the worst-case Covid-19 scenario for South Africa is that the peak would now take place in September. Previously, without the five-week lockdown, South Africa was estimated to reach its peak coronavirus infections in July. However, with the lockdown now in place, and with the worst-case scenario, the government is gaining two more months to prepare for a mass surge in infections.

* * *

Today, on Easter Sunday, as churches stand empty, South Africa officially has 2 173 confirmed Covid-19 cases. I have been reading some news articles and stumbled across an interview that saddens me in a ‘reading about the starving children in Africa’ kind of way. The interview was between correspondents from the World Economic Forum and two refugees in North-western Kenya. They spoke about how the lockdown and curfew had ruined them financially, and explained that they rue the day when the virus reached their refugee community because they all live in such close proximity in the camp, meaning that social distancing will not be possible. If well developed countries are struggling to contain the spread of the virus, imagine the dangers posed by it reaching communities without running water, proper sanitation and food security.

* * *

It’s Easter today. We celebrated with a church service in the morning, and then we just basically chilled the rest of the day. The service was really good. […] Later I tried to take a nap but I was too anxious. It’s so frustrating when you can’t even sleep because you’re so stressed about the future. I think maybe if I start to spend less time on my phone then I will get more done. That is going to be difficult though.

* * *

Today is Easter Sunday, meaning I can finally eat my Easter eggs! You’re never too old for Easter eggs no matter what anyone says. After lunch, my eldest sister and I made origami cranes and butterflies. That’s one new skill I’ve learnt during this time. I’m quite good at it. After mastering my new skill, I had a quick video call with my friends. I’m not very socially active, but I do miss seeing my friends once in a while. I think this is the longest I’ve gone without seeing my best friend. To me, that’s the biggest problem with the lockdown. I usually just rotate between home, friends’ homes and my Stellies [Stellenbosch] home. I never thought I’d say it, but I miss being in Stellenbosch. I miss the people and the atmosphere, honestly not so much the work, but I’m sure I’ll get there. What I do know is that when this is over, going back is going to feel so great. The National Defence force arrived in Paarl yesterday. The municipality announced that they would be deployed in certain parts of Paarl. I do think this was a necessary step as many of our people are not taking this serious enough.

* * *

EASTER SUNDAY! Today was a very interesting day compared to all the other Easter Sundays that I’ve had in my life. My mom went to buy hot cross buns on Thursday, so we’ve actually been having hot cross buns for lunch for a couple days now. At least hot cross buns have remained a normalcy during this period. We didn’t have any Easter eggs this year either. I think this was due to a combination of two factors: namely, Covid-19 and becoming an adult. I guess that the lack of Easter eggs is another disadvantage of growing up. We also didn’t have a big lunch, or have any family and friends over, or visit any family and friends. However, my family did end up having about a three-hour video call with all my extended family.

* * *

I woke up originally at 4:00 am to the sound of pouring rain. It was so calming to hear and just set the mood for this Easter Sunday. I think today is a rather sad day for many people because Easter is highly correlated with family time, and this is obviously not possible this year. I know I was quite sad because it is our tradition to have a massive Easter lunch with my grandparents, but we couldn’t do that this year. However, we are fortunate enough to be living down the road from them, so this morning we dropped a little gift basket and gave a wave through the window. After that our day was filled with a wholesome meal and one too many chocolates.

title: 13 April 2020
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that the impact of coronavirus in Russia was worsening; the country had, at this stage, reported a total of 18 328 cases and 138 deaths. In two days, the Italian police fined almost 23 000 people who had committed lockdown violations. New Zealand’s Prime Minister, Jacinda Ardern, sent a Facebook message to Kiwi Jenny McGee to commend her for her hard work. She was one of the nurses singled out by Boris Johnson for her kindness while he spent time in hospital. To deal with international travellers who could not find space in government-mandated hotels, Tokyo Airport introduced cardboard beds meant for individuals who were awaiting their coronavirus test results.

I find it funny how everyone seems to be dealing with life in quarantine quite differently. My mother distracts herself with ‘small tasks’ around the house – like cleaning out the cupboards and rearranging the bookshelves. My father has reconnected with school friends over Facebook that he has not spoken to in years. My grandmother busies herself by dressing up, and spending hours in front of the mirror doing her hair and her skincare routine (the fact that no one will see her does not seem to matter). I must admit that I have been spending too much time online, but I am trying to cut down on my screen time. I am using this week before classes start to read a bit more. I have already read three books while in quarantine, which is more than I would have been able to do during the semester.

* * *

I woke up feeling a lot lighter today. I called my mom last night and she managed to put my mind at ease. I had way too many things floating around in my mind, and I thought I could feel myself losing it a little.
I have realised that this pandemic is affecting me in ways I did not think it would. Not only do I feel mentally challenged, but I also feel a strong sense of emotional distress. My heart goes out to those that are in this alone because I have no idea how I would cope with absolutely nobody to talk to. I must also admit that these daily journal entries have played an important role in keeping me sane during the past couple of days. The ability to vent and write your experiences down, just to see your words on paper, brings a certain comfort.

* * *

Today is family day, which is a public holiday [in South Africa]. Although, since the lockdown began, it’s been hard to distinguish public holidays from other days, we as a family tried to treat the day as a holiday by playing games, watching movies and not talking about work. I still did my daily physical exercises and planned my academic work week. I video called with some friends and we just talked about life. It is clear that the lockdown is starting to affect everyone and that people are struggling with their mental health. I, myself, sometimes find that I am sometimes overwhelmed by a sudden wave of emotions. I keep my mind busy by watching series and taking naps. Some nights, though, I lie awake for hours just trying to process all of these emotions.

* * *

Today, I shaved off half of each of my eyebrows – really spur of the moment. I wondered how I’d look, so I went for it. Has there been a better time to experiment with your appearance? I shall be making an effort to learn new skills like hairdressing and body piercing, using myself as a test subject, of course.
South Africa’s been in the fight against the coronavirus for over about five weeks now. We are holding our breath but expecting the worst. Our best defense so far has been social distancing, contact tracing and testing. Using a similar approach, South Korea managed to flatten and reverse their infection rate curve in a matter of weeks. The major difference has been their take on contact tracing, which has been largely digital. The South Korean government publicly publishes sensitive information about the infected that can sometimes make them identifiable, and thus the victims of stigma. China’s success can also be attributed to working with large companies that have access to personal information and location services, like Alibaba. There seems to be a difference between collectivist countries and more individualistic countries in the willingness to give up such details. Will this pandemic enable authoritarian regimes, and should we value fighting the virus over our right to privacy?

* * *

One of the major disadvantages of the lockdown is the effect it will have on the education system within South Africa. While it does appear that many tertiary education facilities will be continuing with the academic year through online learning, this may not be the case for high school and preparatory school students.
[…] Will the government let all students write finals, resulting in the majority of those who pass being ‘privileged and wealthy’, while those belonging to predominantly to underprivileged families fail? Or will the government make every student redo the year? Both of the options generate major problems of their own.

* * *

Multiple news sources this morning seem to be focused on what will happen post-lockdown. The consensus seems quite grim. SA’s infection rate will just look more like a delayed exponential curve. Our efforts to stifle the virus so far have been commendable, and nothing short of incredible. We’ve managed to do much better than developed nations with much more resources. However, unless we’ve vaccinated our population and somehow acquired herd immunity, there is nothing stopping it from simply spreading after the lockdown like everywhere else. This view makes the thought of multiple lockdowns, possibly staggered over periods in reaction to infection rates, seem much more likely, and much deadlier for our growth prospects. I think this virus will be affecting us a lot longer than we all hope, or even dread.

* * *

Today, we have decided to become part of a new trend by getting involved in stationary swimming and bike stationary riding. I must admit I have been quite lazy in terms of exercise throughout this lockdown. I prefer working out at the gym and don’t enjoy home workouts.
Today, though, my stepdad built a harness for himself to swim (but remain stationary) in our pool. He used tubing from an old fish tank and some rope, tying it around a huge pot plant which we hope doesn’t move anytime soon.
Building the stationary bike was more of a challenge. We ended up using old pieces of wood and a rolling pin to keep it stationary. The only problem is that it makes such a noise that nobody wants to use it because we don’t want to wake up the neighbours.

* * *

I woke up early this morning, keen to rid myself of the Easter laziness. I did a healthy amount of exercise and academic work to keep my mind and body in check. These small things are extremely beneficial in helping me to remain focused and healthy during the lockdown period. Without the extension, I would be just three days away from ‘freedom’ – but, I still have 17 days of this instead …
