Gangs in the suburb of Mannenberg in the Cape Flats have called a truce during the lockdown period. Rival gangs are working together to distribute food, soap and other essential goods throughout the community. […] This is a really positive and profound story coming out of an area that usually receives so much negative publicity.

* * *

My mom is getting worried about her job and whether she will lose money for all the days she is missing. My parents have a lot of expenses because my sister and I are twins and so everything costs double. I think she also just misses her job which she loves.

* * *

Today was spent doing a group project. We were using Google hangouts and it took me 15 minutes to realise that nobody could hear me … I kept wondering “why does this one team member keep interrupting me?” This was the first time I have experienced a major technical glitch on my side. I felt so dumb and couldn’t figure out how to get my sound back on. In the end, I was that team member that said nothing the whole time.

title: 14 April 2020
text:
The Gauteng Health Department announced that the Johannesburg Expo Centre – which had been selected as the site for a large emergency field hospital – was almost ready to receive its first Covid-19 patients. Some mining operations resumed in the country. The South African Reserve Bank cut the repo rate by one percentage point, and the International Monetary Fund predicted the worst global economic downturn since the Great Depression. US President Donald Trump announced that he would halt funding to the World Health Organisation, specifically because of the organisation’s opposition to the US decision to restrict travel to China.

The path ahead looks daunting. Lockdown was supposed to end in two days, now it has been decided that it will only end in two weeks. The world is facing an epidemic and no one knows what the future will bring. Yet, we as citizens are still critical of the decisions our government is making.
All the negative talk in the news and on social media criticising our government has made me realise that people are impatient and will always blame others when times are tough. I have decided that I will not be one of those people who judge the government and talk negatively about the leaders of our country. I will respect their decisions because I believe that our safety is their first priority.
Nevertheless, I will continue to educate myself on what is happening and will engage critically with the decisions that are being made. I hope the rest of the country does the same.

* * *

Every day I find it harder to write in this diary because every day I feel the same way. There is only so much to do in your own house. In the movie The Breakfast Club, the teacher gives the students an assignment to each write a one thousand word essay, but he explicitly says that it cannot be the same word over and over again. Every day here is the same, though, and so I feel it would make sense to just write “bored” 200 times for this dairy entry.

* * *

News has been circling about the BCG vaccine [the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin vaccine is a vaccine primarily used against tuberculosis (TB)] for quite a while now and now I think it’s becoming significant enough to write about. It has been argued that the BCG vaccine provides at least partial immunity to Covid-19. Since all South Africans by law have to take the vaccine just after birth to prevent against TB, this apparently explains South Africa low infection rate. There is some merit to this theory (although at this stage it is just a theory). Currently scientists around the globe are exploring vaccines related to diseases such as malaria, HIV and TB, so the BCG vaccine could hold some potential. However, this theory has not been tested at all by the scientific community and people who have been vaccinated are still getting the virus.

* * *

Do you know what frightens me? It is failing second year and not coming back to varsity. That is my biggest fear at the moment. I am losing focus and at times I panic but don’t seem to do anything about it. I had a dream that I was writing some maths paper but I don’t remember studying any of the content. I woke up crying. Everyone else in my dream seemed to know what they were doing. I am studying but not with the same effort that I did before. There must be people who are more depressed than me, but at times I just cry and cry and cry.

* * *

The past two days, I have just been revising and catching up on work. Yesterday, I basically spent the entire day doing my Financial Management assignment, while today was spent with revising Political Science. Strangely enough, I feel a bit stressed about all the work that I need to revise, but at the same time, I know that I will do everything that I need to do. I think that I may just be a bit anxious about online learning. I think all my modules will sort of be self-taught, with the opportunity to ask questions. However, I am a rural learner, so it will be quite an adjustment.
All of this has me thinking about how crazy it is that one’s home is stereotypically associated with safety, comfort and consistency; however, there’s so much change and uncertainty that’s taking place while being stuck at home during this lockdown period that the typical association of home is changing. Well, it is for me, at least.

* * *

I baked all day long, using ingredients I could find in the cupboard. I never get to bake when I am staying at my residence at university, so I have really been enjoying being able to do that. I was missing one of the key ingredients so I decided to go to Checkers, expecting the trip to take no more than 20 minutes. When I arrived there was a queue just to get into the supermarket (everyone standing five metres apart, of course). They were probably trying to regulate the number of people inside the building to prevent overcrowding. Almost everyone (including myself ) were wearing a mask as a stark reminder of the freakish times we find ourselves in. The whole atmosphere felt like a scene from a dystopian novel or movie. At the moment I am not reading or watching any sci-fi type books or films because it hits too close to home (silly, I know). When I finally got inside the Checkers, they did not have the ingredients I was looking for. I went to two other supermarkets before I found a place that did not have a long queue and that had what I was looking for. The shelves were mostly empty. The whole experience was a bit disturbing. Today I also heard that the small neighbourhood Italian restaurant that my family has been going to since I was in primary school has been forced to close down. It might sound a bit trivial, but I felt devastated when I heard the news.

* * *

I am finding myself more and more restless each day. The weather is very indecisive. It changes from blue to grey from hour to hour, reflecting my own mood. I am finding that boredom is becoming more common and my routine more and more claustrophobic. Groundhog Day!

* * *

It was one of my best friend’s birthday’s today. My mates and I tried to make it as special for him as possible. We gathered together for a zoom call and chatted for about 2 hours. During the zoom call we also all downloaded an online poker app. We ended up playing poker into the early hours of the morning. It was all fun and games until I lost R100 to my dad!

title: 15 April 2020
text:
The South African government declined the request for a further R10 billion to support an ailing South African Airways. New York City announced that its coronavirus death toll had increased to more than 10 000. The UN started sending ‘Solidarity Flights’ with aid to countries that urgently needed medical equipment. The first flight landed in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) witnessed a new outbreak of the Ebola virus, with three new cases reported.

I have recently been seeing hundreds of posts on Facebook about how the matric class of 2020 have been affected by the virus. There is a strong possibility that matric pupils won’t be able to resume their classes or attend their matric dance, an event I know every grade 12 pupil looks forward to. […] I am so thankful that I have already matriculated and gotten accepted to the university of my choice, and that I do not have to stress about university applications now. These were already so stressful, even prior to the pandemic.

* * *

Today, I shaved my head because I felt like it. It was a fairly impulsive decision, but so far, I have no regrets. I had a huge afro and now it’s all gone. Well, technically I still have an afro; it’s just in a bag until I can figure out how to incorporate it into an artwork or something.
There has been a surge in confirmed coronavirus cases in prisons around the country, particularly in the Eastern Cape. The government’s response is to increase testing, distribute protective equipment to officials and continue contact tracing. The situation in prisons is tricky because a lack of protective gear and because of overcrowding.
The US and some Middle Eastern countries have taken a less conventional approach. America has released hundreds of elderlies and terminally ill inmates, and Iran has released over 100 000 misdemeanor offenders. It’s true that the spread of the virus in densely packed and unhygienic prisons would be catastrophic, and even prisoners should be able to take responsibility for their health. Maybe extraordinary circumstances call for extraordinary action, but at what social cost? I don’t know what the best solution to this problem is, but I think the South African government is acting in its citizens’ best interest.

* * *

My parents put a piece of paper on the kitchen table today and told us all to add whatever groceries we think we need. I wrote a whole bunch of things, but I also tried my luck and added ‘Easter eggs’. IT WORKED. My sisters and I each got a Lindt bunny.
Even though lockdown does have this overarching gloom-and-doom feel, one of the things that I’ve really enjoyed about it is that I’ve really started to appreciate the smaller things again. I’m not referring to the things that I would be doing if it weren’t lockdown, but rather to the things that I am able to do because of lockdown (e.g. finally having the time to read some books that I bought two years ago but had yet to open, as well as catching up with good friends that I haven’t spoken to in a while).

* * *

Today I woke up at 5:00 am, shared a coffee with my brother and my dad, and then accompanied my dad to work. My father’s work is centred around fresh produce, which has been deemed an essential service. We arrived at the fresh produce market before 6:00 am and performed various tasks. I was shocked at the volume of both food and people. Precautionary measures have been put in place – including temperature testing, hand sanitising and social distancing. However, much of the fresh produce was not enclosed or wrapped and was still susceptible to viral contact.
[…] My findings highlighted one main thing for me: the food we eat passes through so many hands and facilities before it lands on our plates. This process translates to nearly all industries. If we are going to go through the effort of lockdowns and quarantines, surely we should be paying more attention to the sanitisation of the products we consume and bring into our homes.

* * *

I woke up to quite a lot of commotion. I went downstairs to find my parents busy putting up drapes for my sister’s birthday. She’s turning 21 tomorrow, and since we’re in lockdown, a party is not an option. So my mom thought she’d go to some trouble to make the dining room look fancier. My eldest sister and I have been making these origami birds to hang them above the dinner table. We’re also planning on putting up fairy lights.
Of course, my sister isn’t even disappointed about having her birthday during lockdown. She’s the introvert in the family so she prefers being alone. This will probably be her favourite birthday yet.

* * *

As of yesterday, I have changed my entire perspective. I have decided to focus on the positive rather than the negative. The number of recoveries has stayed constant and the number of confirmed cases and deaths has grown, but I am still in control of how I take in this information and what I do with it.

* * *

Corona has officially infected and killed someone I know. This gives me an eerie feeling of what is to come. My mother, ouma [grandmother] and gran are starting to run out of cigarettes and alcohol. My ouma and gran are the ones who need the alcohol. Both live on their own and my Ouma’s DStv has lost the bounce from its bungee and is not working. She stays in a home where access is not granted at the moment, and so none of us can enter and help her out. This is not good. I’m worried and would love for her to come and stay here. The only problem with that would be that she wouldn’t be able to go back to her home once she has left.

* * *

I was very unproductive today. I could barely do an hour of work before getting distracted. I haven’t been able to fill my Ritalin prescription yet. I also was not really in the mood for exercise so I took the day off. I did watch an address by Professor Salim Abdool Karim who leads the Coronavirus Ministerial Advisory Committee, though. According to Professor Karim, if the average daily increase in the number of cases is greater than 90 from 10 April to 16 April 2020, we will continue with the lockdown. So far, this seems likely as a result of previous daily increases. What was also interesting to hear is that he said the virus comes in three waves; the first is the introductory wave from international travellers, the second wave is the people who those travellers have been in contact with, and the third wave is general community transmission. We have completed the first two waves and are currently in the third and most dangerous wave.

* * *

While the rest of the world is trying to work together to overcome this pandemic, in an act of destructive nationalism, President Donald Trump has decided to cut funding to the World Health Organisation. This could mean that vulnerable countries in the global South will not be able get the medical supplies and help they need to fight the disease.

* * *

As mentioned previously, my brother has begun his primary-school learning at home. While it will be my parents’ job from next week, it was my duty this week to help him with his work.
I have learned a lot this week, and I sure hope he has too. While his learning came in the form of grade 5 work, my learning was more abstract. It taught me how to be patient, self-controlled and how to reason. It taught me how to teach and interact, and my word, I had fun doing it!
You see I have always known deep down in my gut that teaching is my passion. The reason, however, that I am studying a BCom is because I have always wanted to be financially aware. And now, courtesy of the coronavirus and me having to teach my brother, I know exactly what it is that I want in life.
I am now deadset on doing my PGCE [Postgraduate Certificate in Education] at UCT after my BCom degree in order to teach senior phase (high school) in Accounting and Economics, and perhaps after a few years I could branch into the teaching of History, Mathematics and English. As a hobby, I am hoping to go into Forex and to create an account providing trade signals.
It turns out there is a silver lining, even amongst these dark clouds.
Cheers Covid-19.

title: 16 April 2020
text:
In an unexpected but welcome show of goodwill, gangs in South Africa called a truce to distribute essential goods to the hungry in some of Cape Town’s poorest areas. The South African Defence Force (SADF) announced that it would commence with a probe into the death of a man in Alexandra in Johannesburg who allegedly died as a result of violence from members of the Force. Facebook announced that, in March alone, it had put warning labels on 40 million posts that contained misleading or false information about the coronavirus. In America, 5.2 million Americans filed for unemployment in one week, bringing the total number of Americans filing for first-time unemployment claims since mid-March 2020 to 22 million. The Indian Premier League was suspended until further notice.

I read a beautiful quote today that read: “We are not all in the same boat; we are all in the same storm.” This made me realise that, while the lockdown has been hard on me and my family, there are people in much worse situations; people with no savings to fall back on. In this time, it is our duty to help these people as best we can, but we also need to look after ourselves because no one can pour water out of an empty cup.

* * *

It’s weird to think that today could have been the last full day of lockdown …
I woke up to a flurry of emails and messages regarding the start of the second term. The reality of online schooling has begun to set in. I mean I always knew school would come around, but I didn’t think too deeply about it. Now I am forced to and it’s overwhelming to say the least. The last time I actually did work on the desk in my childhood bedroom was in matric. For the past year or so, coming home always signified rest and was so separate from my school life. And that’s how I’ve been treating the past few weeks – as a holiday.
I have to make a mental shift and focus (and test my self-discipline). I can see it now: Tuesday (the day when I have classes from 8:00 am to 17:00 pm), the whole day by my desk, in silence. It’s crazy to think that days like that are going to be the norm.

* * *

This morning I saw some very worrying videos of people throwing stones and looting in some parts of Cape Town. I was shocked at first but after doing some reading I realised why they were doing this. It was simple, they had not received the food that they were promised. According to ANC [African National Congress, South Africa’s ruling party] Ward 22 councillor, Bongani Ngcani, emergency food supplies worth around R53 million had been set aside by the Western Cape government, but these supplies had not reached residents yet.

* * *

Tensions rose today as everybody is feeling very frustrated and cooped up. Having a daily routine where you can walk around, talk to different people and see different things really does contribute to a sense of individuality and independence. That is why, I think, being in lockdown (even with people that you love and feel safe with) can lead to such a deep sense of dissatisfaction. Of course I am able to say this from a place of privilege. I cannot imagine what it must be like staying in lockdown when circumstances at home are difficult or when one does not feel cared for or even safe.
I have also been wondering what life post-lockdown is going to look like. When will schools be able to reopen, people be allowed to go back to work or shops and restaurants open? At least I have a bit of certainty when it comes to the rest of my university term (more or less – how we are going to be assessed still remains a mystery). On CNN this morning I saw a report on how countries with women as leaders seem to be better controlling the spread of the coronavirus. I wonder what the explanation for that might be …

* * *

Today’s big news is that the lockdown is to be extended indefinitely, although the government will slowly start easing certain restrictions. One of the biggest discussions in my home is how schools will operate. I know universities have measures in place to continue the academic year, but it seems that the continued functioning of schools is still in question. My younger sister, who is now in grade 11, has continued with online learning, but they’re not sure if it’s going to be sustainable. My mom and my sister have spoken about home schooling my sister for the rest of this year because they don’t want my sister to lose out on her academic year. There is just the issue of whether the school will support this by providing learning aids for the subjects my mom doesn’t know much about. My sister also mentioned something today about there being some talk of schools promoting all schoolgoers to the following grade next year, and then having a revision term for this year’s work. As expected, there is just so much uncertainty.

* * *

I made my sister a birthday breakfast. Honestly it was more brunch than breakfast since she doesn’t wake up any time before 11:00 am. Other than that, it was a normal lockdown day. I tried to get as much work done as I could. We had a lovely dinner as a family. My origami birds definitely elevated the room, if I say so myself. Afterwards my sister (birthday girl) and I made a cheese platter and pretended our Grapetiser was wine so that we could have a movie marathon.
In terms of real world things, we’re still waiting for the president’s verdict on lifting the ban on sale of alcohol. The number of confirmed cases is continuing to rise, but I think it’s because they’ve actually now gone out and done the mobile testing which allows them to test on a larger scale. I think the numbers will increase even more rapidly as more mobile tests are done. Today, the number of positive cases stood at 2 605. However, 903 people have fully recovered or have been confirmed negative.

* * *

Today would have been the day that the nationwide lockdown ended, but now they are still weeks remaining. A person can only stay in their house for so long until they are driven to insanity. The global economy is experiencing a financial crisis; GDP is falling, unemployment is rising, stock markets are collapsing and overall the economic future looks quite bleak. Governments all over the world are trying to help their citizens by providing unemployment packages to those who have lost their jobs due to the pandemic. In South Africa, the government is also distributing food parcels to impoverished areas, or so they say. How much is the government actually doing for those who are suffering and whether the money which is being allocated to such programmes is actually being used for this purpose, is not clear. It would not surprise me if corruption was taking place and the money was being used to enrich a member of parliament instead.

* * *

Day 21 of the national lockdown. South Africa is currently standing at 2 605 cases with a death count of 48. In my first diary entry, I mentioned that the virus was dominating most conversations. This is still very much true but the nature of conversation has changed slightly. Back in the early days, words like “self-isolation”, “self-quarantine”, and phrases like “flatten the curve” were frequent, but as time has gone on and we have become more desensitised, our conversations have become less formal. We now joke about the “before times” and the “outside world”. Now, we don’t talk so much about the virus itself, but about the problems surrounding it (e.g. loss of income, the prohibition of certain goods, the economic lockdown, etc.). This change in focus is related, I think, to our acceptance of the problem. In March we were still grasping the idea of the virus itself, whereas now that we have accepted the situation we have begun to consider minor details.

* * *

Today I was woken up a little differently to how I am most days. I got woken up by my girlfriend bringing me coffee in bed! We had not seen each other in weeks, but she lives two minutes away from me in the same estate. After consulting with my mother, she told me that our parents decided it was okay for her to visit me because both families have been on full lockdown for almost four weeks now. This surprise was more than pleasant; it filled me with happiness and comfort knowing that I could spend my time with someone that I love! We started the day off catching up and enjoying each other’s company. After this we decided to bake banana bread just as your typical lockdown couple would do. The entire day was a day filled with happiness and love. After all the fun, we both decided to work for about an hour before we watched a movie to top off probably the best day of lockdown so far!

* * *

Lockdown was supposed to end today (before President Ramaphosa announced the two-week extension period). This week I have felt quite overwhelmed and decided to take a break from analysing the changing world around me. Breaks are very much needed. A system overload only impedes productivity – this is true for businesses, the global economy and individual human beings. And this is also partially the reason for the nationwide lockdown: to buy our already struggling healthcare system a bit more time to get geared with staff and PPE.

title: 17 April 2020
text:
South Africa’s coronavirus death toll spiked with 14 new deaths reported. The government announced some adjustment to regulations for the next two weeks of the lockdown. Hardware components needed for essential repairs were permitted and plumbers, locksmiths, glaziers, electricians and roof repairers could also go back to work. The ban on the sale of alcohol and tobacco remained in place. Shinzo Abe, the Prime Minister of Japan, announced to media that Japan would review its support for the World Health Organisation once the pandemic ended. In Australia, the mayor of Warrnambool was fined after contravening regulations by meeting friends for a beer outside of a liquor store.

The start of online classes is approaching and I’m not ready mentally. I’ve been unproductive academically and I feel stifled. Even writing these (not-so-daily) reflections has proved immensely difficult. I’ve had intense migraines over the past few days that wouldn’t be eased by painkillers, so I’ve been sleeping for the better part of three days. It’s lovely how the days go by when you’re asleep. We received further communication about online learning, so I’m trying to get all my affairs in order before Monday. It’s definitely going to be tough. I left home to get away from domesticated life, and between house chores and academics, I won’t have much time for what I really want to do – design. The whole situation’s left me depressed and uninspired.

* * *

As the virus grows, people remain isolated but healthcare workers cannot do the same. I see my mother wake up every morning to go do her job at clinics all around the city and I worry. However, I can take comfort in the fact that I know she does not work directly with patients, which reduces her risk but does not remove it entirely. Those who are in contact with patients, our frontline healthcare workers, are the ones that are at the most risk of getting infected. Hundreds of [those] workers have sadly died throughout the world due to their exposure to Covid-19. In Italy, over 17 000 health workers have been infected with the virus, representing 10% of the country’s known cases.

* * *

It is amazing how we, as a country with a large population and a low average income, tend to support massive retail businesses that are run internationally, rather than supporting local businesses that will grow our own economy.
Now more than ever, people are starting to see the value in our smaller businesses, as supplies in the big chain stores are running low, and they realise our smaller corner shops are more important than we often give them credit for.
Maybe this time was necessary for us to realise that it is important for us to support our local businesses within our community.

* * *

Today I went grocery shopping. It was my first time outside in four weeks. It is funny how grocery shopping is the nearest thing to an adventure these days. I wore a mask and gloves. On the way to Spar there were more cars on the road than I expected. When I arrived at Spar, I had to wait in a line for more than an hour. In that hour, the workers from Spar sanitised our hands and trolleys three times. While I was waiting, I just observed all the people. Everybody had some form of a mask on. Some were using builders’ masks, others normal headbands and a few even had masks made of underwear.

* * *

Last week Health24 reported that a team of researchers in Australia plan to fast-track the production of the BCG vaccine (a vaccine that prevents severe forms of tuberculosis [TB] in humans) to see how impact corona symptoms. Now a new study has surfaced investigating the correlation between the Covid-19 mortality rate and global BCG vaccine policies. More simply put, scientists are trying to work out if are those nations which make BCG vaccination mandatory are less susceptible to high corona related deaths. This will be very interesting to see, but it is a difficult question to evaluate since there are many different factors contributing to the mortality rates (e.g. cultural norms and health infrastructures).

* * *

Many reports have said that, in some areas, the police and army have been “aggressive” towards certain communities. My opinion is that the police force and the army need to show leadership and to act as calmly as possible. Any bad action will be highlighted by the media and if society does not trust the police we could end up in a bad situation where entire communities and groups of people will rebel the lockdown rules.

* * *

I started this diary a month ago today and all I can say is that life has changed drastically. We used to live in a world in which everything was so fast-paced, routine driven and comfortable. This all came to a halt and we are now finding ourselves in a much slower environment, an environment that has even given us the opportunity to be ‘bored’.
It is so scary to think about. No one ever predicted something like this would happen. […] Luckily, being humans, we are very capable of adapting. Also, as I have mentioned before, we are extremely fortunate to be living in a world where everything is so easily accessible and operational through technology.

* * *

Not much to report today. I got quite a lot of studying done, though I still have so much more to do. My eldest sister’s been stressing a lot lately. She works for a food exporting/ importing company which has been fortunate enough to allow their staff to work from home whilst still paying them. However, it is difficult for the business as they rely heavily on exports/imports. My sister works in the finance department and her workload varies day to day. Today was one of the busier days where she had many deadlines and her computer was giving her problems. Murphy’s law, right? This actually happens quite often. The company didn’t have the means to get everyone laptops to take home, so she came home with her entire desktop. She usually just connects to the company’s server, but some days like today, the computer does not cooperate. My sister usually works till 5:00 pm but because of all the technical delays she was in her study until 8:00 pm.

* * *

Today I woke up at around 6:30 am. I had a sore nose and seemed like I still have flu. I was very worried because now I have tried every medicine for flu and it doesn’t work. I am beginning to suspect that I might be one of the victims of this pandemic. I can’t think straight. I think I will have to isolate myself for about two weeks to see whether I have symptoms. Only then I can go for testing.
At 8:00 am I went back to sleep because I felt very tired. I got up at 11:00 am. I studied as much as I could before going to fetch the food parcels that are being issued to students at the LLL [a residential village for senior students]. When I got to the LLL, I found a group of EFF [Economic Freedom Front, a political party] students debating. I was not interested about the debate because it was not even the reason I was there. Late, I made myself noodles for dinner from out of the food parcel and then fell asleep again.

* * *

As I was reading more on the indefinite extension of the lockdown, I realised how much focus was put on the liquor ban. Many article titles were a version of ‘lockdown’ continues, and so does the ‘liquor ban’. Last Sunday, on the video call with my extended family, my grandma mentioned the looting of liquor stores in Cape Town. Today, I saw that just fewer than 20 stores have been looted. Weirdly enough, I can vaguely understand why liquor stores are being looted. I also understand why so much media focus has been given to this topic as the aim of the lockdown is to save lives, and with the indirect effect that alcohol consumption has on many of the social issues in our country, there’s a huge possibility that public intoxication could reverse what lockdown aims to accomplish.
On a completely different note, something I found quite cool happened today. Our neighbour, who makes his own honey, passed a huge jar of honey to my dad over the wall between our houses.

title: 18 April 2020
text:
President Ramaphosa rejected a request by a liquor forum in Gauteng (representing over 20 000 liquor and shebeen operators) to lift the ban on the sale of alcohol. In Nigeria, the chief of staff to the Nigerian president died after testing positive for the virus. Walmart, the largest US retailer, made it mandatory for employees to wear masks or other face coverings at work. Canada’s minister of transport announced that all airline passengers would need to wear masks or face coverings to cover their nose and mouth while travelling. Although sports of all shapes and forms had been cancelled around the world, Taiwan allowed its baseball league to continue playing. They broadcast their live games to the world at a time when there was a severe shortage of live sporting events to watch.

I am trying to enjoy the last few days before classes start, but honestly I cannot wait for 20 April. I feel extremely stagnant (as I am sure most people are feeling right now). The world seems to have come to a complete standstill. All commercial activities have ceased, the streets are deserted and everything feels very quiet. Every day I try to have my lunch outside for a bit of fresh air and to escape from the suffocation I experience when staying inside with the same people for so long. The standard Johannesburg buzz is gone and I can only hear birds and other subtle sounds of nature.
If there is one positive outcome to all this, I think it must be that the environment will be able catch its breath for a second or two. The canals of Venice are clear, deer are roaming the streets of urban areas in Japan and air pollution is said to be at a sudden low. I know all of this will quickly be eroded once lockdown is lifted and the world tries to carry on as normal, but for just a split second nature shows us who came first and what will carry on once we are gone.

* * *

3 034 cases. 108 021 tests. Two new deaths bringing the count to 52. Very slow day. Played games with the family and painted. More groceries are delivered, and then sent outside to be left in the sun. Some things that needed to be refrigerated or frozen were washed in the sink in soapy water. I felt ridiculous watching my mom do that, but I guess desperate times call for desperate measures. My parents’ companies are waiving wage cuts, and aren’t too sure what to do with pending stock orders, etc. I think many businesses also face ethics of who do they pay first? Staff? Suppliers? Rent?

* * *

Today I took my grandpa on a grocery trip. I had offered to do it alone, but he insisted on coming because he hasn’t left his house in over a month. I can only imagine that this is the case for many elderly people. Fortunately, in our community I have seen many organisations that have started doing grocery shopping on behalf of the elderly. It is always amazing to see something positive in a time like this when everything seems to be so negative.

* * *

This evening my family and I watched the World Health Organisations live virtual concert. The concert featured many global artists and aimed to bring the world together and to encourage people to take meaningful action in protecting our own health and supporting the global response to Covid-19. It was also a way to celebrate and show support for our frontline healthcare workers who are risking their own lives to save others.
We all thoroughly enjoyed the concert, especially Lady Gaga’s performance, and I think it was a great way to try and spread a little bit of happiness and positivity during these daunting and uncertain times.

* * *

I spent the majority of my day studying. I’ve been thinking of the matrics a lot lately. I spoke to a few of my friends and they said their teachers are keeping in contact via Whatsapp groups and Google classrooms. They still have assignments due and are expected to hand them in. So far it seems as if their tests will be taking place through Google forms. I can’t imagine how stressful this time must be for them. This is such an important year, not only academically but socially too. They are missing out on all the lasts of high school.

* * *

Today was an absolute scorcher. […] On such days there really is only one thing to do. Light a fire, throw on a braai, prepare a few salads, laze under the umbrellas, refresh in the swimming-pool, laugh with family and of course feast!
I have decided to take this weekend to kick my feet up, perhaps with just a few preparations for university which will commence via an online process from Monday. I enjoyed alcohol for the first time since the lockdown began after my father managed to convince me to join him in drinking a few gins mixed with dry lemon. A decision I do not regret!
My puzzle-building skills continue to improve, even if I do say so myself. I am currently working on a 1 500 piece puzzle of the African jungle. Needless to say, it’s an absolute nightmare, but ‘boy oh boy’ do I love it!

* * *

Today, just after breakfast, my sister, my girlfriend and I all decided that it would be a really great idea to set up a tent in our garden and to sleep in it tonight. I went to the bottom garages and found a tent that had not been used in about ten years. After considerable planning and procrastination we got ready to set up the tent. Even though there was three of us and it was supposed to be a team activity, I ended up doing 90% of the work while the two ladies just stood and watched me do it. […] I am writing this entry in my room after supper and before we migrate to the tent. I will provide an update tomorrow as to how our ambitious expedition went. Wish me luck!

* * *

Today I decided. No television. No cell phone. No social media. I woke up excited and ran to my mother’s room. I told her that today we are going to paint. I went to the cupboard to get newspapers, paint and everything else we needed. We painted the whole day. It was very relaxing. After that there was a huge storm. We heard a big lightning strike. The next moment our electricity was off. After a few moments, the electricity came back on but our TV and Wi-Fi were broken. Luckily, internet service providers are now designated as essential so we can fix the Wi-Fi on Monday. For now, I am enjoying not to have any internet related distractions. I can focus on myself, take a bubble bath, read a book and sleep tight. This is just what I needed before university starts on Monday … online university.

* * *

Even though there has been a decrease in murders, robberies and hijackings, gender-based violence remains a problem and has actually increased during lockdown. Safe houses set up to serve as first-stage shelters for victims of gender-based violence have been opened. Police Minister, Bheki Cele, was quoted saying that law enforcement had received 87 000 gender-based violence complaints in the first week of the lockdown. This figure is disgusting.
No amount of economic stress, anger or otherwise should ever culminate in the physical, sexual or emotional abuse of another human being. As South Africans (and South African men), we should not behave like this.

* * *

I really thought that I’d be annoyed with my family by now, but surprisingly enough, I feel as though we’re getting along much better than I thought we would under the current circumstances. I think part of the reason is we understand that we all have our work/ studies prioritised, and by figuring out together how to make home our place of work and play, and being respectful of one another’s time and space, we were/are able to get along much better for such a prolonged period of time.

title: 19 April 2020
text:
Americans took to the streets to protest lockdowns a day after Donald Trump encouraged people to protest against strict public health measures. For the first time in two months, South Korea reported single digit cases, with only eight new cases. A humanitarian group found 34 migrants near Malta who were then forced to quarantine on a ship off the coast of Palermo. To deal with bed shortages, Turkey built hospitals on runways at an unused airport. As the UK reached the milestone of one month of being in lockdown, an 11-year-old boy from Lincoln climbed the equivalent of 3 408m, using the staircase in his family’s home, in just over 17 hours.

Today I woke up excited for some reason. It felt like I was back in primary school and it was the day just before the new school term starts. When you iron your clothes and pack your schoolbag and make sure your pencil case has all of its stationery. Only today I won’t be doing any ironing or packing any bag. Stationery is always essential so at least I’ll get to do that. Online learning starts tomorrow and I’m feeling both nervous and excited. I’ve never done an online course or anything similar so I think it will be quite interesting to see how this plays out. It will definitely be an adjustment as most of my modules are quite interactive. Nevertheless, it is a challenge I’m willing to accept if I can do it in my pyjamas. I spent my afternoon studying and started preparing for this week’s classes this evening. I thought it would be a good idea to make a separate folder for all the online learning and then create folders for my respective modules within that folder. I spent my evening downloading all the necessary notes, lectures and videos for the upcoming week. I don’t want to wait until tomorrow as SunLearn is not always reliable.

* * *

My family and I made a terrific Sunday lunch. Each member was responsible for one dish of his or her choosing. We had two proteins, two sides and a delicious pudding. My brothers and I learned a lot. I realised that cooking was easier than I thought, but also that it takes a lot more manual labour.
Throughout this lockdown, I have been given a glimpse of what it must be like to be a parent. It is one thing being an adult, providing for yourself and cleaning up after one person. It is another thing entirely to help with dinner, wash the dishes and clean the house. In my flat, I used to just postpone cleaning my room and could just make a sandwich for lunch if I was tired. Now I have people counting on me to do certain things no matter how tired I am. This is what life is all about. Some days are easy and you can wash an entire sink full of dishes with a smile on your face. Other days you want to hit the person who asked you to wash one cup. Both days you have to do what you promised.

* * *

My mom still makes a big Sunday lunch (even though all the days feel the same) which is nice. We’re lucky that she started a vegetable garden some months ago because we’re starting to see a rise in prices of fresh produce which makes sense going into winter, but it raises concerns about food security at a time like this. A few of the veggies we have include green beans, spinach, pumpkin, tomatoes, carrots and some herbs. I found gardening to be therapeutic for like the first two days, but there’s only so much to do before you’re forced to watch the plants grow.
My sleep cycle isn’t usually regular or normal, but this is getting ridiculous. I finally fell asleep at around 7:00 am today. I’m challenging myself to take a photo a day for the foreseeable self-isolating future. I want to master taking artistic photos in boring locations (such as one’s house). Day one’s photograph was disappointing but that was not unexpected.
My aunt, who works for Doctors on Call, suggested to me that I make masks to sell. I was under the impression that effective masks need to be made from special materials, but the World Health Organisation says you just need 2 ply cotton.

* * *

Our night in the tent was an enjoyable disaster! To the surprise of the entire family there was a massive gust of wind that bent one pole which resulted in the entire tent collapsing right on us. Being the best at situations like these I had to wake everyone up and evacuate the tent in order for me to fix it. After fixing it, I realised just how cold it was outside even within the tent. I struggled to fall asleep again and was woken up by a ray of sun entering the tent and landing perfectly on my face.

* * *

During the Spanish Flu of 1918, my great grandfather, his brothers and their father had the grim job of picking up the bodies of people who had died the previous night. Miraculously none of them caught the flu. My grandmother, when telling the story, always adds that she thinks they all survived unharmed because they were doing such a good thing.

* * *

Today is the last time that I will write in this diary. However I will not stop keeping a journal as I was keeping one long before this project started. That said, I do hope (whatever may come of the coronavirus situation) that the lockdown and restrictions on our behaviour will end soon so that I will have something to actually write in my journal.

* * *

One day to go before online classes start. My parents are building a house in the seaside town of Paternoster that they wish to run as a guesthouse. They have been saving up and planning the construction of this house for 20 years – they bought the last piece of seafront property in the town the year I was born. Obviously this project means the world to them. With recent developments, they have been under an immense amount of pressure financially and are struggling to see how they will be able to finish building by the end of this year. Even if they manage to finish construction, the tourist industry will likely be one of the last industries to recover from this ordeal and it will take much longer for them to break even than they anticipated when they started construction at the end of last year. They are very concerned that they will not be able to carry on with something that they have been dreaming about for years. On top of that, both my parents will soon have to retire and they were hoping that income generated from the guesthouse would assist them when they are not earning salaries anymore. I do not know how we are going to recover from the virus’s long-term economic effects.

* * *

Today marks the end of the penultimate weekend in lockdown. Recently, weekends have lost all meaning. However, that is about to change – I begin lectures tomorrow! I am interested to see how the university and the learners will adapt to this new challenge. Personally, I am relishing this challenge. I believe that I work better out of the lecture environment and this is a time to test that theory. I have prepared myself with the stationery I need and organised my files on my laptop. I have also created a schedule to try and stay motivated. However, I’m sure the process will not be smooth in the beginning and I am expecting some hiccups.

* * *

It feels as though this university holiday has flown by and yet just the other day, I could’ve sworn I had four more weeks. Guess time flies whether you’re having fun or not! Today has been filled with preparations for the weeks ahead.
From tomorrow, the university returns via an online platform - and it’s worth mentioning that this will be a first in Stellenbosch University’s [SU] rich history. The whole reason for me attending SU over studying through UNISA is because I wanted the full experience of the student environment, and not just the process of studying. Guess that’s out the window for 2020.
That said, change is not always bad and all one needs is a positive perspective. While I am incredibly nervous to begin my online studies as I really do not know what to expect, I am also excited to test my own capabilities in facing these drastic differences.
One of the main weaknesses I have identified for myself is time-management and self-discipline. While I have always been punctual and pleased with my hand-ins, I do still believe that I can better my ability. I am thus going to set myself a challenge in these coming weeks to strive and see just how much I can achieve in ‘x’ amount of time. Wish me luck!

* * *

Today was a typical Sunday at our home. We made our family’s favourite meal. We had rice, lamb and vegetables. I baked a cheesecake for dessert. While eating we had an argument about the origin of the coronavirus. My father and brother believe that the corona virus originated in America. I told them they cannot believe this because it has been verified but they wouldn’t listen. […] I realised that there is one thing that spreads faster than the coronavirus … fake news.

title: 20 April 2020
text:
KwaZulu-Natal tightened regulations in the province as the number of cases in Durban rose to 380. China refused to answer a number of questions from leaders around the world, including Donald Trump, regarding its handling of Covid-19. In a hostel in Lisbon, 138 asylum seekers contracted the virus. In light of a dramatic decrease in infections, South Koreans started returning to work, although many companies still followed flexible hours or work-from-home policies to limit travel and physical contact. Details emerged of a mass shooting that took place in Nova Scotia, Canada, which claimed the lives of 22 people.

I feel very anxious about the term ahead. I shouldn’t though, because this is generally how I approach my academics: self-study and barely any contact classes. I think it’ll require more effort to do well.
I completed a short workout for the first time since January and it felt good. I might do that again tomorrow. I thought a bit about well-being (physical and emotional) and how students will need to prioritise it now more than ever if we are to complete the 2020 academic year successfully. I thought, more specifically, about coping mechanisms like exercise, food (if you have it) and memes. I bet it would be fascinating to analyse national trends in BMI changes pre- and post-lockdown. What will the lockdown do to diabetes and malnutrition statistics?

* * *

I am really grateful for today. I finally felt as if I had achieved something at the end of the day, I would even go so far as to say that time flew by …
I know that being able to continue my studies despite the Covid-19 outbreak is a privilege. I am able to sit in various areas of my house and move around if I feel frustrated or bored or the sunny spot that was in the dining room but now is in the study. I am able to do this without losing connection to my uncapped fibre that I have at home. If I feel hungry I can simply open the fridge or go into the pantry and grab something to eat. I don’t have to worry about walking very far and through unsanitary areas to go to the bathroom. In addition to this, I know that I will have more reliable access to water and electricity (due to unpredictable loadshedding schedules and possible waterpipe maintenance that needs to be done which is the case today I can’t claim to have permanent access to these things), but for the most part life is pretty simple.
This isn’t the case for some of my fellow students … the life they are having to live during this time is very different to mine. For these reasons I find myself filled with gratitude for my day, despite the ‘inconveniences’ of the lockdown.

* * *

Classes started today, but within hours the servers and website were overloaded and crashed. They were soon restored, but this is a shaky start. I really miss my friends and my environment I had at campus. I miss being able to get a coffee or a smoothie when walking through the Neelsie [cafeteria].
My parents are donating money to friends and community members that have no income now due to the virus. They also told us to cut down on expenses, as they don’t know what is to come.

* * *

I am so relieved that classes finally started today. SunLearn kept crashing since the entire university was using it at the same time. I wonder if it is going to carry on like this for the rest of the semester. Despite circumstances being less than ideal, I am so grateful that I can carry on with my education and that I have the resources that is necessary to work from home. The university is struggling with helping students who do not have access to computers or the internet to carry on with their studies. My aunt is a lecturer at the University of Cape Town [UCT], and she told me that the university bought an additional 5 000 laptops that they will distribute to students who do not have one. They will have to return the laptops once they return to campus. I am not exactly sure, but I believe Stellenbosch University [SU] is doing something similar. Despite this, I believe that there will still be many students left behind as a result of these interruptions. Financially, I do not know how some families will be able to pay university fees after not receiving an income (or a reduced income) for months. Perhaps this will force the government to rethink the education system (its costs and how it functions) in order not to fall behind on the universal operational shift that is currently happening.

* * *

Day 1 of online classes. Today was the first day since lockdown that I woke up early. I showered, made myself breakfast and then walked around our house that it felt like I was walking to my first class. After I got my ‘mombrew’ [a hybridised version of MyBrew, a local student coffee bar], and then headed to the ‘Van der Sterr’ [building on campus] to start my first class. I opened my laptop and went straight to Sunlearn, but it had crashed. The University’s IT team sent an email that they are trying to fix the problem. So, I waited and after a few minutes the website started to work again. My first class went really well. I enjoyed studying at my own pace. After my first three classes I took a break by walking in our garden. I texted my friends: “Lunch in the Neelsie?” [cafeteria]. They all laughed and sent pictures of their lunch so that we could pretend that we were eating together.

* * *

Today was the first day of term 2 online. As expected, SunLearn crashed multiple times because of all the online traffic. Nonetheless, it was manageable and just as quickly paced as a normal day on campus would be – right back into the full swing of things. Its impressive to see how the lecturers have quickly adapted their teaching styles to suit the online platforms, but is also scary to see how all of this can be done from home and that we don’t actually need to be on campus to learn efficiently. What I did learn ( just from one day) is that I miss the social interactions I didn’t have today – they are definitely necessary for the ‘full university experience’ – which is why I can honestly say that I wouldn’t be able to commit to anything that doesn’t involve social interaction.

* * *

Classes have started and I feel overwhelmed. I am ahead in most of my courses that have textbooks, but I am a little stressed about those that don’t have textbooks. People in my area have been walking around. It seems like people are starting to hate this lockdown. My sister thinks that people are starting to not care. Virus or not, we shall have to go back to daily life at some point. I have been having nightmares, most of them to do with me failing some test. It is scary. I always thought that I was a person who took well to change. I guess that this is not true.

* * *

I have realised that this online learning will be more difficult for us students than I could have imagined. Our lecturers have been posting notes and audio on PowerPoint, but I can’t open some of the files with my tablet. This is making me very worried. We haven’t heard anything regarding the laptops that we have been promised. Maybe things would be easier if I had a laptop.

* * *

I realise I haven’t talked much about the social impacts of Covid-19 in this diary saga, so today I’m writing about something I read and thought about over the past day and a bit: the potential for the youth to become increasingly radicalised in the wake of the virus. People in their 30s have now experienced two ‘once in a generation’ economic shocks. People in their 20s trying to find a job in this market will find it nearly impossible. What the frequency of these downturns could lead to growing antipathy toward the current economic system, even more than we’re experiencing already. This will most likely add to the populist fire and encourage economics focused more on redistribution than growth.

title: 21 April 2020
text:
South Africa reported 1 055 coronavirus recoveries. Unions linked to South African Airways met with Public Enterprises Minister Pravin Gordhan, to discuss proposals to reduce job losses and save the airline. Brazil’s President, Jair Bolsonaro, came under increasing criticism for his response to the pandemic. He appeared at an anti-lockdown rally, which he attended without a mask, and was seen coughing without covering his mouth. Air Canada suspended flights to the US until 22 May, while Vietnam resumed domestic flights after five days of no new cases. Spain eased regulations to allow children under the age of 14 to accompany their parents to shops. The last major cruise ship to be stuck at sea, the Costa Deliziosa, failed to dock because of bad weather.

Second day of classes. Ran a lot smoother than yesterday, but somehow, I feel even more behind than I ever have despite it only being the second day. I find myself struggling to manage my time. My initial plan was to just follow my normal timetable, but now that I can go at my own pace, I find myself going over the usual 50-minute slot allocated to each class. […] I feel like I am spending obscene amounts of time at my laptop. My total screen time yesterday was ten hours! And this is just the beginning.
In world news: oil prices have reached negative levels. When I first read about it I wasn’t too sure what that meant for us as citizens to be honest. Words and phrases like ‘unprecedented’ and ‘first time in history’ kept being repeated.

* * *

I study the whole day. Sometimes I even forget to eat. Is that even normal? I don’t think so, but I mostly end the day with a smile because I do enjoy spending time with my books. If there was a job that paid you simply for reading a book each day I would take it. Now that learning is back on track, I worry about whether I will have enough data to check what is being uploaded every day.
A friend told me that confidence is key at this time; one has to believe that you will make it. What if one’s mentality is not so strong though? […]
I am tired of all of this. The only view I have of outside is from the window or when I stand near to my gate. I miss walking past the shops and seeing how full they were, I miss not being able to just enjoy walking in nature and getting lost in one’s own thoughts. Perhaps I am starting to understand how people finally become insane.

* * *

Online classes have been going well and I have managed to follow my normal class timetable, but I find that I am much more tired at the end of the day than I normally would be after a day of classes at university. Maybe it is because I have to concentrate a lot harder to understand and absorb the material by myself as opposed to the slightly more passive process of listening to a lecturer explain concepts to me. I prefer grappling with the work by myself at first because it helps concepts to sink in faster. However, I hate the isolation that comes with distance learning. Sitting for hours on end in front of your laptop in the same space can be very demotivating.

* * *

So, today’s my birthday, although it really just feels like any other day. Being in lockdown and having online classes especially makes it feel extra ordinary and by that, I mean more ordinary than usual. My mom brought me breakfast in bed this morning and I received countless birthday messages, but besides all that, it was business as usual. I did as much work as I could, or actually as I felt like, but it was productive. It felt quite weird not having family over. We usually always have some family and friends over on birthdays. Even when there’s not a party, our people just show up. Obviously, they couldn’t do that today and it made me a little sad. It feels like we are breaking tradition. But I know that once this is over, we’ll have a good old family gathering and I can’t wait.

* * *

My second day of classes was less exciting. I spent about seven hours studying and attending online lectures. My brother studies at the University of Pretoria and their classes have not started yet. He spent the whole day watching movies, chilling outside and reading. Even though his day sounds more fun, I realised last week that quarantine feels a lot longer and more boring if you do not have work to do. Classes are difficult and they take a lot of effort and dedication, but they provide the purpose that I need during this quarantine.

* * *

The whole household was excited to hear what the president had to say tonight in his address, but at the end of it we realised that we’d have better spent our time on an episode of The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air because the president didn’t even allude to the question that’s on everybody’s mind. Just rip the band aid off already and tell us what the future holds. Despite my frustration, though, I understand that these are important communications.
[…] I’m not adjusting well to these not-so-new conditions. I think I am entering another depressive episode. I’m trying to keep my sleeping patterns healthy, but this seems impossible. I’ll be taking another break from WhatsApp. I haven’t showered in three days.

* * *

Cyril addressed the nation this evening concerning the government’s plans for economic relief. I was wholly surprised by the extent of aid/spending that the government announced. It was much more than I believed we had to spend. My first thought, like most others I’m sure, was, “where will it come from?” Surely we’d have to borrow that money from somewhere. Then I realised we’ve borrowed it from our future. […] The worst part is that even all this spending probably won’t be enough.

* * *

The president spoke to us again today. He announced the details of an economic stimulus package. R500 billion. That is crazy. Billions was every second word. Loans and loans and grants and grants and social services and feeding schemes. I think many people are in trouble. People are looting food trucks. The economy needs to be restarted otherwise starvation will kick in.

* * *

Today is Human Rights Day [in South Africa]. To be honest, I didn’t even remember. My day was interesting. For the first time since coming to Stellenbosch, I went hiking. My friends and I hiked the Coetzenburg Mountain. It was hard. We started around 3:00 pm in the afternoon and it was very hot. I struggled to keep up with the guys (I went with three of my male friends), but it was beautiful seeing Stellenbosch from above.

* * *

A massive decrease has been noted with regard to the demand for oil due to lockdowns and quarantines limiting the movements of people all around the world. As such, the price has steadily declined as the market has produced an excess supply of oil. On Monday, 20 April, an unprecedented event occurred with the price of crude oil falling below zero dollars, into the negative domain. This negative ‘price’ for oil was a result of concerns that there was a lack of space to store incoming crude oil supplies, and investors may have been obligated to accept actual orders of crude oil. Thus, there was a mad scramble to offload this obligation and people were willing to pay for this, resulting in a negative price. This is an incredibly rare and historical event.
In the evening, Ramaphosa addressed the nation again. The nature of his speech was very financial and he detailed an extensive social and economic support package. The president claimed that R500 billion would be spent in order to overcome and alleviate the strain of the virus. R100 billion is to be spent protecting and creating jobs. R40 billion is set aside as an income stipend for unpaid employees. R50 billion is allotted to increases in the social grants system. R20 billion would be immediately spent on health measures. This money was to be sourced from local and foreign sources, including the World Bank and the African Development Bank. He said: “We will follow a phased approach. As we do so, we remain firm in our resolve to contain the virus. We will need to act with flexibility in the weeks and months ahead.”
I believe that the president has taken a strong stance on the large amount of money that is planning to be spent; it will definitely aid the country in the face of the current crisis. However, this could mount to incredibly high levels of debt which would become the burden of the current youth – my generation. It seems that, no matter what our leaders choose, there is always a trade-off that will benefit some and detriment others. I am impressed by Ramaphosa and his level-headedness and prudence in the face of adversity.

title: 22 April 2020
text:
President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a R500 billion support package to help the economy as the country battled the coronavirus. He also announced that social security grants would be increased by at least R250 per month. Spain extended their state of emergency for the third time until 3 May 2020. In South Korea, it was found that some recovered Covid-19 patients re-tested positive, but researchers argued that it was most likely that re-infected individuals would not be contagious. The Costa Deliziosa finally docked in the port of Genoa, Italy. The US Center for Disease Control and Prevention warned that winter in the US could see a second wave of coronavirus infections.

When I went on my phone this morning, I saw that my dad had sent a message to our family group. It was a petition to the government to unlock section 31 of the Bill of Rights and recognise religious institutions as an essential service. I didn’t end up signing the petition because I didn’t agree with everything that it said. I agreed with one of the points, which was that permission should be granted for such institutions to commence or continue providing food and shelter and running feeding schemes. However, I don’t think it is wise to allow such institutions to allow individuals to gather again. There is so much risk that comes along with allowing any major gatherings, regardless of the precautions that are put in place.
There is so much uncertainty that accompanies the circumstances under which we’re living, and it makes sense that amongst great worries, many people want to revert to something familiar in order to experience comfort. However, so many things are changing and we shouldn’t be trying to get back to normal, but rather move forward and embrace a new normal.

* * *

While scrolling through Facebook and seeing all the posts about hunger and after reading the news and checking the updated figures for Covid-19, my stepdad came across one of his old university friends’ Facebook page where she had posted about an organisation that she has been running, known as ‘The Clothing Bank’.
[…] He felt inspired after reading about ‘The Clothing Bank’ and how they supported our poorer communities, and since Freedom Day was on the horizon, he decided that he was going to do a big swim in our swimming pool at home to help raise funds for the organisation. The organisation’s target is to raise R1 million to feed 4 000 families (based on the calculation that R250 feeds a family of four for a week). That is 21 meals and R250 is equivalent to about ten Cappuccino’s and six Beers. We consume that amount of beers and cappuccinos within a few days without even thinking twice, but now instead of spending your R250 on those ‘luxuries’, it can be spent on saving a family from starvation.
After contacting his university friend, it was decided that a fund will be set up on Sunday in my stepdad’s name for people to donate to and spread awareness about ‘The Clothing Bank’.

* * *

3 635 cases today. 65 deaths. Today was my girlfriend and my anniversary. We had a face time call with champagne, but this didn’t come close to the amazing experience we could have enjoyed. It made me feel sorry for the many people who are stranded without their loved ones or families.

* * *

The Police Minister, Bheki Cele, reported a decrease in the crime rate. Our country is notorious for its unusually high rate of crime, and it is refreshing to find that the lockdown has contributed to the decline in criminal activities, such as murder, rape, assault, robbery and domestic violence. Yet, although there has been a reported decline in the crime rates, many NGO’s [Non-Governmental Organisations] say it may be because citizens are unable to report such crimes due to the lockdown. So, we cannot be too sure if the crimes have stopped or if the reporting of the crimes has just become too difficult.

* * *

“Fear is contagious.” These are words to live by during this pandemic. Many of us are afraid of what the future holds. It is important to remember that the fear and stress you experience will affect the people around you. We silently project our feelings onto others. I am trying hard to keep my body language positive and I can see that my parents are trying to do the same. We are all stressed, but if we start to panic and start shouting at each other or losing hope, then we are truely lost. President Ramaphosa is also putting on a brave face; more importantly, he is addressing the difficult issues with confidence and certainty. This puts my mind at ease and I believe that many South Africans trust Cyril. I sometimes wonder how different the situation in the US would have been if Barack Obama was still in office. He was clearly a much more caring and compassionate individual. Ramaphosa also possesses these characteristics. In a time of trouble and hardship, you need someone who not only cares about the big corporations who run the country, but also the little man. The pensioner selling cupcakes from home or the little girl who started her own lemonade stand.

* * *

A Mitchells Plain family – consisting of a father and his two daughters, aged nine and thirteen – have been using 3D printers to create protective visors that work as facemasks. The visors prevent the cross-contamination of oral particles and prevent the spread of the virus. […] Incredibly, the family are donating these masks to the community for free! The father says that he understands the economic disadvantages that many members in the community are facing, what with unemployment and low-income jobs. […] I thought this was such a touching story and an incredible initiative!

* * *

Today on the news they showed a story about a 29-year-old who makes facial masks and shields using recycled materials. What touched me about his story is that he is an unemployed graduate; he studied mechanical engineering at UJ [the University of Johannesburg]. He usually makes money by recycling things, but due to the lockdown he cannot. He donates the facial masks and shield that he created. […] As a student working towards my degree, it’s a little bit scary to see a graduate unemployed.

* * *

I accomplished a lot more today in terms of school, but still not enough. It is as though I am playing catch up; which isn’t the best feeling to be experiencing right now. I’ve come to the conclusion that what I am missing about contact classes is the communal aspect that comes about from being in the same room as your fellow classmates – even though most times a lot of my classmates were strangers to me. It is weird being next to no one in an ‘academic’ setting. It’s also a bit weird having this much freedom in determining my school routine.
I have always thought myself to be someone who didn’t like routine, preferring constant change. But this whole online schooling thing has me questioning that. Under normal circumstances, I don’t think I would say this: but I kind of also miss the routine that school gave us (i.e. having to be in a classroom at a certain time for a certain period). Now I determine all of that, and it’s kind of a lot of pressure. At least when I was at university and I was kind of distracted in class, I could make myself feel better by saying at least I went to the class. Now I have no excuse. Because besides having to make sure I submit all my work, EVERYTHING is up to me. I’m hoping with time it will all get easier.
A lot of my friends are saying that we shouldn’t put pressure on ourselves, that adjusting to all the change will take time, but I feel as though I don’t really have the time to ‘adjust’. School is right now. Deadlines are now. Work needs to be done now.
Wow that sounds really gloomy and ominous…

* * *

I went to the grocery store today and was shocked at the length of the queue outside of Woolworths and Pick n Pay. I live in a small town with an even smaller population; therefore, I would think that there wouldn’t be as many people wanting to buy groceries.
I wonder if the measures and precautions taken now will stay in place in the long run. Will we ever return to a world where wearing a mask outside while running or going to the shops is not normal? Will we always restrict the number of people allowed in a shop at a time? Will money be a factor in deciding whether or not you must wait in these lines or not?
Currently I am imagining a world where every supermarket has a bouncer, and some of the supermarkets are charging entrance into their store. If you pay this entrance, you can skip the queue. Entrance into better supermarkets costs more. However, there you will have access to better produce of a greater variety, and an unlimited amount of stock. Those who cannot afford to pay entrance will have to wait in the queue for the grocery stores that allow people in free of charge.
While this is very hypothetical and unrealistic, it has occurred to me that, when all of this is over, money will begin to create a greater divide than ever.

title: 23 April 2020
text:
On the 28th day of lockdown in South Africa, President Ramaphosa announced the implementation of a five-level alert system to be used to determine future restrictions. In Cape Town, police struggled to control looters who attacked food delivery vehicles and shops. The World Health Organisation announced that the world was ‘weeks to months’ from finding a drug to fight Covid-19. The preliminary results of a large-scale study showed that the drug hydroxychloroquine was not effective for those who were very sick with the coronavirus. It’s estimated that, at this stage, a third of the world’s population is under coronavirus movement restrictions.

Increase of ten deaths. 1 000 tests conducted today. Western Cape has become the new epicentre of the virus, overtaking Gauteng.

* * *

Personally I do not like Mondays, but who does! The usual, I woke up late, did the basics. I had a brunch together with the other ladies from res [student accommodation]. There are just eight of us left. We thought it would be a nice thing to do, as some of the ladies haven’t been eating well. […] We had an interesting conversation. The international students are worried. They are facing a lot of uncertainties and the all rumours and fake news are making things worse. Many students are also worried that if this pandemic continues, they might lose their bursary. That’s also my worry.

* * *

This morning I struggled. Statistics is difficult to self-study. I am stressed because all my test and assignments are scheduled for in two weeks time. This means that I must make sure that I watch all my classes during the day and study for my tests at night. I am usually tired at night, but I feel a lot more tired now than I would have had if I attended ‘real’ classes. I think it is because, with real classes I can just go to the class and listen but with virtual classes I must listen, read and teach myself. It is quite difficult to be my own lecturer and a student at the same time.

* * *

(Covid) 19 Reasons to NOT shoot my brains out before the end of lockdown: 1. I don’t own a gun. 2. I miss my friends. 3. My fashion design career hasn’t taken off yet. 4. I need at least one last sit-in McDonald’s meal after 1:00 am. 5. My dog deserves his late afternoon walks to the park for being such a good boy. 6. I want to rock my new hairstyle outside. 7. My Economics 281 class average will drop. 8. I miss the smell of stale urine in Stellenbosch on a Thursday morning. 9. I haven’t seen life outside of SA borders. 10. The drugs will hit that much harder after months of sobriety. 11. I want to sleep through traffic. 12. I got a Pulp membership after years of protest. 13. I haven’t been mugged in the Joburg CBD yet. 14. I want to skate again. 15. I didn’t put all this effort into my academics not to get a degree. 16. I need to continue my annual tradition of paying for a gym membership and not go. 17. The Anime Society owes me a refund. 18. I must write an inappropriate name on my RocoMama’s menu for the waiter to announce, for old time’s sake. 19. I’ll have kept this diary for nothing.

* * *

I watched the president’s speech again tonight. I’m really glad that around this time next week, measures will be put in place to initiate the gradual recovery of our economy. I was chatting to my mom the other day, and she mentioned how these lockdown restrictions are most likely just delaying the spread of the virus, and that South Africa’s curve will probably only peak in September. Therefore, I really hope that the incremental actions taken to lift the lockdown are done with extreme caution.
The more I think about it, though, while the aim of lockdown is to protect lives, the truth is that it mainly protects the livelihood of those who can afford it, while threatening the livelihood of those who are vulnerable. The current condition of the country is really such a catch 22 situation. On the one hand, there is the recognition and understanding of the seriousness of the virus and that we need to be in lockdown to protect our livelihoods. On the other hand, the livelihoods of vulnerable individuals and families are being threatened because unemployment is higher and money is even tighter (because of the lockdown). At least the amount allocated to social grants has increased – I just hope it enables purchasing power to be maintained.

* * *

President Ramaphosa finally gave the country an update regarding the virus situation tonight, but his message was rather cryptic. Stage 5 lockdown will officially end next Thursday (I only became aware of the fact that there are different stages of lockdown during his speech). I still do not understand what exactly we are allowed to do and what we still cannot do after next Thursday. Certain businesses will be allowed to operate (which will hopefully prevent the economy from completely collapsing), like clothing stores. Stores will be allowed to sell cigarettes once again, but the alcohol policy was not directly addressed, which suggests that the ban will probably stay in place.
